Over the course of the 20th century, the car became America’s dominant mode of transportation. As vehicle miles travelled soared well past the rate of population growth, demands on the roadway surged. Congestion became a major issue. So transportation planners made the roads wider and added traffic lanes.
Today, we now know that bigger roads and extra traffic lanes do nothing to solve congestion. In fact, it tends to induce even more traffic. So we didn’t fix the congestion issues, and on top of that, we built wide roads that are relatively unsafe.
Transportation planners in the 21st century recognized that many of the roads that were overbuilt could be redesigned to calm speeding and add space for newer multimodal transportation options. And thus, the road diet was born.
The video above explains why road diets are implemented, and how planners survey the feasibility of a lane reconfiguration. You can learn more about road diets with the following resources:
https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/publications/research/safety/10053/10053.pdf
https://safety.fhwa.dot.gov/road_diets/guidance/info_guide/rdig.pdf
https://nacto.org/docs/usdg/conversion_of_four_lane_undivided_urban_roadways.pdf


Transcript

What is a road diet
0:01 · This road might not look like anything special.
0:03 · But what if I showed you the same road, a few years earlier —notice anything different?
0:09 · Here’s a better angle of that: The old road has 4 lanes for traffic.
0:17 · The new one has two.
0:18 · And now there’s this middle lane for left hand turns.
0:22 · There’s also a new bike lane.
0:24 · This is what transportation planners call a road diet.
0:28 · And it’s a very popular to make the roads safer.


History of overbuilt roads
0:33 · Over the course of the 20th century, four lane roads became an American institution.
0:37 · It started with the release of Ford’s model-T in 1908.
0:42 · A few decades later, there was one car for every two households in the states.
0:47 · By the 1960s, many roads became so busy, that traffic engineers had to figure out how to add capacity.
0:54 · So, they added lanes.
0:56 · A lot of pavement was getting put on the ground.
1:00 · Even where maybe when the population and traffic volumes weren’t so high that we needed that pavement.
1:09 · But we wanted that pavement.
1:11 · Sometimes your eyes are bigger than your stomach.


Safety benefits
1:14 · Fast forward to the present day and we’re left some overbuilt roads that are pretty unsafe.
1:20 · And crash reduction is a major benefit that planners can achieve with just a bit a paint.
1:26 · Four lane roads have quite a few conflict points – these are places where accidents could happen.
1:31 · These ones represent merging accidents.
1:32 · These are rear ends, and there are multiple left turn crash scenarios.
1:37 · Now look at what a 3 lane reconfiguration does — There are far fewer crash points.
1:43 · A road diet can also make left turns suck way less.
1:47 · The shared middle lane takes left turners out of the traffic flow, so they won’t hold up drivers who want to continue through.
1:53 · And now, left turners will only have to cross 1 lane of traffic instead of 2, which will eliminate broadside accidents.
2:00 · And the benefits don’t end there.


Speed and multi-modal use
2:03 · By slimming each lane in the road, the road diet reduced the travel speed by almost 7 miles per hour.
2:09 · Narrower lanes can cause that psychological impact on the driver to slow down a bit.
2:22 · And while a 6 mile an hour difference in speed may seem modest, it can make an auto accident much less deadly … Narrower lanes also leave more space for expanded sidewalks or bike lanes.
2:33 · your pedestrians will feel safer.
2:34 · It might’ve given you more green space to separate from your vehicles.
2:39 · And your bicyclists might have a dedicated space to ride.
2:45 · In the midst of these changes, the number of traffic lanes has gone from 2 to 1.


Maintaining traffic flow
2:50 · So if you drive a car, you might assume that the tradeoff of a road diet would be congestion…
2:55 · How could traffic not increase?
2:58 · That’s usually their concern before a road diet is implemented.
3:03 · That’s not what happens.
3:05 · The volume of the roadway is still sustained.
3:08 · We wouldn’t want to put a 4 to 3 conversion on a piece of roadway that would then push half your traffic somewhere else.
3:14 · And what we found in a couple of places, it actually makes moving through town easier.
3:23 · But traffic flow is only one part of the equation — you’ve got to also balance commercial and safety benefits too.
3:29 · especially if this is through an urban corridor where you’ve got businesses, coffeeshops, it works.
3:34 · it keeps people moving, it doesn’t take traffic away from that corridor, and it reduces those rear-ends that thendo stop the road.


Contextual success rates
3:45 · Iowa is conducting this road survey because so far, the plan has worked really well for them.
3:49 · A study of 15 streets in the state saw a crash reduction rate of nearly 50%.
3:53 · At the same time, the diet didn’t substantially disrupt other activities along their corridors.
3:58 · A key factor was the traffic volume, measured by engineers as ‘Annual Average Daily Traffic’.
4:05 · Most road diets will run into problems as you approach that 15,000 vehicles number.
4:10 · In Iowa, many roads don’t get that much traffic.
4:13 · The same could not be said for the suburban contexts in California.
4:16 · A study comparing road diets in Iowa to corridors in California showed that California’s streets average about double the amount of daily traffic.
4:25 · The same kinds of road diets resulted in a 17% crash rate reduction – significantly lower than the reductions in Iowa.
4:33 · This is not to say that the road diets in California are an outright failure.
4:36 · It’s just a difference context for the road diet.
4:39 · And the success of a road diet is driven by so many other factors – economic impact, land use, or level of service to name a few.
4:46 · What works in Iowa may not be the right fit for California, and vice versa.
4:48 · So the case for road diets is pretty clear: they do slow streets down and they do reduce crashes.


Conclusion
4:54 · But whether or not that’s worth the trouble depends very much on the context of the world that surrounds the road.

Description
The state of U.S. infrastructure is improving, but not great, according to Samantha Silverberg MPP 2012, a former Biden administration official and visiting fellow at the Taubman Center for State and Local Government at Harvard Kennedy School. In this video, Silverberg discusses the challenges that face federal, state and local government officials who endeavor to fix the country’s infrastructure, from roads and bridges to tap water and transmission lines. Topics covered include:
• The importance of infrastructure to our daily lives
• Why it’s often challenging to get new infrastructure built
• What infrastructure priorities policymakers should focus on in the coming years.
You can read more about Ms. Silverberg’s thoughts on our website: https://www.hks.harvard.edu/centers/taubman/state-and-local-perspectives/interview-samantha-silverberg-mpp-2012-taubman-center
About Harvard Kennedy School:
The John F. Kennedy School of Government at Harvard University is a graduate and professional school that brings together students, scholars, and practitioners who combine thought and action to make the world a better place.
Our mission is to improve public policy and public leadership across the United States and around the world so that people can lead safer, freer, and more prosperous lives. Harvard Kennedy School teaches current and future leaders the skills they need to effectively advance the public purpose in the public, nonprofit, and private sectors. Our renowned faculty and trailblazing research centers pioneer bold new ideas. And as the most international school at Harvard, we convene global leaders in the Forum, host visiting experts in the classroom, and attract a diverse community of faculty, students, and staff.


Transcript

The importance of infrastructure
0:00 · Listen, right now it takes too long and it costs too much to build infrastructure in the United States, and we need to do something about that.
0:10 · Infrastructure is so important for everything we do in our daily lives.
0:15 · Think about the roads you drove on or the train that you took to get to school or work today, the tap you turned on and the water you drank, the internet that you use, even the electricity that powers everything in our homes.
0:28 · But infrastructure is something that we really only pay attention to when it fails.


Current state and challenges
0:33 · The state of infrastructure in the US right now is better than it was, but still not great.
0:40 · The American Society of Civil Engineers gave US infrastructure a grade of C in its most recent infrastructure report card, and that’s really because of decades of underinvestment in our infrastructure that has led to crumbling roads and bridges, unreliable transit systems, power networks that are unable to withstand the impacts of climate change and so much more.
1:06 · There are tens of thousands of bridges in this country that are in poor condition.
1:12 · There are millions of Americans that still don’t have access to high-speed internet, which is far worse in rural America.
1:20 · Our airports and ports lag their peers in other parts of the world, and the list goes on and on.
1:27 · Infrastructure is funded and financed in a shared way through both the federal, state, and local government, primarily through taxes and user fees.


Funding and historical context
1:38 · There are some privately-funded projects, particularly things like power plants or electricity transmission.
1:44 · And then there are some that are a mix of private and public funding.
1:48 · You can think of airports or ports or toll roads are often common examples of public-private partnerships.
1:56 · Some of the most remarkable investments in infrastructure were accomplished by the United States government.
2:03 · You could think about the Hoover Dam, the Bay Bridge, LaGuardia Airport.
2:12 · These were all built during the New Deal.
2:15 · When there was a real national effort that provided the resources, the trust, and the commitment of the entire American population behind what the government is doing.
2:25 · I think there’s a real and meaningful tension between efficiency and democracy.


Overcoming bureaucracy
2:32 · When you want communities and the public to have a voice, which is a necessary and appropriate thing of any democratic process, there are often many veto points.
2:43 · That process can be exploited by actors who are trying to stop good things from getting done.
2:50 · The system right now is overly litigious.
2:53 · Things like environmental permitting, which have an important and good purpose, have been used as a tool to stop good projects, even clean energy projects that have an overall positive benefit on the environment.
3:05 · And as a result, these systems are getting in the way of progress.
3:09 · If we want to get things done, we need to take a hard look at the way things are currently done within our governments and within our companies.
3:17 · This means re-looking at rules and regulations and requirements that maybe each individually made sense, but when layered over years have created a process where well-intentioned public servants can’t get anything done.


Investing in public capacity
3:31 · The same time, we need to make sure that those public servants have the resources they need to do their jobs.
3:37 · My colleague and friend Zach Liscow at Yale Law School has recently published research that shows how state departments of transportation have actually shrunk over time.
3:47 · And those reduced staff have real impacts on the cost of projects.
3:52 · Zach has shown that as staffs have declined, prices have gone up.
3:57 · His team has also shown that experienced engineers actually save money on projects.
4:03 · So if we’re going to get things done, we need to invest in our public institutions, we need to invest in public servants, and we need to make sure that they have the tools to get their jobs done.


Successful projects and efforts
4:13 · When we think about infrastructure projects, it’s important to think of both the mega projects and the backyard projects because both of those types of projects have meaningful impacts on our communities.
4:23 · On the mega project side, one of the examples that many people raise is the Mario Cuomo Bridge in New York.
4:29 · This was the replacement of the Tappan Zee Bridge.
4:31 · It was executed using an innovative procurement method at the time.
4:36 · It also went through an expedited environmental permitting process, and as a result of both of those activities, it was delivered on time, on budget, and, by some estimates, saved billions of dollars for the taxpayer.
4:49 · At the same time, I think it’s really important to think about those smaller backyard projects.
4:55 · In the Biden Administration, one of our priorities was to replace lead pipes.
4:59 · There are still 9 million lead pipes serving our homes, which are a source of toxic chemicals.
5:05 · Through money provided by the federal government, the city of Milwaukee has already replaced thousands of lead pipes.


Future priorities
5:12 · I think the top three infrastructure priorities for the next 10 years are, number one, climate resilience.
5:18 · We need to protect our communities from the impacts of climate change.
5:21 · The second is clean energy generation and transmission so that we could power our future.
5:26 · And the third is to close the digital divide, because we know that affordable, reliable high-speed internet is important for everything from remote school to work to accessing telehealth.
5:37 · I also want to say, though, that every community knows what their own priorities are and they can’t just be told by Washington where they need to invest.
5:45 · And so the feds need to continue to invest in infrastructure carrying forward the legacy of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act so that our communities can invest in what they need.

Transcript

The role of city roads
0:00 · What makes a city? People? Buildings?
0:04 · Horrific traffic jams? That’s not too far off.
0:08 · It turns out that roads are what connect all the parts of a city.
0:12 · We need easy paths to travel from place to place and for moving materials, supplies, and services.
0:18 · And in some parts of cities—slums— that’s not happening.


Infrastructure issues
0:23 · The world’s slums lack not only large, easy to travel roads, but they’re also missing a lot of the infrastructure that goes along with them: street signs, building numbers, and vehicle access to building exteriors.
0:35 · That lack of connectivity means that the billion people living in slums can’t reliably get their mail, get to work, or even get to the hospital in an emergency.
0:45 · Trash removal and sanitation are difficult at best.
0:49 · Now, scientists are trying to transform slums with a mathematical approach to urban design called “topology”.


Using topology for design
0:56 · Slums can be broken down into two components: infrastructure, like homes and stores, and the access network that links them.
1:05 · Nodes and connections.
1:07 · With this framework, connections –in effect access– can be optimized.
1:13 · This new approaches already been used in two slums within Cape Town, South Africa.


Case study in Cape Town
1:19 · In one of the two neighborhoods, most essential services provided by the city— water, toilets, electricity, trash removal— are on the outskirts where road access exists, but the inner portions of the settlement— where temples are—are completely cut off.


Mapping and optimization
1:37 · In this study scientists used satellite data and detailed maps handmade by locals to diagram all the nodes and connections of the settlement.
1:45 · They then used their topological algorithm to figure out which areas were inaccessible by roads, then generated the most cost effective ways to build roads and connect them to outside services.
1:57 · In topology since one block of buildings surrounded by roads is considered equivalent, settlements with a wide range of shapes and sizes, from the suburbs of Las Vegas to the slums of Mumbai, can be analyzed in the same way.


Empowering local communities
2:13 · The scientists who designed the program hope to come up with a user-friendly interface that can be used by communities around the world.
2:19 · That, they say, would put the decision-making power into the hands of locals who can determine if proposed access roads will accommodate their priorities, then reroute them accordingly.

Why cities are full of uncomfortable benches

Description
That bench won’t be yours forever.
Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO
When designing urban spaces, city planners have many competing interests to balance. After all, cities are some of the most diverse places on the planet. They need to be built for a variety of needs.
In recent years, these competing interests have surfaced conflict over an unlikely interest: purposefully uncomfortable benches.
Enter the New York City MTA. They’ve installed ’leaning bars’ to supplement traditional benches & save platform space. But designs like this carry an often invisible cost: they rob citizens of hospitable public space. And the people who experience this cost most directly are those experiencing homelessness.

Why did we build high-rise public housing projects

Description

In the spring of 2007, the Chicago Housing Authority demolished the last of the 28 buildings in the Robert Taylor Homes housing project. Robert Taylor Homes is one of several high profile housing project demolitions, from St. Louis’s Pruitt-Igoe to fellow Chicago project Cabrini Green. The demolitions serve as an admission that high-rise public housing wasn’t a good idea. The housing that replaced them are all low rise projects better integrated within existing neighborhoods. So why did anyone back then think it was a good idea? Why did housing authorities build these high rise projects in the first place?

Why don’t we just burn our trash
DW Planet A, 08 13, 2021

Video (10:45)




Description
Waste to energy plants are seen as green innovations for countries where landfills dominate, as they reduce methane and generate renewable energy. But will these incinerators really make our trash problems go up in flames?
We’re destroying our environment at an alarming rate. But it doesn’t need to be this way. Our new channel Planet A explores the shift towards an eco-friendly world — and challenges our ideas about what dealing with climate change means. We look at the big and the small: What we can do and how the system needs to change. Every Friday we’ll take a truly global look at how to get us out of this mess.
Read More (Links):
Open burning: https://theconversation.com/health-crisis-up-to-a-billion-tonnes-of-waste-potentially-burned-in-the-open-every-year-152778
Waste around the world: https://datatopics.worldbank.org/what-a-waste/trends_in_solid_waste_management.html
Waste to energy as a solution (IEA): https://www.iea.org/articles/will-energy-from-waste-become-the-key-form-of-bioenergy-in-asia
Waste to energy as a solution (Project Drawdown): https://drawdown.org/solutions/waste-to-energy/technical-summary
Waste management in India (Pritpal Randhawa): https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/frsc.2020.00014/full
Environmental impacts of waste to energy: https://www.eunomia.co.uk/reports-tools/greenhouse-gas-and-air-quality-impacts-of-incineration-and-landfill/
Waste to energy in Europe: https://e360.yale.edu/features/in-europe-a-backlash-is-growing-over-incinerating-garbage
0:00 Intro
0:39 Why we need better waste management
2:00 Waste to energy
6:04 The Waste Hierarchy
6:51 A waste solution for the Global South?
6:47 Decentralization & Diversification
9:34 When incineration makes sense
Reporter: Amanda Coulson-Drasner
Video editor: Amanda Coulson-Drasner, Cem Springer
Supervising editor: Kiyo Dörrer


Transcript

Intro
0:01 · These skiers are all here because of trash.
0:05 · That’s because underneath this slope is a huge garbage incineration plant.
0:10 · It processes 400,000 metric tons of waste a year and turns it into energy and heat for Copenhagen.
0:18 · It also recycles 90% of the city’s metal waste.
0:22 · Some say such incineration plants could be key for solving our global trash problem.
0:28 · But is that true?
0:30 · Or are we going to end up just getting burned?


Why we need better waste management
0:39 · Globally, we produce over two billion tons of household waste annually, with high income countries generating an outsized amount compared to their populations.
0:50 · 37% of global waste ends up in landfills, polluting groundwater and producing methane.
0:57 · Less than 20% of the world’s trash is recycled or composted.
1:02 · In the Global South many people have no access to trash collection, and it often ends up in rivers — a primary source of ocean plastic.
1:12 · To get rid of as much trash as possible, as fast as possible, around one billion tons of waste are openly burned every year.
1:22 · “Open burning generates high levels of black carbon, which is soot, which has a really strong global warming effect.”
1:31 · Zoë Lenkiewicz is one of the founding members of Wasteaid, and has been a waste manager for over 20 years.
1:38 · “It also generates dioxins and furans, which are known to cause cancer.
1:41 · All of this is going into the local air, wherever people are burning waste.”
1:48 · Women are more directly impacted, as they are often responsible for disposing of household waste.
1:53 · Burning trash this way is a serious problem. But done differently, there are advantages to it.


Waste to energy
2:01 · Here’s where controlled burning, aka incineration, comes in.
2:04 · Incinerators first appeared where it was hard to landfill, in London in 1874, then in New York City, in 1885.
2:12 · “The incineration process itself, it reduces the volume of the waste [by] 90 percent.”
2:19 · Ella Stengler is the managing director of the umbrella organization for European waste to energy operators.
2:25 · “And it fulfills the kind of sanitary task because it destroys the pollutants which are embedded in the waste.”
2:32 · The generated heat can also be turned into energy. It’s called, unsurprisingly, waste to energy.
2:38 · In the US, where there’s a lot of space and cheap energy in the form of oil, waste to energy wasn’t so competitive, and many plants were closed.
2:46 · But more and more plants were built in the EU.
2:50 · Today they provide power to 18 million Europeans, and heat to 15 million.
2:56 · They’re a common waste management option for countries like Denmark and the Netherlands, which have almost completely eliminated landfilling.
3:05 · Environmental organizations see potential in waste to energy as a transition step toward a more circular economy, especially in countries without much space, that need more energy.
3:18 · Here’s how the plants work: The garbage is dumped into a big pit — from there it’s fed into the furnaces.
3:25 · They burn extremely hot, and the waste is reduced in a matter of minutes.
3:30 · The heat from the fires generates steam, which turns turbines to create electricity.
3:35 · The steam can also be used for heating.
3:38 · The 10% that doesn’t burn is called bottom ash, and metals can be recovered from it.
3:44 · The rest can then be used as construction material.
3:50 · So the process reduces the volume of waste, creates energy, and part of the residue can even be recycled.
3:58 · What’s not to love?
4:01 · Well, there are a few reasons why the world isn’t full of waste to energy plants with ski slopes on top.
4:07 · One of those reasons is fly ash, which is everything caught by the filters.
4:11 · It needs to be disposed of in a hazardous waste facility.
4:15 · Another reason is cost.
4:16 · “If there would be a waste to energy plant built, it should be equipped with a state-of-the-art technology, which is expensive.
4:27 · And you need to train the staff to properly operate it and also authorities to monitor it.”
4:33 · Even without ski slopes, waste to energy plants can cost over one billion US dollars to build.
4:39 · Without the latest technology and monitoring, pollution can reach unsafe levels, and impact people living nearby.
4:47 · And they also emit a lot of CO2: in the EU, around 52 million tonnes per year.
4:56 · That’s like 430,000 cars each driving a million kilometers.
5:02 · “Policymakers and industries put incineration in the same type of energy group as renewables, like wind or solar or even nuclear.”
5:15 · This is Tatiana Lujan.
5:16 · She leads the plastics team for ClientEarth, and is also working to implement the EU’s circular economy directive.
5:24 · “But when you look at the greenhouse gas emissions of incineration, they’re actually pretty close to coal and gas, and way far from wind, solar, nuclear.
5:36 · A study commissioned by ClientEarth found that controlled incineration generates between 59 and 73% of the emissions that coal would.
5:44 · Classifying this energy as renewable can divert funding from more sustainable waste management technologies like recycling.
5:51 · So, where it can be correctly built and managed, controlled incineration is better than a landfill – but it’s by far not the cleanest option to handle waste, no matter how much energy is won.


The Waste Hierarchy
6:04 · Have a look at this “waste hierarchy pyramid” – bear with me, it’s less complicated than it looks.
6:09 · At the very bottom of the pyramid is open burning or dumping, the worst possible way to get rid of trash.
6:15 · Disposal without energy recovery is next, so landfilling or incineration without energy generation.
6:22 · Then here’s where waste to energy, which is an umbrella term for a few different methods, comes in.
6:29 · Then comes recycling.
6:31 · Even better is to re-use things, often called upcycling, and at the top is prevention and reduction.
6:38 · Yeah, the whole world is pretty far from the top.
6:42 · That is why waste to energy is seen by some as a quick “solution” for countries struggling with their waste.


A waste solution for the Global South?
6:51 · Not surprisingly, plants are opening up around the world, like in China, Indonesia and India.
7:02 · Africa’s first waste to energy plant just opened, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.
7:08 · But it has proven to be more complicated than just opening up plants and burning the problem away.
7:14 · One reason is that the composition of waste varies widely throughout the world.
7:22 · “You can’t take one model that works in a wealthy country like a cookie cutter and expect it to work in a low-income country because it’s a completely different market.”
7:34 · In India, household waste is around 50 percent organic matter, like food scraps, which are too wet to burn.
7:41 · And because of the lack of centralized waste collection, trash there is often mixed together.
7:48 · “I don’t think segregation is happening at all in majority of the Indian cities.
7:55 · So that’s a major, major problem.”
7:57 · Pritpal Randhawa has been conducting long-term studies on waste management in India for the past 10 years.
8:02 · “The waste has to be segregated and the undesirable material should be separated from that waste, and only the waste with high calorific value should be burned.
8:14 · But that is not something which is happening actually.”
8:18 · Calorific value is a measure of a substance’s heating power — in other words, how easily it burns.
8:24 · Crude oil and mixed plastics come in at around 40 megajoules per kilogram.
8:29 · Food is about 16.
8:31 · Without waste separation, lots of food scraps find their way to the furnaces, forcing the plants to add additional fuel.
8:39 · This makes the whole facility extremely inefficient.
8:42 · Countries also need to have a place to store the hazardous waste.
8:46 · So if incineration isn’t a silver bullet for the Global South, what are other options?
8:52 · “It’s not very complicated at all – the ideal situation would be management of waste at the decentralized level.”
9:01 · And not only decentral, but diversified: specifically suited to the environment and economy of an area.
9:10 · In many cities in India, for example, waste pickers collect recyclables, which are processed informally.
9:15 · Biogas generated from organic waste can be a source of fuel from Benin to Mumbai.
9:20 · And plastic can be made into building material.
9:25 · “With waste management, absolutely one size does not fit all.
9:28 · And you really need to look at what’s most appropriate for that local area.”


When incineration makes sense
9:34 · Waste to energy plants can work, but a trash collection system and a strong environmental regulator are both necessary.
9:41 · These can be really hard to come by.
9:44 · Even with them, countries need to do some careful reflection before building new plants.
9:48 · “When you create incineration, you’re making huge investments and locking yourself in a system that you’re going to have to continue feeding and feeding and feeding.
10:00 · And that creates a disincentive for transitioning to a real circular economy.”
10:08 · So before more trash burning facilities join the global system, policymakers should look at funding more sustainable methods of waste disposal – like recycling, reusing and most importantly, reducing our waste in the first place.
10:22 · So what do you think?
10:24 · To burn, or not to burn?
10:28 · If this video made you think at all…
10:30 · If this video make you think at all, come back every Friday for new ones.
10:33 · And don’t forget to subscribe.




Why don’t we just turn empty offices into housing
DW Planet A, 12 01, 2023

Video (12:13)




Description
Many offices are sitting empty following the rise of working from home, while cities around the world face housing crises. Building new housing is extremely carbon intensive. Could converting unused offices into housing help solve both problems?
We’re destroying our environment at an alarming rate. But it doesn’t need to be this way. Our new channel Planet A explores the shift towards an eco-friendly world — and challenges our ideas about what dealing with climate change means. We look at the big and the small: What we can do and how the system needs to change. Every Friday we’ll take a truly global look at how to get us out of this mess.

Transcript

Intro
0:00 · If you live in a city, there’s a pretty good chance you’re living through a housing crisis.
0:05 · Rents in major cities are skyrocketing…
0:10 · And this is happening all around the world.
0:15 · At the same time housing has grown scarce, some buildings stand empty.
0:22 · Downtown Frankfurt looks like just about any other big city’s central business district.
0:26 · But the gleaming high-rises do hide an alarming fact — nearly 10% of the city’s offices are vacant.
0:35 · Other major cities around the globe have vacancy rates that high…
0:38 · or even higher.
0:41 · So why don’t we just convert empty offices into housing for people worldwide?


The Vacancy Problem
0:52 · While many of us are back in the office, working from home is here to stay.
0:56 · For instance, 35% of US workers who can work from home still do.
1:01 · And plenty only come into the office on occasion.
1:04 · But vacant workspaces aren’t a new problem.
1:07 · Long before the pandemic, aging offices were already becoming less desirable.
1:11 · “There’s been for about the last 10 years a trend that we called ‘flight to quality.’”
1:17 · Steven Paynter, an architect at one of the world’s biggest firms, focuses on adaptive reuse.
1:22 · “People weren’t renewing their leases in older buildings, they were going to the new ones that were being built, because they offered the kind of amenities and kind of locations people wanted.”
1:32 · All these empty offices aren’t just a waste of space: they mean less rent for owners, lower tax revenue for cities, and the decline of entire neighborhoods.
1:42 · “We have beautiful buildings, we have the wonderful plazas, we have sort of all of the physical assets – we just have vacant buildings.
1:49 · And so you don’t see that vibrancy.
1:51 · You used to, you know, kind of look down these key corridors, and you would see just streams of people, you know, coming down the street, and you don’t see that as much anymore.”
2:00 · Lily Langlois is a planner in San Francisco, another city addressing high vacancies.
2:06 · “Almost 95% of our tax revenue comes from business tax, from downtown.
2:12 · About 80% of our GDP came from downtown companies in 2021.
2:17 · It is our economic engine.
2:19 · And so, it needs to thrive so the city can thrive.”
2:24 · Roughly 1/3rd of offices are vacant in San Francisco – the third-most expensive housing market in the US.


Housing’s environmental Impact
2:31 · At the same time, the ongoing construction of new housing is causing a whole different host of problems.
2:37 · Construction accounts for 13% of global energy-related carbon emissions, more than five times that of the aviation industry.
2:44 · “In order to meet climate targets, but also other sustainability targets, we will need to actually stick with what’s already built.”
2:53 · Pernilla Hagbert researches urban sustainability at Stockholm’s Royal Institute of Technology.
2:59 · “Even if this new production of housing and buildings is done with very energy efficient and optimized technologies, this won’t be enough.
3:10 · We will also need to reduce the total amount of new production.”
3:16 · And this is what brings us to Frankfurt.
3:18 · I checked out an ongoing conversion project – an office tower built in the 90s will soon be reborn as around 150 furnished apartments.
3:28 · Benjamin Albrecht, the developer’s regional European head, is excited about adaptive reuse.
3:50 · But it doesn’t only save on emissions.
3:53 · Revamping an office building can be up to 30 percent cheaper and construction can be done in half the time…
3:59 · Though that depends on the project.
4:00 · This one wasn’t much cheaper than a new build, but speed played a big part.


Adaptive Reuse
4:13 · Repurposing an old building to serve a new function is called adaptive reuse, and can extend a structure’s life.
4:19 · Think of turning old factories into artists’ lofts, or warehouses into ubiquitous street food halls.
4:25 · There are plenty of empty offices, tons of people need housing – it seems like a pretty simple solution.
4:32 · Plus it’s environmentally friendly.
4:33 · So why isn’t this constantly happening?
4:37 · Retrofitting an existing structure is a lot more complicated than planning everything from scratch.
4:43 · As developers have found out, apartments and offices aren’t always a 1-1 fit – it depends on when and where they were built.
4:52 · Modern open-plan offices weren’t built for living in.
4:54 · First, you must divide up large areas while ensuring rooms get enough sunlight.
4:59 · And you can’t just have one big bathroom for a whole floor.
5:03 · Each room needs ventilation, heating and power, too.
5:08 · And for all you know the old building is full of asbestos – not every challenge is clear before renovations start.
5:26 · Steven Paynter, the adaptive reuse specialist, has even developed an algorithm to measure whether offices are good candidates to be reincarnated as housing.
5:36 · “So it looks at say, over 100 different aspects.
5:38 · Some of the key ones are things like the distance between the elevators and the windows.
5:44 · You want your one-bedroom apartment to have a nice bedroom with a window and a nice living space with a window, and then have maybe the kitchen and the bathroom at the back.
5:54 · That’s great.
5:55 · A lot of office buildings actually have way too much space between the elevators and the glazing to make that happen.”
6:02 · This means to end up with shiny new apartments, many conversions essentially rebuild everything except existing foundations and facades.
6:10 · Turns out its just slightly more complicated than just clearing out some cubicles and throwing up a bit of sheetrock – especially if you like luxury amenities like bathrooms in every apartment and windows in every bedroom.
6:23 · These constraints make many offices just too much work to convert.
6:27 · According to Paynter’s research, roughly 30% of offices are ideal candidates.
6:33 · And while not every office building is ripe for conversion, adding up all of those that would be a good fit would still make a massive difference.
6:40 · “If you look at the US market where we’re doing a lot of this work, there’s about 100 billion square feet of office space.
6:47 · And if you’ve converted just the vacancy, or about seven precent of that, you could create between six and seven million new homes.”


Improving City Planning
6:55 · But just turning offices into apartments isn’t going to be enough.
7:00 · Neighborhoods that are just office blocks can be a bit inhospitable – crawling with finance bros by day, morphing into ghost towns outside of business hours.
7:08 · Ensuring people live, not just work there could change that.
7:14 · As we saw for ourselves…
7:18 · This neighborhood of Frankfurt, Niederrad, was a sprawling set of offices in the 60s and 70s with the wildly creative nickname of the ‘Bürostadt’ or office city.
7:28 · But by the mid-2000s, nearly one in three of the offices was sitting empty.
7:43 · In 2006, the city began converting the empty office towers into housing, creating true mixed-use development.
7:50 · Now it’s filled with places to live, shop, eat and go to school, instead of just places to work.
7:58 · Frankfurt rezoned the area, and turned parking lots into green spaces and kindergartens.
8:02 · It brought in developers to build apartments and shops.
8:06 · When they’re done, there’ll be 6,000 apartments here.
8:19 · We took a tour of one of the converted office buildings, a 20-story tower turned into 150 apartments in 2020.
8:26 · Its former life made for some quirks.
8:28 · Every room has sprinklers and architects built around load-bearing beams.
8:32 · But they boasts high ceilings and great views, too.
8:36 · As you can see, many conversions end up as relatively upscale housing.
8:41 · That might take a bit of pressure off the housing market, but it’s not going to bring relief to the masses.
8:45 · If we want this to be more than just some kind of luxury niche we don’t need anything crazy – just a bit of political will.


Cutting Red Tape
8:53 · The Canadian city of Calgary, which started working with Paynter to revitalize its downtown in 2021, is a case in point.
9:01 · “Calgary had about a 38% vacancy in their office market.
9:04 · And that was at the time one of the worst in the world.
9:07 · They very quickly put a program together, which gives you $75 a square foot to convert the building, and moved all of the red tape out of the way to make these projects move more quickly.
9:17 · The first five projects are now under construction.
9:20 · That represents about 750 new homes, and they have 10 more approved.”
9:26 · Paynter says much of this housing will be affordable and built with families in mind, thanks to the financial incentives provided by the city.
9:35 · Adaptive reuse often has even more red tape than new builds – that will have to change if we’re going to use its potential to curb emissions.
9:42 · “If you take Toronto where I am, as an example, there’s a rule in all of downtown that you cannot remove office space: it’s protected as employment lands.
9:51 · That was created in the ’70s, and it just never got updated because there was no need to change it.
9:56 · But now there’s a desperate need to change it and it’s kind of holding up these projects happening.”
10:02 · Such arbitrary regulations are quite common.
10:04 · And approval for conversions often takes as long as it would for a new build, even though the structure’s already in place.
10:11 · Ideally, it’d be the other way around.
10:14 · “In both legislative and sort of from a governance perspective, we need to think of how to actually make it difficult to, for example, tear down a building and build a new building, through zoning and through harder legislation.
10:32 · But also through sort of soft legislation like taxation and financial incentives.”


Potential
10:41 · Frankfurt’s leading the way in Germany, converting offices to nearly 10,000 houses in the last decade.
10:47 · And according to recent studies, there’s room for plenty more in cities all over the map.
10:52 · Frankfurt did it with careful city planning, like in Niederrad.
10:56 · Plus, the more we learn implementing such projects, the greater the savings.
11:01 · Since their first office conversion projects have gone well, Benjamin Albrecht thinks his firm will focus more on adaptive reuse.
11:10 · Many developers have shown interest in these projects, and cities like San Francisco are supporting office conversions.
11:17 · “I don’t think that we’re naive in any way, thinking that we’re going to build hundreds of 1000s of units downtown.
11:23 · But I think it’s, you know, part of the solution.
11:26 · And it is an amazing opportunity, to take advantage of these existing assets.”
11:31 · The kind of support offered may determine the type of housing we get.
11:35 · Flipping offices into housing is clearly no quick fix, and it’s not going to solve the global housing crisis overnight.
11:42 · But Frankfurt and Calgary do show it can make cities vastly more livable and it can drastically reduce the environmental impact of relying solely on new builds.
11:51 · Let us know in the comments if your city has started converting offices to housing.
11:55 · And don’t forget to subscribe, we’ve got new videos for you every Friday.

Why safe playgrounds aren’t great for kids
Vox, 02 20, 2019

Video (5:43)




Description
There’s a case for making playgrounds riskier.
This video is presented by Wix, sign up at https://www.wix.com/go/vox
Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO
The stereotypical modern playground — with its bright colors and rubberized flooring — is designed to be clean, safe, and lawsuit-proof. But that isn’t necessarily the best design for kids.
US playground designers spent decades figuring out how to minimize risk: reducing heights, softening surfaces, and limiting loose parts. But now, some are experimenting with creating risk. A growing body of research has found that risky outdoor play is a key part of children’s health, promoting social interactions, creativity, problem-solving, and resilience.
Some communities are even experimenting with “adventure playgrounds,” a format with origins in World War II Denmark, where bomb sites became impromptu playgrounds. Filled with props like nails, hammers, saws, paint, tires, and wood planks, these spaces look more like junkyards than play spaces — and parents are often kept outside of the playground while children are chaperoned by staff. Now, that question of keeping children safe versus keeping children engaged is at the heart of a big debate in playground design.

0:00 · When you imagine a playground, chances are it looks something like this.

0:19 · Here, there are no plastic play structures – just things like old tires, wood planks, hammers and nails.
0:25 · Places like this represent one of the most debated ideas in play architecture: that playgrounds should be designed to let kids take more risks.
0:33 · Now, this nightmare for helicopter parents is the hottest new thing in American playgrounds, because there’s growing evidence that play like this is a whole lot healthier — and safer — for kids.
0:50 · They can play with very dangerous tools, they can take really dangerous risks and overcome them.

History of junk parks
1:04 · She was a British landscape architect and children’s welfare advocate around the middle of the century.
1:09 · In 1945, she visited Copenhagen, where she met an architect named Carl Theodor Sorensen.
1:15 · Two years earlier, during the German occupation of Denmark, Sorensen noticed a problem: kids in his neighborhood weren’t using playgrounds.
1:22 · In fact, they were playing just about everywhere else — even in construction sites and bombed out buildings.
1:27 · So in a housing development in the suburbs of Copenhagen, Sorensen closed off an empty lot and filled it with building materials, discarded objects, and tools.
1:35 · Here, kids could dig, build, and invent on their own.
1:40 · The play structures were ultimately designed by the kids themselves.
1:45 · Sorensen called it a junk playground — and kids and parents loved it.
1:49 · When she returned to England, Marjory Allen started opening similar playgrounds across London.

1:57 · From there, they became a global phenomenon.


Controlled risk design
2:00 · They spread to Minneapolis, Boston, Toronto, Tokyo, Houston, Berkeley, Berlin.
2:05 · And to create these playgrounds, designers had to introduce a critical element: Controlled risk.
2:11 · In this context, a risk isn’t the same thing as a hazard.
2:14 · When you’re climbing a tall tree, a rotten branch is a hazard: the threat is unexpected.
2:19 · But how high you climb is a risk: it’s manageable, and requires you to actively make a decision.
2:25 · You can break the elements of controlled risk down into six categories: heights, speed, tools, dangerous elements, rough and tumble play, and the ability to disappear, or become lost.
2:36 · And a good adventure playground includes a mix of these.
2:39 · Designers also focus on separation of space.
2:42 · To give kids the feeling of discovering things on their own, parents have to stay out.

3:05 · The idea behind all these design elements is that kids respond well to being treated seriously: if they’re presented with risky items with a serious functional purpose, they’ll respond cautiously and conduct more experimentation.
3:17 · But if presented with an overly safe, static space, they often wind up seeking dangerous thrills that the built environment fails to provide, which can result in higher injury rates than risky play at adventure playgrounds.
3:28 · In the US, a culture of lawsuit-proof playscape design means that overly safe playgrounds are the norm.
3:34 · And design philosophy has focused on how to reduce height, movement, and hard materials.
3:38 · That hasn’t made playgrounds better.

3:47 · But adventure playgrounds have recently begun to catch on in the US — perhaps due to an effort to introduce more unstructured play.

Zoning Matters How Land-Use Policies Shape Our Lives
Urban Institute, 06 12, 2019

Video (2:28)




Description
Zoning is a way for communities to separate land by use or form. But from the start, zoning has separated more than just land uses. It has also separated people. As a result, we pay the cost in public health, racial and economic injustices, higher housing costs, and more. Learn more at http://www.urban.org/zoning


Transcript
0:00 · ♪♪♪ Zoning is a way for communities to separate land by use or form.
0:07 · For example, an area could be dedicated to commercial or industrial use, or there could be a restriction on how many housing units can be built.
0:16 · Zoning shapes the places where we live, but it also shapes our lives.
0:20 · Local zoning regulations determine where we can find housing, schools, and parks, and who gets to use them.
0:26 · Policymakers initially created zoning codes to protect public health- for example, to stop residents from getting sick from living too close to factories.
0:35 · But from the start, zoning has separated more than just land uses.
0:39 · It has also separated people.
0:41 · In the early 20th Century, many communities explicitly used zoning ordinances to racially segregate neighborhoods— effectively declaring that different skin colors were as incompatible as a family’s home and a smokestack.
0:54 · By the late 20th century, civil rights legislation outlawed overt housing discrimination.
1:00 · But those explicit racial barriers were quickly replaced by subtler methods.
1:04 · Even today, exclusionary zoning policies that restrict lower-cost or higher-density housing limit racial and economic diversity and raise housing costs.
1:14 · By driving up housing costs, restrictive zoning can exclude people from equal access to public resources, like schools and parks, and leave lower-income workers unable to afford housing close to available jobs.
1:27 · When regions are more economically and racially segregated, everyone loses.
1:32 · Local economies see slower growth and residents of all races are less upwardly mobile.
1:38 · And finally, despite being created to protect public health, zoning often pushes multifamily buildings closer to highways and areas with higher concentrations of air pollutants.
1:48 · As a result, low-income people and people of color are more likely to live in places that could make them sick.
1:55 · It doesn’t have to be this way.
1:57 · When done thoughtfully, zoning can connect people and places, not divide us.
2:02 · Communities across the US are beginning to reexamine the role of zoning and change their restrictive zoning rules— opening neighborhoods to multifamily housing, walkable densities, and more.
2:14 · For more information and resources, and to find out what other communities are doing to improve their zoning policies, go to urban.org/zoning.

We actually have elderly housing, public housing, combined with healthcare, which is a medical center, commercial and some social programs, and a food court, yeah.
Shane: Oh, wow.
So that’s why it’s not gated.
It’s very open.
Anybody can actually come in and use the facilities here.
Shane, voice-over: Singapore is the third most densely populated city in the world.
The entire country is an island with only 281 square miles of land, but 5.5 million people live here.
In a city this dense, you wouldn’t expect much room for nature.
But it’s like they say: where there’s a will, there’s a way.
And by will, I mean law.
Legislation enables it to happen.
The building took the land.
So we need to do replacement.
The legislation actually requires a building to give back 100% landscape.
Oh!
100% of the site footprint has to be replaced into the building.
Every square inch of, like, green space that you take up, you have to put back in…
Put back in, yeah.
into the building somehow.
Into the building.
Shane, voice-over: A few years after completing the building, Pearl’s firm surveyed the animal life in Kampung Admiralty’s gardens.
50 different species had moved in.
Pearl: The species in this building is higher than the species on the ground park.
Oh, really?
Yeah, which is right nearby.
So…
Wait, so there’s more species within this construction than in, like, a natural space of the same amount of greenery?
Yeah, correct.
That’s incredible.
Thinking about an entire city built like this, basically, you’re talking about reforestation and urbanization as sort of one and the same.
Correct.
[Crows] Shane, voice-over: This development is a microcosm of what’s happening all over Singapore.
It’s not just one building or designer or architecture firm.
The whole city is teeming with life.
Narrator: It’s hard to believe that not so long ago, war surged around it and even in it.
Singapore, cosmopolis of the East.
Malays, Chinese, Indians, and British have taken time by the forelock, and the shops and market stalls dazzle the eye and make our mouths water.
As you sort of, like, move around the city now, you know, do you, you know, like, do you go to places and you’re like, “Oh, this is my baby”?
Yeah, yeah.
All the time.
[Laughter] Shane, voice-over: Professor Cheong Koon Hean is a music lover and life-long Singaporean.
She’s also a legendary urban planner.
A lot of folks credit her with shaping Singapore’s singular urban landscape.
BAER: Raise a toast to the GOAT, yeah Cheong: This is one of my favorite neighborhood centers in a public housing estate.
Because in Singapore, 80% of the people live in public housing in estates like this.
Oh, wow.
In highly affordable housing.
Shane, voice-over: Kampung Admiralty, the building Pearl Chee designed, is public housing, too.
And these places are cush.
The apartments are modern and clean, the amenities are incredible, and most developments are a 10-minute or less walk from public transportation.
And, of course, everything is draped in greenery, from the street level to the tops of the skyscrapers.
Where I come from, when we say “public housing,” basically, like, we call it “the projects.”
And I was actually raised a lot in public housing.
And that public housing and this public housing are not the same thing.
Well, you can’t believe it when you come to Singapore today, but, say, about 60, 70 years ago, actually, Singapore was a nation of slums and squatters.
It was also polluted and lots of traffic congestion.
Shane, voice-over: When Singapore gained its sovereignty from Britain in 1959, it was a city of 1.5 million people and massive, unplanned sprawl.
Tens of thousands of people had no place to live.
So the newly elected government created the HDB, or Housing and Development Board.
Cheong: And within 5 years, the HDB, they already built 51,000 units of flats.
It started from very basic housing, but now, of course, the quality is a lot better, as you can see around you.
Yeah.
Shane, voice-over: And public housing is just the beginning.
Singapore is a very small city-state.
It’s actually only half the size of metropolitan London.
Oh, wow.
But we are a country.
We’re not just a city.
So everything you need about a country, whether it’s for water, power generation, ports, airports, plus housing, shops, offices, industry, all has to be built within this tiny island city-state.
And so biodiversity and ecological balance became really quite an important concept.
Now, as we developed the land, of course we start to lose space for planting.
So what did we do?
We decided to move the greenery upwards into the sky.
And so, what you did is you just created new space.
And suddenly, you bring back all the biodiversity.
Back in the States, urban areas and wildlife are sort of like oil and water.
They don’t mix very well.
But what you’ve done here is something very, very different.
Over the years, we moved from being a garden city to a city in the garden because we started to plant so extensively.
And in the last decade or so, we moved from a city in a garden to city in nature.
In a place where you have limited space and you have this growing population that there are two very sort of competing needs.
Shane, absolutely, there’s always competing needs, right?
So it’s really this very important balancing act of allocating the right amount of land for different uses to create this type of an environment.
Shane, voice-over: And who orchestrates this balancing act?
It’s the Singaporean government, with their comprehensive “Master Plan” for managing the city-state’s ongoing growth.
By centralizing the control of urban development, Singapore paves the way– you see what I did there– for projects that fuse function and form.
Cheong: If you look behind us, the Punggol Waterway is actually a man-made river.
We dammed up two rivers to become freshwater reservoirs.
Now, the engineers wanted to connect the two reservoirs with a pipe– very functional.
But then the architects and the planners say, “Why do a pipe?
Why don’t we make a river?”
And so, this river connected the two reservoirs to balance and optimize the storage of water, but at the same time, it became a leisure facility.
So Punggol has a nickname.
It’s the Venice of Singapore.
Oh, that’s amazing.
Because we brought in water, right?
It has its aesthetics, but everything also serves… Function, yes, a function.
a very specific function.
Even the Punggol Waterway, there’s a family of otters that have come back.
Oh, that’s incredible.
They live on the Punggol Waterway.
Shane, voice-over: Singapore challenges a lot of what I thought I knew about cities.
No one’s saying that we should all be like Singapore, or even that we could be.
This place is unique.
90% of Singapore’s land is publicly owned.
The government determines what gets built and where.
And with everyone sharing the same tiny island, by definition, they’re all in this together.
Most places don’t have all that.
But I’m not sure we need it to re-imagine what cities can be.
I think the thing that stands out to me about Singapore is the intentionality.
I’m not sure if this specific model can be applied anywhere or everywhere, but I think they’re doing things that I think other cities can learn from.
We have to get our act together to make cities effective.
Creativity, innovation, and that will to survive and to want to do well are very, very strong drivers.
That’s human beings, right?
That’s what we are.
Shane, voice-over: Cities might just be humankind’s most remarkable invention.
Because we thought we were building ourselves a place to live, but we were really creating a new ecosystem, a place where nature has to adapt to live alongside us and some of our urban neighbors are more welcome than others.
City living brings challenges– for us and all the species that share our urban spaces.
But we shouldn’t forget that cities can also help us flourish.
In Oakland, Chris said something that stuck with me.
We are a communal species.
So for folks to think, “Well, if you just get outside the city, you’ll be OK,” nah, nah, nah, it doesn’t work like that.
We need to be able to have connection.
Shane, voice-over: That’s why cities aren’t going anywhere and why we need to make them better.
With a little creativity and vision, they can deliver that connection– to each other and maybe to the rest of our incredible planet, too.
Human Footprint is available with PBS Passport and on Amazon Prime Video.

About this episode:   Long flights at high altitudes can expose pilots and flight attendants to dangerous levels of cosmic radiation over their careers, potentially increasing their risk for a variety of cancers and posing special dangers to pregnant crewmembers. Fenwick is an accomplished pilot with over 21,000 flight hours spanning military, corporate, VIP, and major airline operations. He also has extensive experience in aviation safety management. What Ever Happened to the Ozone Hole?



What Ever Happened to the Ozone Hole?


Duration: 00:39:21
Released: 2026
Series: Are We Doomed?

Open Episode in Spotify
Open Series in Spotify
A dark blue wound across the bottom of the world — that’s what NASA images showed in the 1980s. It was a hole in the ozone layer, eight million square miles across. Human activity and convenience had quietly, but rapidly, eaten away  Earth’s crucial shield against the sun, one that likely helped make life on land possible in the first place.Ben Bradford goes back to re-examine the story of the ozone hole: how people discovered it, how they fought over what to do, and what finally happened. It’s a tale of hairspray, human progress, exploding refrigerators, scientists balancing on icy Antarctic rooftops, and Ronald Reagan’s ranch. And from it, maybe, we can find a map for building consensus on our most pressing environmental challenges today.Guest:Susan Solomon, MIT atmospheric scientist and one of the key figures in solving the ozone crisis.Support Are We Doomed?, get bonus episodes, and more: https://doompod.com/support/ Watch earlier episodes on Youtube! https://www.youtube.com/@arewedoomedpod To manage podcast ad preferences, review the links below:See pcm.adswizz.com for information about our collection and use of personal data for sponsorship and to manage your podcast sponsorship preferences. Superfund sites are some of the most polluted areas in the country, containing highly toxic waste such as asbestos, lead, and dioxin. Cleaning them up, which follows a systematic, science-based process as required by law, can take decades.There are more than 1,300 of these sites across the US, from Florida’s Panhandle to the banks of the Rio Grande in New Mexico. They’re found in nearly every state, often near residential areas. The EPA estimates that 78 million people live within three miles of a Superfund site—nearly 1 in 4 Americans.But these waste dumps face a growing threat: the worsening effects of climate change. The EPA has determined that more than 300 Superfund sites are at risk of flooding. The actual number of flood-prone sites, however, may be more than twice that amount, according to a 2021 Government Accountability Office report. Floodwaters can move toxic waste into neighboring communities, which threatens drinking water, agriculture, and broader ecosystem health.Read more at sciencefriday.comTranscripts for each segment will be available after the show airs on sciencefriday.com. A new approach to fighting malaria



May 31, 2019: A new approach to fighting malaria


Duration: 00:25:28
Released: 2019
Series: Better Off

Open Episode in Spotify
Open Series in Spotify
Each year, more than 200 million people around the world are infected with malaria and more than 400,000 die. For the past two decades, the most successful method of malaria prevention has involved treating bed nets with long-lasting insecticides that kill mosquitoes. But that progress is being threatened as mosquitoes increasingly grow resistant to the most commonly used insecticides. Now, new Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health research offers a potential fresh approach to fighting malaria: directly target the parasite responsible for the disease. A recent study showed that mosquitoes that landed on surfaces coated with the antimalarial compound atovaquone were completely blocked from developing Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite that causes malaria. The study was led by Flaminia Catteruccia, professor of immunology and infectious diseases and Doug Paton , a research fellow at the Harvard Chan School. In this week’s episode we sit down with Paton to discuss the findings—and how they could be used to make progress in the fight against malaria. Full Transcript: hsph.me/malaria-pod

Though discovered relatively recently, Oropouche virus has been making headlines as an emerging vector-borne infectious disease on the rise. Not transmitted by the usual suspects (like ticks and mosquitoes), this virus is instead spread through the bites of midges or no-see-ums. Since these arthropods are already widely distributed and their range is growing thanks to climate change, this is a recipe for potential disaster. In this episode, we take you through the story of Oropouche virus, from how it makes us sick to what the construction of a highway has to do with its discovery, from surprising prevalence statistics to the history of One Health. Dotted across the Great Basin of the American West are salty, smelly lakes. The largest of these, by far, is the Great Salt Lake in Utah.But a recent report found that water diversions for farming, climate change and population growth could mean the lake essentially disappears within five years. Less water going in means higher concentrations of salt and minerals, which threatens the crucial ecological role saline lakes play across the West, as well as the health of the people who live nearby. On today’s episode, Kirk takes Short Wave co-host Aaron Scott on an audio field trip to the endangered Great Salt Lake, and explains why losing the lake could be devastating for everyone from brine flies to the humans that live next door. Most of the 600 billion pounds of waste that Americans produce every year ends up in landfills. All that trash can have huge impacts on the environment. But modern landfills have found a new use for all that trash — they’re turning it into energy. In spite of their reputation as “dumps,” these landfills are feats of engineering, more akin to construction sites.
One of North America’s biggest landfills lies on the outskirts of Las Vegas. The Apex Landfill is not only one of the country’s largest, it’s also one of the busiest. Landfills like Apex are required to deal with the toxic chemicals they produce, like methane, a greenhouse gas that’s 84 times more potent than carbon dioxide. At Apex, they capture that methane and turn it into energy that powers 11,000 homes in southern Nevada.

John Yang reports.

The climate crisis isn’t a distant threat — it’s already here, and it’s deadly. But keeping people cool is surprisingly complicated.
In Sydney, Australia, physiologist Ollie Jay is tackling the problem by studying how the human body responds to extreme heat. The ultimate goal is to create low-cost cooling strategies for people without access to air conditioning — those most at risk from extreme heat. Science journalist Miles O’Brien puts himself in the hot seat — literally — to find out what it feels like when the body’s cooling system starts to fail.

Resolve to Solve with Miles O’Brien
Miles O’Brien travels the globe searching for solutions to climate, water, and health crises. From building sea curtains in Antarctica to restoring wildlife in Argentina, the answers are closer than we think thanks to people with a “Resolve to Solve.”



0:01 · MILES O’BRIEN: At the iconic Sydney Opera House, I met a scientist looking for an answer.
0:06 · Ollie Jay runs the Heat and Health Research Center at the University of Sydney.
0:13 · Lay the context for us a little bit on Australia, its climate, and the heat impacts you deal with here.
0:21 · We have an increased prevalence of heat waves.
0:23 · They’re greater intensity, the maximum temperature records are being beaten regularly.
0:28 · Among, uh, high income countries, we’re actually the most susceptible to the impacts of extreme heat on human health and well-being.
0:35 · For a researcher such as yourself, trying to find solutions, ways to adapt, this is the perfect laboratory, isn’t it?
0:41 · JAY: Absolutely.
0:42 · We take time to understand the nature of the problem before we start trying to develop solutions, because we don’t want to go down that route that a lot of academics do of finding solutions to problems that don’t exist.
0:52 · O’BRIEN: Ollie and his team are looking for smarter, more efficient ways to keep people safe and cool as the global thermostat rises.
1:01 · ♪ ♪ That was on his mind when I met him on a steamy Saturday at the University of Sydney Cricket Club Oval.
1:11 · (bat cracks) A match like this can last two long days, six to eight hours each.
1:19 · That was big!
1:20 · (cheers and applause) On the sidelines, Ollie Jay and his team were setting up a curious contraption they call the EMU.
1:30 · It’s a flightless Australian bird, but also something called the Environmental Measurement Unit.
1:35 · O’BRIEN: Mm-hmm.
1:36 · Like MaRTy in Phoenix, EMU measures four key parameters: air temperature, humidity, radiant temperature and wind speed.
1:47 · We measure temperature in this device right here.
1:50 · We can move air in a certain way across that temperature sensor to get a very accurate read on what the temperature of the air is in the shade.
1:57 · O’BRIEN: Humidity is measured in that same white chamber.
2:01 · Above it is a copper sphere that is painted matte black.
2:07 · It measures radiation that comes directly from the sun and bounces off the various surfaces surrounding an athlete.
2:15 · JAY: And then using all of this information, we can model how hot someone’s going to get, and therefore what their rate of dehydration might be.
2:21 · And, you know, potentially how much water they need to drink in order to maintain hydration.
2:29 · O’BRIEN: A short walk away from the cricket oval is Ollie’s lab.
2:33 · And that’s where he’s built another novel tool to better understand how heat affects the human body.
2:39 · It’s a climate chamber.
2:42 · Think of it as a science oven, and I’m on the menu.
2:47 · JAY: Just be careful of the step there.
2:49 · Here we go, Miles.
2:50 · O’BRIEN: You’re not messing around.
2:52 · JAY: No, we’re not messing around. O’BRIEN: All right.
2:54 · Reporting for scientific duty.
2:55 · I was finally going to find out what it’s like to be an order of French fries, waiting under the heat lamp on a short-order shelf.
3:05 · Before I got this far, I swallowed a horse pill.
3:08 · Right down the gullet there.
3:10 · A thermometer with a tiny transmitter inside that tracked my core temperature.
3:15 · I’m hot stuff.
3:16 · They took my blood pressure.
3:18 · Applied a strap to track my heart rate and a mask that measured the amount of oxygen I was consuming, to help estimate how much heat my body was generating on its own.
3:30 · JAMES SMALLCOMBE: If you can just blow out for me.
3:31 · (blows) Yep, that’s tight enough, that’s perfect.
3:34 · Your cardiovascular system seems to be in pretty good nick, uh, Miles, we’ve got, you know, great blood pressure and your resting heart rate’s nice and, uh, nice and low, so.
3:43 · Objective evidence demonstrating your very good health.
3:46 · O’BRIEN: He put it to the test by simulating one of the worst weather disasters in modern U.S. history: the heat wave in Chicago in 1995.
3:57 · More than 700 people died.
3:59 · Researchers concluded a working air conditioner would have prevented half the fatalities.
4:05 · And living alone doubled the risk of death.
4:07 · It became a stark lesson in how vulnerability and isolation can turn extreme heat into a mass-casualty disaster.
4:17 · Almost for the first time, it placed extreme heat on the radar of public health officials and actually seeing that it is responsible for excess death and morbidity.
4:27 · O’BRIEN: The tragedy exposed something deeper than weather.
4:31 · It was about inequality, and neglect.
4:35 · That summer, Chicago made it painfully clear heat doesn’t strike evenly, and it kills quietly.
4:44 · We’re doing this from the perspective of trying to understand the settings that the most vulnerable are going to be in, and then developing solutions that are fit for purpose in those settings.
4:54 · O’BRIEN: Here in the chamber, the temperature was 104 degrees Fahrenheit, with humidity between 50% and 60%.
5:03 · It was pretty miserable.
5:06 · I feel like a cheeseburger just off the grill.
5:08 · The human body cools itself by sweating, but that only works if the sweat can evaporate.
5:14 · At this temperature and humidity, it can’t.
5:19 · The air is nearly saturated.
5:21 · The sweat just sits there, and the body keeps heating up.
5:27 · It’s a huge challenge for human survival.
5:30 · What we know is that the people who are most vulnerable won’t have access to air conditioning.
5:34 · They most likely won’t have access to things like cooling shelters as well.
5:38 · They’ll be sheltering at home in place.
5:40 · So the question is, what type of activities, what type of risk reduction cooling strategies can these people use that is most effective at blunting that physiological heat strain that generates inside the body that we know is harmful to human health?
5:53 · O’BRIEN: He’s exploring cooling strategies for people who can’t afford to live in air-conditioned comfort.
6:00 · Practical, low-cost ways to survive the heat.
6:04 · Things like immersing your feet in water so they act like radiators.
6:09 · And using fans which, under the right conditions, can significantly reduce the effects of heat stress.
6:16 · These are the kinds of things that can help the most vulnerable among us, during a heat wave like Chicago in 1995.
6:26 · With the proper prior planning on that, could those deaths have been preventable?
6:31 · Most of them?
6:32 · There’s a, there’s a saying, um, in the heat health space that every heat-related death is preventable.
6:40 · O’BRIEN: Globally, heat kills about a half-a-million people every year.
6:45 · And in the U.S., the fatalities are growing at an alarming rate.
6:50 · In 2023, more than 2,300 died from heat in the U.S.
6:55 · About three times more than a decade ago.
6:58 · Far greater than the average toll for hurricanes and wildfires.
7:03 · They grab the headlines, but heat has always been the most lethal consequence of climate change, by far.
7:11 · Outside this window in Sydney, intense heat is everywhere– quiet, invisible and relentless.
7:20 · Ah.
7:22 · (sighs) Sheesh.
7:23 · After I’d mopped myself up, Ollie and I went from the frying pan to the fire.
7:31 · He took me on a walking tour of the University of Sydney campus.
7:35 · Born and raised in Wales, with a stop in Canada along the way, Ollie actually earned his PhD studying cold temperatures.
7:45 · But in 2014, Sydney beckoned.
7:48 · Suddenly, he was on the opposite end of the earth and the thermometer.
7:53 · Australia being a hot place, and it is a hot place, I figure that if, Australian-based researchers, if we can’t get a handle on these problems, and we can’t find a solution, then there’s very little chance that anyone else will.
8:06 · O’BRIEN: Plenty of scientists study the climate and the relentless rise of temperatures.
8:10 · But far fewer connect the dots to the impact on human health.
8:15 · How heat affects real bodies, in real time, in a warming world.
8:20 · It’s a mistake to overlook human physiology as you try to come up with some answers here, right?
8:25 · If you think about it from a health perspective, obviously, the hot weather is a problem.
8:29 · But the real problem is the hot person in the hot environment.
8:32 · ♪ ♪ O’BRIEN: It was time for us to solve that problem.
8:36 · We met up with his partner Allison and their adorable, precocious daughter Lottie.
8:41 · ALLISON: Ready to go to the beach?
8:43 · O’BRIEN: They took me to Coogee Beach, a short walk from their home in Sydney.
8:49 · Becoming a parent has changed the way he thinks about his work.
8:54 · It’s sharpened his focus and redoubled his resolve to solve.
9:00 · There are lots of solutions, but I think what we’ve got to do is focus on not just climate change mitigation, ensuring that the choices that we make don’t aggravate the problem in the future, but also got to face that we’ve got to adapt to a warmer world.
9:13 · We need to do both of them at the same time.
9:15 · It would be bad if all of that back and forth led to inertia and apathy. JAY: Well, it’s exactly right.
9:21 · People need to have hope in order to act.
9:22 · Otherwise, we just bury our head in the sand and try to pretend it’s not happening when it is.
9:26 · O’BRIEN: In the sand. JAY: Here we are.
9:28 · O’BRIEN: I see what you’re doing there, man.
9:30 · Nicely done, nicely done. (Ollie laughing) ♪ ♪

0:06 · Ollie Jay runs the Heat and Health Research Center at the University of Sydney.
0:13 · Lay the context for us a little bit on Australia, its climate, and the heat impacts you deal with here.
0:21 · We have an increased prevalence of heat waves.
0:23 · They’re greater intensity, the maximum temperature records are being beaten regularly.
0:28 · Among, uh, high income countries, we’re actually the most susceptible to the impacts of extreme heat on human health and well-being.
0:35 · For a researcher such as yourself, trying to find solutions, ways to adapt, this is the perfect laboratory, isn’t it?
0:41 · JAY: Absolutely.
0:42 · We take time to understand the nature of the problem before we start trying to develop solutions, because we don’t want to go down that route that a lot of academics do of finding solutions to problems that don’t exist.
0:52 · O’BRIEN: Ollie and his team are looking for smarter, more efficient ways to keep people safe and cool as the global thermostat rises.
1:01 · ♪ ♪ That was on his mind when I met him on a steamy Saturday at the University of Sydney Cricket Club Oval.
1:11 · (bat cracks) A match like this can last two long days, six to eight hours each.
1:19 · That was big!
1:20 · (cheers and applause) On the sidelines, Ollie Jay and his team were setting up a curious contraption they call the EMU.
1:30 · It’s a flightless Australian bird, but also something called the Environmental Measurement Unit.
1:35 · O’BRIEN: Mm-hmm.
1:36 · Like MaRTy in Phoenix, EMU measures four key parameters: air temperature, humidity, radiant temperature and wind speed.
1:47 · We measure temperature in this device right here.
1:50 · We can move air in a certain way across that temperature sensor to get a very accurate read on what the temperature of the air is in the shade.
1:57 · O’BRIEN: Humidity is measured in that same white chamber.
2:01 · Above it is a copper sphere that is painted matte black.
2:07 · It measures radiation that comes directly from the sun and bounces off the various surfaces surrounding an athlete.

2:21 · And, you know, potentially how much water they need to drink in order to maintain hydration.

2:33 · And that’s where he’s built another novel tool to better understand how heat affects the human body.
2:39 · It’s a climate chamber.
2:42 · Think of it as a science oven, and I’m on the menu.
2:47 · JAY: Just be careful of the step there.
2:49 · Here we go, Miles.
2:50 · O’BRIEN: You’re not messing around.
2:52 · JAY: No, we’re not messing around. O’BRIEN: All right.
2:54 · Reporting for scientific duty.

3:08 · Right down the gullet there.

3:15 · I’m hot stuff.

3:30 · JAMES SMALLCOMBE: If you can just blow out for me.
3:31 · (blows) Yep, that’s tight enough, that’s perfect.

3:43 · Objective evidence demonstrating your very good health.

3:57 · More than 700 people died.
3:59 · Researchers concluded a working air conditioner would have prevented half the fatalities.
4:05 · And living alone doubled the risk of death.
4:07 · It became a stark lesson in how vulnerability and isolation can turn extreme heat into a mass-casualty disaster.
4:17 · Almost for the first time, it placed extreme heat on the radar of public health officials and actually seeing that it is responsible for excess death and morbidity.
4:27 · O’BRIEN: The tragedy exposed something deeper than weather.
4:31 · It was about inequality, and neglect.
4:35 · That summer, Chicago made it painfully clear heat doesn’t strike evenly, and it kills quietly.
4:44 · We’re doing this from the perspective of trying to understand the settings that the most vulnerable are going to be in, and then developing solutions that are fit for purpose in those settings.
4:54 · O’BRIEN: Here in the chamber, the temperature was 104 degrees Fahrenheit, with humidity between 50% and 60%.
5:03 · It was pretty miserable.
5:06 · I feel like a cheeseburger just off the grill.
5:08 · The human body cools itself by sweating, but that only works if the sweat can evaporate.
5:14 · At this temperature and humidity, it can’t.
5:19 · The air is nearly saturated.
5:21 · The sweat just sits there, and the body keeps heating up.
5:27 · It’s a huge challenge for human survival.
5:30 · What we know is that the people who are most vulnerable won’t have access to air conditioning.
5:34 · They most likely won’t have access to things like cooling shelters as well.
5:38 · They’ll be sheltering at home in place.
5:40 · So the question is, what type of activities, what type of risk reduction cooling strategies can these people use that is most effective at blunting that physiological heat strain that generates inside the body that we know is harmful to human health?
5:53 · O’BRIEN: He’s exploring cooling strategies for people who can’t afford to live in air-conditioned comfort.
