11:01 · And that’s really the key to all of this. Right now, there is no crystal ball, just small incremental ways scientists are learning how to buy precious seconds, maybe even minutes. But trying to prevent or even predict the inevitable, National Geographic referred to these glaciers as cryogenic time bombs, a reference to our changing climate and how frozen water that makes up this kind of glue that binds the Earth together, the cryosphere, it’s melting.
11:33 · Is that to blame in Nepal?
11:36 · We may never know directly, but it is why scientists [music] are so certain something like this will happen again. It’s just a question of when and where.

Hurricanes, typhoons, and tropical cyclones are Earth’s most powerful storms, capable of unleashing destruction and death on coastal areas worldwide. As climate change warms Earth’s oceans, we face more risk of storms rapidly intensifying into category 5, sometimes in less than a single day. Being able to predict these rapidly intensifying storms will save lives, but studying hurricanes in detail is difficult and dangerous. So in order to improve our understanding of hurricanes, scientists have built a machine that can create hurricane conditions indoors. weather hurricanes

0:12 · These are Earth’s most powerful storms up to a thousand miles across and capable of devastating coastal areas with massive rains, surging waves and sustained winds of more than 160 miles per hour.
0:26 · Hurricanes, also known as typhoons or tropical cyclones, form over warm tropical oceans, where they draw up huge amounts of heat, energy, and moisture.
0:36 · A hurricane’s intensity depends on how much energy it can pull from warm ocean water.
0:41 · And as humans have changed the climate, the oceans have heated up creating the potential for more intense hurricanes happening more often.
0:50 · So in order to better predict the destructive impact of these swirling superstorms and to save lives, scientists have built this, a machine that can create the worst imaginable hurricane conditions indoors.

2:26 · The models simply aren’t refined enough.
2:29 · To create better tools to make these predictions, scientists have to get up close and study hurricanes in detail.
2:35 · Scientists have created many advanced tools to study hurricanes using remote instruments by flying into them and even following them from space.

6:43 · One of the key gaps in hurricane prediction has been the intensity.
6:48 · And that can be a huge problem if something like this happens. In 2017, hurricane Maria intensified from a category one to a category five storm in just 18 hours, leaving those in its path little time to prepare or seek shelter and ultimately causing more than 3000 deaths on the islands of Dominica and Puerto Rico. Hurricanes can grow from dangerous to potentially historic levels of destruction in basically no time flat.



7:19 · So being able to predict several days in advance whether a hurricane will be powerful could allow more time for evacuation and save lives. This storm machine is already helping scientists better understand how hurricanes grow. As a hurricane’s winds blow over the waves, the rough surface of the ocean exerts a drag on the storm, sucking energy out of it similar to how friction slows down a sliding object by removing its kinetic energy.
7:49 · What we’d expect is as a hurricane gets stronger, rougher seas, and bigger waves would suck out even more energy, preventing storms from growing too quickly. AMNA NAWAZ: Welcome to the “News Hour.”
The scale of the disaster in the Himalayas is becoming clearer tonight after catastrophic flooding tore through parts of Nepal and neighboring Tibet.
Scientists now believe the disaster was likely triggered by the collapse of a glacier high in the mountains, unleashing a torrent of water, mud, and debris that swept away bridges, roads, and entire communities.
GEOFF BENNETT: President Trump today called the devastation in Nepal brutal.
The death toll stands at least 390, with more than 1,400 others still missing.
That’s as rescue crews race to reach survivors in some of the world’s most difficult terrain.
In the valleys that carve through the highest peaks in the world, villages are now buried in mud.
This is Nepal’s Nuwakot district.
Yesterday’s floods left behind a layer of sludge so high, it reached rooftops and trapped trucks as if in quicksand.
Survivors recounted the terror as it all unfolded without warning.
JANAK BAHADUR, Flood Survivor (through translator): It came in suddenly and exploded like a bomb.
The river looked small from a distance, but it suddenly started overflowing and swept through this place.
GEOFF BENNETT: Geological experts believe a glacier collapse some 30 miles north of Kathmandu was likely what caused the disaster.
These satellite images show the glacier along those snowy peaks there at the bottom before the collapse.
And this is what it looks like now, the surrounding rivers swollen by the floodwaters and debris rushing downstream.
Cell phone video showed the torrent starting to barrel toward this hydroelectric dam.
Within seconds, it bursts through the other side and engulfs the entire site, this border crossing between Nepal and Tibet, the autonomous region in China, now completely destroyed by the ensuing landslides.
Nepalese officials say the floods have swept away dozens of bridges and damaged some 25 miles of roads.
That, combined with the already treacherous terrain of the Himalayas, have made rescue efforts especially difficult.
Nepal’s army says it’s airlifted more than 100 people to safety using helicopters.
On the ground, crews trudge through knee-deep mud with the aid of search dogs to locate the missing, hoisting them onto their backs, many survivors transported to hospitals in Kathmandu.
But as the search grinds on, many families have no choice but to wait for news they fear may never come.
SUBINA TAMANG, Wife of Missing Man (through translator): All I want is that my husband comes back to me safely in one piece.
I do not want anything else.
CHAMINDI SHRESHTHA, Mother of Missing Man (through translator): My son is stuck in the floods.
He is a truck driver.
And he said he was driving.
There is no news of him.
We are not able to find out anything.
GEOFF BENNETT: The scale of this catastrophe is being felt across the region.
Officials in China say they’re searching for hundreds of people still missing in Tibet, where floodwaters stretched for miles across the vast plateau.
Authorities said a new lake was formed in the deluge.
A spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry vowed to send aid to Nepal, which has significantly fewer emergency resources than its neighbor.
LIN JIAN, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson (through translator): The mudslide has caused massive casualties and left many missing in both China and Nepal.
The two sides are having close communication and coordinating efforts for search-and-rescue.
GEOFF BENNETT: Among the missing, some 500 foreign nationals.
The U.S.
State Department this morning confirmed three Americans had been rescued, but as many as 90 may have been affected by the floods.
SADHGURU JAGGI VASUDEV, Indian Spiritual Leader (through translator): I wish to bring to your notice that there has been a terrible… GEOFF BENNETT: In an emotional message today, the Indian spiritual leader known as Sadhguru said a group had been on a holy pilgrimage in the area and got caught in the floods.
He said 22 of them were U.S.
citizens.
And for more on what caused the devastating floods, we’re joined now by Dan Shugar, who heads the waterSHED Lab at the University of Calgary.
Thanks for being with us.
DAN SHUGAR, waterSHED Lab Director, University of Calgary: Thank you.
GEOFF BENNETT: So scientists believe the deadly flood in Nepal may have started when a massive chunk of ice snapped off a glacier high in the Himalayas, unleashing this devastating cascade into the valley below.
Walk us through how that might have happened.
DAN SHUGAR: That was certainly our initial thought as to what happened based on the information that we had yesterday from some preliminary satellite information.
It’s changed a little bit since then, but the general story is still the same.
At about just under 5,000 meters elevation is a glacier that in the satellite imagery that we saw yesterday essentially two days ago was there, yesterday was gone, and the flood resulted downstream.
Since then, we have found that glacier ice - - chunk of glacier ice that essentially disappeared downstream was part of a much larger mass of bedrock, so a gigantic chunk of the mountainside that collapsed, essentially exploding as it descended a vertical kilometer to the valley bottom, melting all that ice, and then flowing out and generating the floods that we saw in those horrific videos.
GEOFF BENNETT: What makes that part of the Himalayas so vulnerable?
DAN SHUGAR: That’s a good question.
I suppose it would be a couple of things, one, incredibly steep topography and then huge relief, so massive differences between the low points and the high points, lots of glaciers, lots of glacial lakes, which weren’t an issue in this particular disaster, but certainly in other ones.
A lot of seismic activity.
The Gorkha earthquake wasn’t that long ago, and we saw very similar sort of disasters unfold, in fact, just on the other side of this mountain.
And the human part of that equation, I think, is important.
Unlike in Western North America, in much of the Himalaya, you have settlements in these incredibly high, narrow valleys that essentially are putting people and infrastructure and livelihoods at risk when these landslides or these floods come down.
GEOFF BENNETT: The other human element at play, it strikes me, is climate change.
What role does climate change play here?
What can scientists say with confidence about the connection between rising temperatures, retreating glaciers, and disasters like this one?
DAN SHUGAR: We can speak in generalities, because it’s a little bit hard to speak about the specific event just yet because we haven’t done any sort of attribution study.
As temperatures rise, glaciers will melt, will thin vertically, destabilizing the valley walls that they formerly were sort of help – hoping – or helping to hold up.
Additionally, as air temperatures rise, the permafrost is changing, and so permafrost is just ground that remains frozen year-round year after year.
But in some areas, both at high altitudes, but also in the north, permafrost is destabilizing because of warming temperatures.
And that can cause large landslides like this as well.
And then a third factor, I think would be changes in precipitation patterns, not only in terms of intensity, but in terms of when during the year they occurred.
Water can get underneath the glaciers, allowing them to slide a little bit more rapidly, any number of ways that that extra water can sort of enhance or increase the likelihood of one of these kinds of events.
GEOFF BENNETT: Dan, what lessons can be learned from this disaster?
DAN SHUGAR: I think that these landscapes, these steep mountain landscapes, are continually evolving due to climate change.
And the global community, not just the government of Nepal or China or India, need – the global community, we need to be stepping up to help mitigate these risks and to enhance the resiliency of people living in these environments that are subject to these disasters that, when there’s a climate change link, we in the rich West are largely responsible for.
GEOFF BENNETT: Dan Shugar with the waterSHED Lab at the University of Calgary, thanks for joining us this evening.
DAN SHUGAR: Thank you.

6:48 · What you’re seeing here is a 26-hour time-lapse [music] from the same Swiss company, GeoPrevent, just before the glacier collapse. Maybe seemingly slow, but alarmingly fast [music] for a mountain. The Earth was moving 10 m a day.
7:09 · With this kind of information, you [music] can’t predict the exact timing of the collapse itself. But this kind of observation is what allowed scientists to recognize [music] the increasing chance that something bad might happen at some point. The danger [music] was progressive and predictable.
7:27 · It’s easier to access some of those cliff sides in Switzerland, get sensors and monitoring equipment in those locations so that we can keep get real-time data. Here in Nepal, um the extreme elevations we’re looking at, there’s just there’s no trail to the top, there’s not a cable car there.
7:43 · The capacity and the resources necessary are going to be very difficult to replicate in places like the Himalayas.
7:50 · It’s one thing when you’ve been noticing changes over a long period and you decide to point a whole bunch of measuring devices at a very specific spot. But the problem with the Himalayas is scale.
8:01 · The physical scale of the range, the difficulty in working with it, the fact that it’s often covered in clouds as it is due to the monsoon season now, it it presents tremendous challenge for prediction and monitoring.
8:14 · This part of the world isn’t just a mountain range. It is an entire wall of mountains stretching thousands of kilometers containing some of the highest peaks and deepest valleys on Earth.
8:28 · Glaciers and the lakes they melt into are a key concern because they can overflow. But there are thousands of them across Asia and [music] scientists do their best to track every single one with reports like this one from 2020 creating a meticulous inventory of the most dangerous sites like one giant catalog of risk. There’s promise there, maybe, you think. And looking in hindsight at what happened in Nepal, they are indeed finding clues that suggest maybe these types of events are predictable.
9:02 · A new report published after the collapse refers to how movement of the ice surface sped up just prior, how meltwater had turned visibly brown suggesting mountain sediment was shifting. Also, noticing a crack propagating in the days leading up to the disaster. Even learning to better track events as they occur, noticing that the mass movement caused a seismic signal at a magnitude larger than four. So, maybe there’s promise in deploying more seismic sensors.
9:33 · And imagine tying all that knowledge together, pushing it to the limit using AI, combining susceptibility maps [music] with real-time data to inch closer and closer to predicting the unpredictable. But then you remember, once again, the problem of scale. I think one Washington-based think tank put [music] it best. The Himalayan region offers more slopes capable of failing at this magnitude [music] across greater vertical relief than anywhere else on Earth.
10:04 · Then it goes on to this point of how hard it can be to gauge risk even when you think you’ve found it. Of roughly a dozen extreme flow events in the region in the [music] past 10 years, only one originated in a place already known to be a risk. Every other one of these events also came from somewhere no one was watching.
10:26 · It’s very challenging to predict exactly where and when these rock collapses are going to occur.
10:33 · It would be terrific if you could put sensors in in all the locations where events like this potentially were going to happen, but it’s just not practical to monitor so many different locations all at once. As remote sensing technologies improve, as computing improves, we’ll be more and more able to watch the landscape and detect small amounts of change, but that’s still a work in progress.
11:01 · And that’s really the key to all of this. Right now, there is no crystal ball, just small incremental ways scientists are learning how to buy precious seconds, maybe even minutes. But trying to prevent or even predict the inevitable, National Geographic referred to these glaciers as cryogenic time bombs, a reference to our changing climate and how frozen water that makes up this kind of glue that binds the Earth together, the cryosphere, it’s melting.
11:33 · Is that to blame in Nepal?
11:36 · We may never know directly, but it is why scientists [music] are so certain something like this will happen again. It’s just a question of when and where.
11:46 · [music]

ANDY THAPA: Nothing is visible - no houses, no roads, no any greenery in those areas and no blue water. Now it’s muddy water now.
CHANG: Andy Thapa is one of the rescuers trying to get to as many survivors as he can. He’s a charter and rescue pilot for a helicopter company in Nepal, and in 20 or so flights over the last two days, he shot some video and shared that video with us.
THAPA: We saw many people stuck in the middle of the mud. Half of the body were inside the mud and they were just seeking for help. But there were no place to land, even no place to drop for the rescue.
CHANG: Thapa said he was able to find survivors in some accessible parts of the mountainous region, but many were in bad shape.
THAPA: Personally, for me, I evacuated more than 120 people. They are muddy, like in their face, in their legs, might be body scratched, hand broken, leg broken and they terrified, you know, unable to speak.
CHANG: He told us about one man who was able to talk with him.
THAPA: He had 10 people in the family, out of which he lost nine in front of his eye.
CHANG: Thapa has been flying the most critically injured people to Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu, and the rest to a closer staging area. But there are so many people still stranded. Today, he said he had to leave several hundred people sheltering in a tunnel because the weather just got too bad to fly.
THAPA: But they are very safe and they have enough food to eat. We will just continue with such missions.
CHANG: CONSIDER THIS - climate change is accelerating the frequency of deadly natural disasters. What do we know about the role climate change is playing in the Himalayan region?
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
CHANG: From NPR, I’m Ailsa Chang.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
CHANG: It’s CONSIDER THIS FROM NPR. These deadly flash floods on the border of Nepal and Chinese-administered Tibet are not a surprise to many climate scientists. NPR’s Julia Simon joins us now to explain why. Hi, Julia.
JULIA SIMON, BYLINE: Hello, Ailsa.
CHANG: So the way I understand it, this flooding - it came from a glacier - right? - that collapsed. Is that correct?
SIMON: Yeah. So the reports are still preliminary, but many scientists think this was a glacier collapsing - this giant chunk of ice that snapped off, triggering the floods. This mass of ice and rock and mud and water - it started ripping down this Himalayan river valley, down through these villages, destroying communities. If you’ve seen the videos, you can see it’s this avalanche of deadly debris.
CHANG: Yeah. And I mean, these glaciers, they’ve been around for thousands of years, right? So…
SIMON: Right.
CHANG: …To have a chunk of glacier just snap off now seems like a huge deal.
SIMON: It does. But sadly, many scientists are not so surprised that this could happen, Ailsa, and that’s because of human-caused climate change. These glaciers that were once stable - they’re disappearing. NPR has been reporting on Nepal’s glaciers for years. A team from NPR traveled to Nepal in 2022. They were climbing up a moraine. That’s a massive pile of boulders created by a glacier. But when NPR’s Rebecca Hersher got to the top, there was no glacier in sight.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)
REBECCA HERSHER: Oh, wow.
(SOUNDBITE OF WATER SPLASHING)
SIMON: That’s the sound of water. There was only water - this huge lake - where a glacier should have been, Ailsa. The glacier had melted, and glacial lake floods are a growing threat. In recent years, multiple glacial lake floods have displaced and killed people. Scientists warn that an estimated 15 million people around the world are at risk from such floods.
CHANG: Wow. So just how unstable are these melting glaciers?
SIMON: Yeah. So NPR spoke with Alton Byers about this. He’s at the Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research at the University of Colorado at Boulder. He says he’s surprised how fast the permafrost - that’s the continuously frozen ice, soil and rock that’s held the mountains together for millennia - it’s now changing.
ALTON BYERS: The analogy I and my colleagues use is take a stick of butter out of the refrigerator and put it on the counter. It’s going to get softer and it’s going to lose its structural integrity.
SIMON: Yeah. So these melting glaciers - they pose deadly risks to the communities in their path.
CHANG: I mean, we’re seeing it right now. So…
SIMON: Yeah.
CHANG: …What are some solutions here to prevent the kind of disaster that we are seeing in Nepal, for example, a disaster that is caused by melting glaciers?
SIMON: Well, the first thing is better alert systems. It seems right now, like, Nepal’s flood warning system wasn’t equipped to handle this, despite quite a bit of investment in those warning systems over the last decade or so. And it’s important to mention this area has seen flash floods before. But we also know the primary driver of global warming is the burning of fossil fuels, like oil, gas and coal. The solutions to transition away from fossil fuels are out there, Ailsa. They are scalable. They’re affordable. They’re reliable. They include solar energy, wind energy and batteries.
CHANG: That is NPR climate and energy correspondent Julia Simon. Thank you, Julia.
SIMON: Thank you, Ailsa.

In August 2005, one of the most powerful storms ever recorded in the Gulf of Mexico barrelled toward the United States. When Hurricane Katrina finally struck land, it devastated hundreds of miles of shoreline, but the disaster that captured the world’s attention unfolded in one place above all: the city of New Orleans.   Within hours of the storm passing, the flood defence levees meant to protect the city broke, and it began to fill with water. What followed the natural disaster was a crisis that raised profound questions about preparedness, inequality, and the ability and willingness of a modern nation to protect one of its own great cities.   But why was New Orleans so vulnerable in the first place? What was the response in the wake of the hurricane and flooding? And what did the disaster reveal about the systems of engineering, government and society that were supposed to protect it? This is a Short History Of Hurricane Katrina. A Noiser podcast production. Hosted by John Hopkins. What Worsening Floods Mean For Superfund Sites

Series: Science Friday

Open Episode in Spotify
Open Series in Spotify
Superfund sites are some of the most polluted areas in the country, containing highly toxic waste such as asbestos, lead, and dioxin. Cleaning them up, which follows a systematic, science-based process as required by law, can take decades.There are more than 1,300 of these sites across the US, from Florida’s Panhandle to the banks of the Rio Grande in New Mexico. They’re found in nearly every state, often near residential areas. The EPA estimates that 78 million people live within three miles of a Superfund site—nearly 1 in 4 Americans.But these waste dumps face a growing threat: the worsening effects of climate change. The EPA has determined that more than 300 Superfund sites are at risk of flooding. The actual number of flood-prone sites, however, may be more than twice that amount, according to a 2021 Government Accountability Office report. Floodwaters can move toxic waste into neighboring communities, which threatens drinking water, agriculture, and broader ecosystem health.Read more at sciencefriday.comTranscripts for each segment will be available after the show airs on sciencefriday.com. citizens.
And for more on what caused the devastating floods, we’re joined now by Dan Shugar, who heads the waterSHED Lab at the University of Calgary.
Thanks for being with us.
DAN SHUGAR, waterSHED Lab Director, University of Calgary: Thank you.
GEOFF BENNETT: So scientists believe the deadly flood in Nepal may have started when a massive chunk of ice snapped off a glacier high in the Himalayas, unleashing this devastating cascade into the valley below.
Walk us through how that might have happened.
DAN SHUGAR: That was certainly our initial thought as to what happened based on the information that we had yesterday from some preliminary satellite information.
It’s changed a little bit since then, but the general story is still the same.
At about just under 5,000 meters elevation is a glacier that in the satellite imagery that we saw yesterday essentially two days ago was there, yesterday was gone, and the flood resulted downstream.
Since then, we have found that glacier ice - - chunk of glacier ice that essentially disappeared downstream was part of a much larger mass of bedrock, so a gigantic chunk of the mountainside that collapsed, essentially exploding as it descended a vertical kilometer to the valley bottom, melting all that ice, and then flowing out and generating the floods that we saw in those horrific videos.
GEOFF BENNETT: What makes that part of the Himalayas so vulnerable?
DAN SHUGAR: That’s a good question.
I suppose it would be a couple of things, one, incredibly steep topography and then huge relief, so massive differences between the low points and the high points, lots of glaciers, lots of glacial lakes, which weren’t an issue in this particular disaster, but certainly in other ones.
A lot of seismic activity.
The Gorkha earthquake wasn’t that long ago, and we saw very similar sort of disasters unfold, in fact, just on the other side of this mountain.
And the human part of that equation, I think, is important.
Unlike in Western North America, in much of the Himalaya, you have settlements in these incredibly high, narrow valleys that essentially are putting people and infrastructure and livelihoods at risk when these landslides or these floods come down.
GEOFF BENNETT: The other human element at play, it strikes me, is climate change.
What role does climate change play here?
What can scientists say with confidence about the connection between rising temperatures, retreating glaciers, and disasters like this one?
DAN SHUGAR: We can speak in generalities, because it’s a little bit hard to speak about the specific event just yet because we haven’t done any sort of attribution study.
As temperatures rise, glaciers will melt, will thin vertically, destabilizing the valley walls that they formerly were sort of help – hoping – or helping to hold up.
Additionally, as air temperatures rise, the permafrost is changing, and so permafrost is just ground that remains frozen year-round year after year.
But in some areas, both at high altitudes, but also in the north, permafrost is destabilizing because of warming temperatures.
And that can cause large landslides like this as well.
And then a third factor, I think would be changes in precipitation patterns, not only in terms of intensity, but in terms of when during the year they occurred.
Water can get underneath the glaciers, allowing them to slide a little bit more rapidly, any number of ways that that extra water can sort of enhance or increase the likelihood of one of these kinds of events.
GEOFF BENNETT: Dan, what lessons can be learned from this disaster?
DAN SHUGAR: I think that these landscapes, these steep mountain landscapes, are continually evolving due to climate change.
And the global community, not just the government of Nepal or China or India, need – the global community, we need to be stepping up to help mitigate these risks and to enhance the resiliency of people living in these environments that are subject to these disasters that, when there’s a climate change link, we in the rich West are largely responsible for.
GEOFF BENNETT: Dan Shugar with the waterSHED Lab at the University of Calgary, thanks for joining us this evening.
DAN SHUGAR: Thank you.

A new approach to fighting malaria



May 31, 2019: A new approach to fighting malaria


Duration: 00:25:28
Released: 2019

Open Episode in Spotify
Open Series in Spotify
Each year, more than 200 million people around the world are infected with malaria and more than 400,000 die. For the past two decades, the most successful method of malaria prevention has involved treating bed nets with long-lasting insecticides that kill mosquitoes. But that progress is being threatened as mosquitoes increasingly grow resistant to the most commonly used insecticides. Now, new Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health research offers a potential fresh approach to fighting malaria: directly target the parasite responsible for the disease. A recent study showed that mosquitoes that landed on surfaces coated with the antimalarial compound atovaquone were completely blocked from developing Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite that causes malaria. The study was led by Flaminia Catteruccia, professor of immunology and infectious diseases and Doug Paton , a research fellow at the Harvard Chan School. In this week’s episode we sit down with Paton to discuss the findings—and how they could be used to make progress in the fight against malaria. Full Transcript: hsph.me/malaria-pod

Why do we believe what we believe? Is what we believe the truth? How can we convince others of our beliefs? If you’ve ever found yourself pondering these questions, you know that the answers are rarely clear-cut. We need to form beliefs in order to navigate the world, but how skilled are we at evaluating evidence for those beliefs or weighing new data that contradicts them? In this week’s TPWKY book club episode, Adam Kucharski, Professor at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine joins me to discuss latest book, Proof: The Art and Science of Certainty. With this book, Dr. Kucharski presents a compelling and thoughtful examination of the concept of proof, delving into topics ranging from the justice system (what’s a reasonable doubt?) to infectious disease, clinical design to the founding of this country. And he leaves us with a powerful lesson: what convinced you of something might not convince someone else. Tune in for a fascinating conversation! In epidemiology, this central character is known as Patient Zero—the case at the heart of an outbreak. This hour, Radiolab hunts for Patient Zeroes from all over the map. 14:58 · It uses hooks, called tarsal claws, to flip over ledges.
15:02 · [cymbal ta-da] [cymbal ta-da] And not even a wall can stop it.
15:21 · Better to keep up the momentum and figure it out as you go.
15:28 · The roach is both tough and flexible.

15:42 · They’re held together by lots of pliable joints.
15:46 · And they use all those bendy joints to fold up, origami-style, and push through impossibly small cracks … … like that gap you never knew existed in your kitchen cupboard.

title: Environmental Justice
text:
Dates: 2026-09-03T16:00:00
Introduction to Environmental Justice 





ProPublica, 08 04, 2017







Landfills, chemical waste facilities and power plants are more often built in poor and minority communities, which don’t have the power or money to advocate for themselves.
For decades, these communities have called for environmental justice: the idea that people shouldn’t be forced to deal with more pollution because they belong to a certain race, national origin or income bracket.
It’s a simple notion, but America has struggled for decades to implement any policies that actually protect poor and minority communities from environmental toxins. Now, President Trump’s budget seeks to end the Office of Environmental Justice and cut overall funding to the EPA by 31%. What will happen to the marginalized communities that most need a government advocate?
Images:
CNN, Fox News, MTV, AP, The EcoLogic Channel, José da Vede, Chicago Sun Times, St. Louis Public Radio, Leroy Woodson via The Atlantic, Frank J Aleksandrowicz via The Atlantic, Harry Shaefer via The Atlantic, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Julie Dermanksy, CBS News
Music:
“Climbing the Mountain” - Podington Bear
“Falcon Hood Tight” - Podington Bear





0:06 · Nationally the facilities where we dump our garbage and process dangerous chemicals tend to be located in poor and minority communities.
0:14 · The people who live there have little or no protection from the industries around them.
0:18 · And things could get worse.
0:22 · So, there’s this idea of environmental justice.
0:24 · It’s pretty simple: Communities shouldn’t be forced to deal with more pollution because they belong to a certain race, national origin or income bracket.
0:33 · Yet, America has struggled over the years to implement any serious policy that actually protects these communities.
0:38 · So, let’s lay out the ways the government has failed them.



0:42 · “We will not allow Warren County to become a dump site.”
0:47 · The fight for environmental justice took off in 1982 when residents of Warren County, North Carolina mounted mass demonstrations against a plan to dump contaminated soil in a landfill in their community.
0:59 · The EPA investigated four similar landfills in southern states and found that they were all located in black or low-income neighborhoods.
1:07 · In 1987, the United Church of Christ Racial Justice Commission found that around the country, hazardous waste facilities were more likely to be located in mostly minority communities.
1:18 · Amid mounting proof, the federal government was forced to act.



1:23 · So, in 1992 President George H.W. Bush founded the Office of Environmental Justice inside the EPA.
1:30 · Two years later, President Bill Clinton signed an executive order requiring federal agencies to consider environmental justice in all of their policies, as well as extending civil rights protection to environmental discrimination.
1:42 · But Congress never passed a bill to make Clinton’s executive order law.



1:47 · Then came George W. Bush.
1:50 · His administration shifted the focus of the Office of Environmental Justice from protecting low-income and minority communities to “all people,” Leaving vulnerable populations without a federal environmental advocate.
2:02 · “80% of New Orleans, including much of downtown, is under water.”
2:05 · Under Bush, many environmental civil rights claims were rejected or delayed for years.
2:11 · In 2009, after President Barack Obama’s election, his administration recommitted to environmental justice.



2:18 · Generally speaking, in this country a lot of environmentally problematic facilities tend to be located in places where poor folks live.
2:30 · Yet, during the two years Democrats controlled the House, the Senate and the White House they didn’t file a single bill focused on strengthening environmental justice protections.
2:40 · Passing major environmental legislation faded further when Republicans took control of Congress in the 2010 midterm elections.



2:47 · Now, President Donald J. Trump is making good on his vow to weaken the EPA.
2:52 · “Environmental protection, what they do is a disgrace.”
2:55 · “Every week they come out with new regulations.”
2:57 · “Who’s going to protect the environment?”
2:59 · “We’ll be fine with the environment.”
3:00 · “We can leave a little bit.”
3:04 · This budget–a 31% cut to the EPA, $2.6 billion cut away from the EPA, that’s what the president wants.
3:10 · As the EPA loses funding and regulations are rolled back, vulnerable communities may very likely fall through the cracks.
3:18 · I’m Talia Buford. I’ll be covering these communities and digging into systemic environmental injustice.
3:23 · If you have something to tell me, email me at Talia.Buford@ProPublica.org.

Optional Material (Dive Deeper)

Podcasts

10 Years After Flint, The Fight To Replace Lead Pipes Continues



10 Years After Flint, The Fight To Replace Lead Pipes Continues


Duration: 00:13:12
Released: 2024
Series: Short Wave

Open Episode in Spotify
Open Series in Spotify
Ten years ago, Flint, Mich. switched water sources to the Flint River. The lack of corrosion control in the pipes caused lead to leach into the water supply of tens of thousands of residents. Pediatrician Mona Hanna-Attisha recognized a public health crisis in the making and gathered data proving the negative health impact on Flint’s young children. In doing so, she and community organizers in Flint sparked a national conversation about lead in the U.S. water system that persists today. Today on the show, host Emily Kwong and science correspondent Pien Huang talk about the state of Flint and other cities with lead pipes. Efforts to replace these pipes hinge on proposed changes to the EPA’s Lead and Copper Rule. Have questions or comments for us to consider for a future episode? Email us at shortwave@npr.org — we’d love to hear from you!See pcm.adswizz.com for information about our collection and use of personal data for sponsorship and to manage your podcast sponsorship preferences.NPR Privacy Policy




Transcript
EMILY KWONG, HOST:
You’re listening to SHORT WAVE…
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
KWONG: …From NPR.
Hey, SHORT WAVErs. Emily Kwong here. So 10 years ago, Dr. Mona Hanna-Attisha was a pediatrician at Hurley Medical Center, living in Flint, Mich. The city was near bankruptcy, and to save money, Flint decided to switch water sources from Lake Huron to the Flint River on April 25, 2014.
MONA HANNA-ATTISHA: We had greenish and brownish water, and it smelled weird, and it was giving people rashes, and they were losing hair.
KWONG: And families in Flint kept telling her, something’s not right with the water.
HANNA-ATTISHA: They were asking, was it OK to use this tap water to mix their baby’s formula?
KWONG: State and city officials said there was nothing to worry about. And Mona told her patients the same thing.
HANNA-ATTISHA: For a year and a half, I was telling my patients that, of course, everything’s OK. Like, how can - how could our drinking water not be OK? Like, this is America. It is the 21st century. All the folks in charge, despite all these concerns, were saying everything was OK.
KWONG: But everything was not OK.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
KWONG: Over a glass of wine, one of Mona’s high school friends who used to work at the EPA implored her to look into this issue.
HANNA-ATTISHA: And she literally stared me down. She was like, Mona, it doesn’t have corrosion control.
KWONG: The Flint water system lacked something important called corrosion control. Corrosion control changes the chemistry of the water to make it less likely to leach lead from the pipes. And without that corrosion control, the lead in Flint’s pipes got into the water supply.
HANNA-ATTISHA: And that is the moment that I heard about the possibility of lead being in the water, and that’s the moment my life changed.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
HANNA-ATTISHA: We need water to survive. It’s a medical and public health necessity. And the younger you are, the more our bodies are made up of water.
KWONG: The CDC says that no amount of lead in children is safe. For kids, lead poisoning can have serious consequences. It can damage their brains and nervous systems, causing learning and behavioral problems and issues with hearing and speech down the line. Mona saw a crisis in the making and began looking for any data she could on kids’ blood lead levels. And in September 2015, a year and a half after that water switch, she went public with her results…
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
HANNA-ATTISHA: This research is concerning. These results are concerning.
KWONG: …Showing that the number of children in Flint with elevated levels of lead in their blood had gone up.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
HANNA-ATTISHA: And when our national guiding organizations tell us primary prevention is the most important thing and that lead poisoning is potentially irreversible, then we have to say something.
KWONG: At first, the state dismissed her findings. But Mona Hanna-Attisha was right. It’s been 10 years, and the city’s water quality has improved. Flint switched back to Lake Huron, and thousands of lead pipes have been replaced.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
KWONG: But there is still a lot of work to be done in Flint to replace them all. And the truth of the matter is there are cities and towns all over the country facing their own issues with water quality, aging infrastructure and inadequate laws that don’t protect people from lead poisoning. Flint is an example of how speaking up with science can turn a crisis around. So 10 years on, we’re bringing in science reporter Pien Huang to focus on those trying to stop another crisis in another city - Chicago. You’re listening to SHORT WAVE, the science podcast from NPR.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
KWONG: So to help us understand the emerging lead crisis in Chicago, we’ve got science reporter Pien Huang in the studio. Hi, Pien.
PIEN HUANG, BYLINE: Hey, Emily.
KWONG: Hello.
HUANG: It’s great to see you.
KWONG: Good to see you, too.
HUANG: And it’s also so cool that you got to talk to Dr. Mona.
KWONG: It was so cool. And Mona is still on the front lines of trying to make life better for kids in Flint, where more than two-thirds of children live in poverty. She’s the founding director of the Pediatric Public Health Initiative, which connects families to programs and services to alleviate that poverty. One of them, Rx Kids, gives new moms in Flint a no-strings-attached check of $7,500.
HANNA-ATTISHA: In a city that so many folks know as a city that failed kids is a city that’s learning, that’s leading with science, that’s leading with prevention to promote kind of the health and development of kids by boldly kind of eradicating infant poverty.
KWONG: I asked her what she thought of the situation in Chicago, and she didn’t hold back on her thoughts and feelings.
HANNA-ATTISHA: Chicago has a long history of lead advocates, but also a long history of lead misuse. Chicago continued to use lead in their service lines until it was restricted in 1986 and built into the code - if you wanted water from the main, you were mandated to use lead in your plumbing. So Chicago has the most lead lines than any other city in our nation. And, you know, if you respect the science of lead, if you understand that it has no safe level, lead should not be the straw that is delivering our drinking water to so many children and families.
HUANG: And, Emily, that lead is still in the water even now. So there was a recent JAMA Pediatrics study that found that most children under the age of 6 in Chicago are probably drinking leaded water.
KWONG: Most children - wow. OK. And that research was spearheaded by Benjamin Huynh at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, right?
HUANG: Yeah, exactly. Yeah. So he is an assistant professor of environmental health and engineering there, and his focus is on data science and environmental justice. In this case in particular, he’s got personal ties to the topic.
BENJAMIN HUYNH: So I’m from Chicago. And, you know, those of us in Chicago, we’ve known for a long time that most of our pipes are made out of lead.
HUANG: Including the house that his parents live in. In Chicago, there are around 400,000 homes that have lead pipes connecting the water main to the house. And Ben wanted to know, what does that actually mean for people drinking water from those taps?
KWONG: So how did Ben figure this out, like, that so many kids were drinking leaded water? What data did he use?
HUANG: Yeah. So it’s rooted in the fact that Chicago has a free water testing program. It’s for people who want to test their tap water for lead. And so far, this program has run about 38,000 tests. People have voluntarily collected water samples from their home, sent them to the city. And while these tests are free, Ben says not everybody uses them.
HUYNH: We found that the people who took those tests - they’re more likely to be in white neighborhoods, like, wealthier neighborhoods, and also neighborhoods that are less likely to have lead in the first place.
KWONG: Oh, so there was a huge sampling bias in this data.
HUANG: Right, exactly. And he had to correct for that. So he took that data, and he combined it with other sources of data, so data on local health, demographics, survey results on how many people use tap versus filtered or bottled water as their main drinking source. And then with the help of machine learning, he and his team figured out an estimate. They figured out that 68% of young children in Chicago are drinking tap water with lead.
HUYNH: On top of that, you know, we’re seeing Black and Hispanic neighborhoods are more likely to have lead exposure, but also less likely to be tested for lead.
KWONG: But the federal government does allow for some lead to be in the water. So at what point does the Environmental Protection Agency say, this is too much lead in the water - this is the cutoff?
HUANG: The EPA does have something called the Lead and Copper Rule. And this rule sets an action level for lead at 15 parts per billion.
KWONG: OK.
HUANG: And when water systems find that amount of lead in the water, they’re supposed to initiate that corrosion control that we mentioned earlier.
KWONG: So is Chicago in compliance with this 15-parts-per-billion limit?
HUANG: Yeah. I mean, the city says that it is, and they’ve done everything that they’re supposed to be doing.
KWONG: Sure.
HUANG: But there are other places that might not be.
KWONG: OK.
HUANG: I talked to Elizabeth Southerland. She’s formally with the EPA. And she says that audits from the agency actually showed that in some 90% of these cases where there are excess levels of lead in the water, those cases never even got reported to the federal government.
ELIZABETH SOUTHERLAND: This was probably the worst reported and enforced regulation in the history of the drinking water program.
HUANG: Yeah. And many researchers and advocates say the rule was weak and inadequate. Now even the EPA itself says that those regulations need to change. So last year, the EPA proposed the Lead and Copper Rule improvements, and those are expected to be finalized by October this fall.
KWONG: OK. I’m pulling up their website now. So let’s see what could happen if these proposed changes to the Lead and Copper Rule were to take effect. One proposed rule change is that every water system in the country produce a map of where their lead pipes are. That could be huge.
HUANG: Yeah, totally.
KWONG: Also on this list are calls for improving water sampling and lowering that lead action level from 15 parts per billion to 10 parts per billion. OK.
HUANG: There are some people who think that it should be even less than that, but that would significantly lower the trigger level for lead.
KWONG: OK. And then the last thing - ah, requiring the vast majority of water systems to replace all their lead pipes within the next 10 years.
HUANG: And many people are saying, because the lead protections for the drinking water haven’t really been working, this is what we really need to fix the problem. But you said the vast majority, and I want to…
KWONG: Yeah.
HUANG: …Point that out, because that’s a really important point, because in that proposed rule, Chicago gets an exemption because it simply has too many pipes. The regulation, as it’s proposed, is really concerned with what’s realistic and feasible. And so what the EPA is saying is that it’s realistic to expect a city to replace around 10,000 lead service lines a year, and this is based on what other cities have already done. So since most cities have under 100,000 pipes, they should be able to make that deadline. But Chicago, with its 400,000 lead pipes, would get around 40 years or more to switch out their pipes.
KWONG: Wow.
HUANG: And that 40-year timeline has community advocates, like Chakena Perry with the Natural Resources Defense Council, pretty upset.
CHAKENA PERRY: That’s decades, that’s generations of children and adults, you know, consuming lead-contaminated water. It’s incomprehensible to tell a resident that they have to wait that long for safe drinking water.
HUANG: Chakena and others are really pushing for the EPA to close up those exemptions when they issue the final rule in the fall.
KWONG: So to be determined, really, how this rule might impact Chicago in the long run.
HUANG: Yeah. Meanwhile, people have to grapple with the reality of their lead pipes. Remember when I said earlier that Ben’s parents have lead pipes? Well, a few weeks ago, Ben’s mom got sick with symptoms that were consistent with lead poisoning.

American cities were once built around people on foot. Downtown streets were packed with shops, apartments, streetcars, theaters, restaurants, and neighborhoods where daily necessities could often be reached without getting into a car. Then, after World War II, America began rebuilding its cities around the automobile.This video explores how highways, suburban expansion, urban renewal, zoning, and massive parking requirements transformed the American landscape. The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 accelerated construction of the Interstate Highway System with the federal government covering 90% of Interstate construction costs. Meanwhile, suburbanization surged: in 1950, 23.3% of Americans lived in suburbs, but by 2000 that figure had reached 50%.Entire urban neighborhoods were demolished or divided by freeways and redevelopment projects, while historic buildings and downtown blocks were increasingly replaced by roads, garages, and surface parking. Parking minimums later reinforced car-oriented development by requiring businesses and housing projects to dedicate substantial amounts of land to automobiles.Discover how America went from compact, walkable neighborhoods to sprawling suburbs and parking lots—and why many cities are now trying to reverse the transformation.ResourcesInterstate System – Federal Highway Administration – FHWA Interstate System History1950 Census Records: A Window to History – U.S. Census Bureau – U.S. Census BureauAmerican Place: The Historic American Buildings Survey at Seventy-Five Years – National Park Service – National Park ServiceUrban Renewal and the Post-War American City – U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development – HUD ArchivesParking Spaces/Community Places – U.S. Environmental Protection Agency – U.S. EPA

In August 2005, one of the most powerful storms ever recorded in the Gulf of Mexico barrelled toward the United States. When Hurricane Katrina finally struck land, it devastated hundreds of miles of shoreline, but the disaster that captured the world’s attention unfolded in one place above all: the city of New Orleans.   Within hours of the storm passing, the flood defence levees meant to protect the city broke, and it began to fill with water. What followed the natural disaster was a crisis that raised profound questions about preparedness, inequality, and the ability and willingness of a modern nation to protect one of its own great cities.   But why was New Orleans so vulnerable in the first place? What was the response in the wake of the hurricane and flooding? And what did the disaster reveal about the systems of engineering, government and society that were supposed to protect it? Monsanto or MonSatan? How—and Why—a St. Louis Startup Became a Hated Herbicide Giant



Monsanto or MonSatan? How—and Why—a St. Louis Startup Became a Hated Herbicide Giant

Open Episode in Spotify
Open Series in Spotify
A chemical that kills the plants you don’t want—weeds—and keeps the plants you do—food!—seems kind of like magic. After all, weeds are the bane of farmers’ lives, causing tens of billions of dollars in lost yield every year. So why is the world’s largest herbicide company, Monsanto, so unpopular that it’s been referred to as MonSatan? How harmful are today’s herbicides for us humans, and for the environments they’re seeping into? And do we need weedkillers to feed the world? In part two of our three-part series on weeds, we take on the big questions around this “bad seed” of the farming world—and the fascinating story behind the scrappy St. Louis startup that hooked the world on herbicides. Superfund sites are some of the most polluted areas in the country, containing highly toxic waste such as asbestos, lead, and dioxin. Cleaning them up, which follows a systematic, science-based process as required by law, can take decades.There are more than 1,300 of these sites across the US, from Florida’s Panhandle to the banks of the Rio Grande in New Mexico. They’re found in nearly every state, often near residential areas. The EPA estimates that 78 million people live within three miles of a Superfund site—nearly 1 in 4 Americans.But these waste dumps face a growing threat: the worsening effects of climate change. The EPA has determined that more than 300 Superfund sites are at risk of flooding. The actual number of flood-prone sites, however, may be more than twice that amount, according to a 2021 Government Accountability Office report. Landfills, chemical waste facilities and power plants are more often built in poor and minority communities, which don’t have the power or money to advocate for themselves.
For decades, these communities have called for environmental justice: the idea that people shouldn’t be forced to deal with more pollution because they belong to a certain race, national origin or income bracket.

US road design favors speed over pedestrian safety.

Most American roads aren’t just unpleasant for pedestrians, they can be dangerous. Pedestrian fatalities have been rising in the past few years, and urban planners point to the way roads are designed as the culprit.
A group of urban planners identified 60 pedestrian fatality hot spots throughout the US, and a 1,000-meter corridor of US-19 in New Port Richey, Florida, topped their list. Seventeen pedestrians lost their lives along this short stretch of road in the study period of 2001 to 2016.
The fatality hot spots on the study’s list shared a lot of design characteristics. Many of them are arterial thoroughfares: roads historically built to keep high-speed traffic off of nearby residential streets. But the way US communities developed in a sprawling fashion along these roads meant these roadways also became business centers that pedestrians might need to access. The number of lanes and distances between crosswalks are among other dangerous design elements.
For this video, we went to New Port Richey to walk along US-19 and document the design characteristics identified in the study.

Extreme Heat Is the New Normal
New York Times Opinion, 08 28, 2026

Video (15:42)




Description
We filmed “A New Inferno,” the short documentary above, in Phoenix, one of the hottest cities in America, through some of the city’s hottest days of 2025, during one of the hottest years on record globally. On one of our production days, temperatures reached 118 while we were filming outside.
In the face of extreme heat, we documented firefighters and paramedics of the Phoenix Fire Department saving lives in real time. We wanted to call attention to a specialized technique of ice bag immersion for people facing life-threatening heat stroke. We hope that telling their story and showcasing the efficacy of this strategy will encourage wider adoption of this protocol across the country.
Yet this procedure is ultimately a stopgap, as firefighters do their best to adapt to the climate crisis in front of them. The underlying story of heat in Phoenix is one of broader, interlocking crises: homelessness and substance use disorders that are deeply entangled with urban heat, each amplifying the other, illustrating how climate change affects the disenfranchised most brutally.
With our film, we aim to reframe how the public thinks about heat: as an invisible, silent killer reshaping the rhythms of urban life.

How America’s hottest city is trying to cool down

Description
Can trees help save Phoenix from extreme heat?
Subscribe and turn on notifications 🔔 so you don’t miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO
It’s time to stop looking at trees as a form of “beautification.” They are, instead, a living form of infrastructure, providing a variety of services that include stormwater management, air filtering, carbon sequestration, and, most importantly for a city like Phoenix, Arizona, they cool the environment around them.
Trees can lower neighborhood temperatures in three ways: 1) Their shade prevents solar radiation from hitting paved surfaces like concrete and asphalt, which absorb energy and rerelease it into the air as heat. 2) Their leaves pull heat from the immediate area in order to evapotranspirate water that’s drawn from the soil. And, 3) If you’re standing under one, a tree protects your body directly from the sun’s rays. If you’ve ever made a summer visit to a dry, hot city like Phoenix, you’ll know how important shade is for making any outdoor experiences tolerable.
As Phoenix deals with a rising frequency of extreme heat waves — which aren’t only deadly, but also cause worrisome spikes in energy demand — the city is looking to trees as part of its heat mitigation strategy. Phoenix isn’t devoid of trees, but they’re distributed unevenly across the city. A quick glance at a satellite image of the metro area reveals substantial green splotches in the north and east and brown ones in the south and west, where many lower-income neighborhoods are located.
So Phoenix recently pledged to reach “tree equity” by 2030, under an agreement with American Forests, a national tree organization. I visited Phoenix recently to take a look at the current state of the city’s urban forest. In this video, we use drone imagery and thermal cameras to understand how the urban design of the city contributes to extreme heat, and what it can do to cool down.

Most of the 600 billion pounds of waste that Americans produce every year ends up in landfills. All that trash can have huge impacts on the environment. But modern landfills have found a new use for all that trash — they’re turning it into energy. In spite of their reputation as “dumps,” these landfills are feats of engineering, more akin to construction sites.
One of North America’s biggest landfills lies on the outskirts of Las Vegas. The Apex Landfill is not only one of the country’s largest, it’s also one of the busiest. Because it serves a non-stop city, the landfill must operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year. It receives upwards of 16 million pounds of trash per day or 5 billion pounds per year.
Landfills like Apex are required to deal with the toxic chemicals they produce, like methane, a greenhouse gas that’s 84 times more potent than carbon dioxide. At Apex, they capture that methane and turn it into energy that powers 11,000 homes in southern Nevada.

Transcript

The Katy Freeway’s scale
0:01 · The Katy Freeway in Texas connects Houston’s western suburbs with the city’s downtown.
0:08 · At its widest point, right here, it spans 26 lanes including parallel roads, before it intersects with another freeway, creating this massive web of pavement. The Katy Freeway is among the widest in the world. But it didn’t start out this big. The freeway was initially built in the 1960’s with 6 lanes in most places. But as the suburbs and office space around Houston started growing in the 1980’ s and 90’s and more people began using the freeway— it became a traffic nightmare. By 2004, it was ranked the second worst bottleneck in the country.


Expansion and continued traffic
0:40 · To accommodate the growing commuter class, the city began a nearly 3 billion dollar expansion project, to add the additional lanes. The solution seems natural — more lanes equals less congestion. But traffic didn’t get any better. In fact, it got worse, in both the morning and afternoon commutes.


Economic theory of traffic
1:02 · The reason why hinges on a simple economic theory. One that is often overlooked, because actually reducing traffic is far from simple. Highway expansion has gone hand in hand with the suburbanization of American cities like Houston. It becomes a self-fulfilling recipe for urban sprawl: a highway gets built to connect suburbs to a city center, which encourages more development along it, which necessitates even more highways when those get congested — and on and on and on.
1:33 · The instinct to widen highways to relieve traffic makes sense—but there’s a reason it doesn’t work: due to a concept called “induced demand.” These represent 3 highway lanes. And these balls are the commuters that drive on them. These particular commuters — the red ones — will sit in traffic no matter how bad it gets, because they have to. Driving to work on the highway is their only option. Let’s say this is what congestion looks like, during peak rush hours. Once a certain number of cars get on the highway, traffic slows to a crawl. Now let’s add a new lane.


Understanding induced demand
2:04 · These drivers now have more room to spread out — which should make traffic flow better. That might happen at first, but it doesn’t stay that way. That’s because there’s another set of people who will take the highway under the right conditions — even though they have other commuting options. When a highway is congested, they might take local roads instead. Or be able to drive during off-peak hours. They might use other modes of transportation, like public transit or biking.
2:34 · Or maybe they can work from home that day and skip the commute altogether. In a few years, these people will start taking the highway, enticed by less congestion. This is induced demand at play: the more supply there is, the more demand will follow, to exhaustion. And in this case, the supply is highway lanes. And sometimes, like on the Katy freeway, congestion gets even worse after a highway expansion, until some of those people with more options go back to their old ways. But in the end, you’re still left with more drivers, and congestion that’s at least as bad as it was before.
3:02 · When our transportation system is so reliant on highways and private automobiles, there’s almost no way around it because that’s the system that we’ve created. This is Kyle Shelton, an urbanist based in Houston. The endless reduction of congestion… should that be…the driving, honestly the driving policy question for a lot of our transportation funding? Big expensive highway infrastructure projects are still the prevailing band-aid to congestion in the US.


Challenges to the system
3:32 · The transit advocacy group Transportation for America found that between 1993 and 2017, the US added over 30,000 miles of new freeway lanes in 100 metro areas. Building more highways may provide some short-term relief. And it’s easier than most infrastructure projects to get federal funding to do a highway expansion. But if we want less traffic and fewer drivers, giving flexible commuters better choices is a good place to start. Like by improving public transit by adding more and better bus routes or trains.
4:06 · That alone might not be a silver bullet for congestion relief, for the same reason that adding another lane isn’t: new drivers will take the place of transit commuters on the highway. And for many people living off highways in sprawling US cities, public transit may never be an adequate solution.
4:23 · ‘Cause it’s not just about the infrastructure. It’s also about individual behaviors. It’s about where job opportunities are located. And most of our cities have now been constructed in this way where the car is the prime mode. Another option is to enact policies that actively disincentivize people from using the highway. Like congestion pricing, which charges people who drive on highways during rush hours. Or remote work programs that deter people from traveling during the highest traffic times — or make it so they don’t have to commute at all.


Alternative solutions
4:54 · And in the long-term, better land use policies can help as well, like by building communities that put people closer to where they need to go. And if building more highways results in more drivers and congestion, then removing them could have the opposite effect.


Highway removal and future
5:10 · For example, the city of Boston removed a freeway in its city center in the 1990s, and replaced it with a boulevard with biking and bus lanes and more space to walk. It reduced congestion by 62%. And now the Democratically controlled Senate is considering nearly $10 billion in funding for similar highway-removal projects in other cities. What we build and invest in in the world of transportation truly changes our behavior.
5:38 · If building more roads makes us drive on them more. Then giving people better choices by investing in the right things, will make us drive less. Because, if we build it, they will come.

Description
The term “redlining” refers to the practice by banks of excluding Black and Brown Americans from receiving loans to buy homes and make improvements to their communities. Redlining arose during the Great Depression, when the federal government sought to boost homeownership by encouraging banks to lend to more Americans. Many neighborhoods, specifically those with majority Black and Brown residents, were deemed undeserving of these loans. Though redlining was made illegal by the Fair Housing Act, the effects of this practice still reverberate to this day.
In this video, Khalil Gibran Muhammad, Ford Foundation Professor of History, Race, and Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School and director of the Institutional Antiracism and Accountability Project, provides background on the history and legacy of redlining.

Our renowned faculty and trailblazing research centers pioneer bold new ideas. 0:24 · In 1933, in the midst of America’s Great Depression, when unemployment rates were 25% and millions of people were not only out of work, but many of them were houseless, the federal government under President Franklin Delano Roosevelt established an agency called the Home Owners Loan Corporation.

0:55 · Millions of Americans participated, except that when the Home Owners Loan Corporation began to issue mortgages, it came up with a scheme to decide which communities were deserving of loans and which ones weren’t.

1:36 · This created a system that came to be known as redlining because communities that were deemed risky by the mere presence of people of color, most especially black people, were disqualified from getting direct support from the federal government to purchase homes.

Transcript
0:01 · The urban environment is a feat of human decision-making— from where to develop street grids lined with large glass office buildings, to which green spaces to preserve for outdoor recreation.
0:13 · How humans make these choices, and the natural environment’s response, can create extremely different ecosystems in neighborhoods just a few blocks away from each other.
0:23 · Researchers delved into dozens of studies to understand what drives these variations.
0:29 · One well documented phenomenon in cities is the relationship between wealth and biodiversity.
0:35 · More affluent areas generally have greater canopy cover, with larger, mature trees, as well as a higher diversity of birds.
0:45 · This is known as the “luxury effect.”
0:48 · Low-income areas typically have more man-made surfaces— including major heat-absorbers like asphalt and concrete, compared to higher-income areas.
0:59 · The lack of shade from trees and vegetation, combined with more asphalt and concrete, makes it hotter in these neighborhoods— a phenomenon known as an “urban heat island.”
1:10 · These communities are also more likely to be near sources of air pollutants, like expansive interstates pumping car exhaust.
1:19 · Although wealth can sometimes predict the outcomes of an urban ecosystem, there isn’t always a clear relationship.
1:26 · In some cases, the racial make-up of a neighborhood is better than income when forecasting canopy cover.
1:33 · Researchers explored studies that highlight how systemic racism shaped our build environment.
1:39 · One glaring example in the United States is residential segregation.
1:44 · From 1933-1968, the federal government limited access to homeownership among Black Americans through a practice known as redlining.
1:55 · Neighborhoods were graded based on the riskiness of providing a mortgage in the area.
2:00 · The grades ranged from A, the most desirable areas, full of wealthy businessmen, to D, neighborhoods considered high-risk investments due to a combination of factors: from their environmental quality and distance from large industrial factories to the main determinant, the presence of foreign-born and Black people.
2:22 · The inability for Black people to buy homes in these neighborhoods meant many types of capital investments left— landlords abandoned their properties, and public services, such as transportation and park maintenance, weren’t prioritized.
2:36 · Today, many U.S. cities still exhibit long-lasting environmental impacts from this discrimination.
2:42 · Neighborhoods which had a “D” grade in the 60s have about half the canopy cover of historically white communities.
2:50 · Some studies evaluate how the current environment relates to historically redlined communities, but researchers did not find any research that traces how ecosystems changed over time because of this segregation.
3:03 · They propose that because habitable regions are more spread out in these areas, animal populations struggle to breed since they are cut off from each other.
3:14 · The reduced breeding options for animals could have decreased gene diversity, an important way for animals to adapt to changing environments.
3:23 · And decreased gene flow of native species could promote the abundance of pest species, like mosquitos and brown rats, which carry diseases that can infect humans.
3:34 · The combination of all these outcomes— from urban heat islands to increased pests— make low-income, marginalized communities far more vulnerable to risks like climate change.
3:47 · Scientists say such evidence shows that conservation and social justice cross paths— especially along neighborhood streets.

How the US made affordable homes illegal

The rules that keep American housing expensive.
Subscribe and turn on notifications (🔔) so you don’t miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO
Over the past year, housing prices in the US rose precipitously. Low interest rates and millennials’ entry into the market spiked demand across the nation, leading housing prices in some cities to increase by more than 20 percent in one year, and crushing the dreams of many would-be homeowners.
But housing prices in the US were a problem long before 2020 — and while demand is a big part of the story, there’s an even bigger reason it’s increasingly difficult for Americans to find affordable housing: We don’t have enough houses. According to one estimate, the US is now facing a nearly four-million-home shortage. And the primary reason for that shortage is what’s called exclusionary zoning.
Zoning laws are the local rules and regulations that decide what types of homes can be built where. These rules can sometimes have good intentions. But they also have a dark history in the United States as a tool to keep certain races, religions, and nationalities out of white neighborhoods. And while zoning laws in the US are no longer explicitly racist, their effect remains basically the same: to keep affordable housing, and the people who need it, away from the wealthiest Americans.
Today, in the majority of the US, especially in cities with good jobs, it’s illegal to build many affordable types of housing. And it’s led to a widespread affordability crisis. Watch the video above for more.

Transcript

The role of city roads
0:00 · What makes a city? People? Buildings?
0:04 · Horrific traffic jams? That’s not too far off.
0:08 · It turns out that roads are what connect all the parts of a city.
0:12 · We need easy paths to travel from place to place and for moving materials, supplies, and services.
0:18 · And in some parts of cities—slums— that’s not happening.


Infrastructure issues
0:23 · The world’s slums lack not only large, easy to travel roads, but they’re also missing a lot of the infrastructure that goes along with them: street signs, building numbers, and vehicle access to building exteriors.
0:35 · That lack of connectivity means that the billion people living in slums can’t reliably get their mail, get to work, or even get to the hospital in an emergency.
0:45 · Trash removal and sanitation are difficult at best.
0:49 · Now, scientists are trying to transform slums with a mathematical approach to urban design called “topology”.


Using topology for design
0:56 · Slums can be broken down into two components: infrastructure, like homes and stores, and the access network that links them.
1:05 · Nodes and connections.
1:07 · With this framework, connections –in effect access– can be optimized.
1:13 · This new approaches already been used in two slums within Cape Town, South Africa.


Case study in Cape Town
1:19 · In one of the two neighborhoods, most essential services provided by the city— water, toilets, electricity, trash removal— are on the outskirts where road access exists, but the inner portions of the settlement— where temples are—are completely cut off.


Mapping and optimization
1:37 · In this study scientists used satellite data and detailed maps handmade by locals to diagram all the nodes and connections of the settlement.
1:45 · They then used their topological algorithm to figure out which areas were inaccessible by roads, then generated the most cost effective ways to build roads and connect them to outside services.
1:57 · In topology since one block of buildings surrounded by roads is considered equivalent, settlements with a wide range of shapes and sizes, from the suburbs of Las Vegas to the slums of Mumbai, can be analyzed in the same way.


Empowering local communities
2:13 · The scientists who designed the program hope to come up with a user-friendly interface that can be used by communities around the world.
2:19 · That, they say, would put the decision-making power into the hands of locals who can determine if proposed access roads will accommodate their priorities, then reroute them accordingly.

When designing urban spaces, city planners have many competing interests to balance. After all, cities are some of the most diverse places on the planet. They need to be built for a variety of needs.
In recent years, these competing interests have surfaced conflict over an unlikely interest: purposefully uncomfortable benches.
Enter the New York City MTA. They’ve installed ’leaning bars’ to supplement traditional benches & save platform space. But designs like this carry an often invisible cost: they rob citizens of hospitable public space. And the people who experience this cost most directly are those experiencing homelessness.

First to Historian A. Roger Ekirch who kindly got me up to speed on the expansion of streetlights in historic western city districts.

Those numbers come from a variety of annual ‘Point-In-Time’ counts. The problem with benches
0:00 · Why are cities full of uncomfortable benches?
0:06 · This one has armrests to prevent you from dozing off.
0:09 · to prevent you from taking a nap.
0:11 · Here’s another — again with the arms, the stiff metal.
0:16 · And this one — it’s brand new.
0:18 · The MTA in New York began installing them as part of a subway enhancement plan.
0:23 · And they don’t call it a bench.
0:25 · They prefer the term “leaning bars.”
0:28 · So what if i told you it was designed with discomfort in mind?


Defining defensive design
0:34 · New York City is filled with some of the most innovative architecture and urban planning in the world.
0:39 · Today, nearly every kind of public space here is has been developed with close attention to detail.
0:45 · So these benches are no mistake.
0:47 · They are designed to allow you to sit but not get too cozy.
0:51 · And that is intentional.
0:53 · The concept stems from a school of thought that goes by many names, but today we’ll use “defensive design.”
1:00 · Defensive design is about moderating behavior.
1:03 · The goal is to limit the ways an object can be misused.
1:07 · These benches have armrests because that will prevent anyone from laying down.
1:11 · Their short back is another nod to say, “This bench isn’t yours forever.”


Examples of hostile design
1:16 · This trend is worldwide.
1:17 · And it’s not just in the benches.
1:20 · When you start looking for defensive designs in New York City, you’ll find examples everywhere.
1:25 · It’s the presence of security cameras in subway turnstiles or Times Square.
1:31 · It’s these spikes on this column, meant to deter birds.
1:34 · It’s the knobs on these ledges, to discourage skateboarders.
1:38 · And there were once sprinklers underneath the awning of this bookstore, to prevent people from sleeping there.
1:44 · It’s sidewalk barriers.
1:45 · It’s even these regular streetlights.
1:48 · Streetlights are probably some of the most recognizable defensive designs.
1:52 · When they surfaced in the 19th-century Western cities, the dynamic of urban life changed.
1:58 · More people spent time outside at night, which drove economic development and a reduction in crime.


Controversy and impact
2:04 · Most hostile architecture tries to influence behavior in a similar way.
2:08 · The designs attempt to make public space a bit more hospitable, more ideal.
2:13 · Defensive designs can deter crime.
2:15 · It can prevent the destruction of public property.
2:19 · And it can prevent loitering.
2:21 · But there is a reason why defensive design is characterized as “hostile.”
2:25 · Take the example of the bench again.
2:30 · Disability advocates have a problem with that appearing in the MTA.
2:33 · One advocate pointed out that “People who travel who have disabilities or just get tired sometimes need a bench to sit on, not a wall to lean against.”


Targeting homelessness
2:41 · And while no one likes an uncomfortable bench, these additions mean something more for people who are experiencing homelessness.
2:49 · The United States is currently experiencing a decline in the overall homeless population.
2:57 · But in New York, the homeless population is growing.
3:01 · About 1800 people were found to have been sleeping in the subway.
3:06 · That’s because emergency shelter isn’t always a viable option.
3:13 · There are several examples of hostile architecture that target people who are homeless.
3:18 · These designs imply that public space is not where homeless people should be.
3:22 · As it goes, city planners have a dilemma — how do they design inclusive cities?


Designing inclusive cities
3:29 · As for the enhanced subway initiative, the MTA’s mock designs highlight new USB ports and electronic signage in stations.
3:36 · But you won’t find any press materials highlighting this uncomfortable bench.
3:40 · Excuse me, the “leaning bar.”
3:42 · That’s because it makes for an uncomfortable discussion about who we design public space for — and who gets left out.

Why don’t we just burn our trash
DW Planet A, 08 13, 2021

Video (10:45)




Description
Waste to energy plants are seen as green innovations for countries where landfills dominate, as they reduce methane and generate renewable energy. But will these incinerators really make our trash problems go up in flames?
We’re destroying our environment at an alarming rate. But it doesn’t need to be this way. Our new channel Planet A explores the shift towards an eco-friendly world — and challenges our ideas about what dealing with climate change means. We look at the big and the small: What we can do and how the system needs to change. Every Friday we’ll take a truly global look at how to get us out of this mess.
