11:58 · But we also have to invest in nature’s carbon sinks —such as soils and forests— which pull carbon out of the atmosphere and back into the land, where it can’t keep heating things up.



12:09 · It won’t be the easiest breakup.
12:12 · We’ve designed whole societies and global systems around fossil fuels.
12:16 · We should fully expect to be listening to Jazmine Sullivan on repeat with a gallon of Rocky Road.
12:21 · But this is one relationship we can’t afford to stay in.
12:24 · So, in order to halt emissions, we have to both invent new systems and work more efficiently within old ones, and to do that, we’ve got to get a whole planet’s worth of people on board.
12:35 · And if you’ve ever been part of a group project, you know that last part isn’t easy.
12:39 · Thankfully, when faced with global crises, humans have one great thing going for us: we are creative.
12:46 · I mean, we’ve been to space, we’ve got electric cars, we made furbies for some reason.
12:53 · So yes, It’s going to take all of our creativity and cooperation to tackle.
12:58 · But the only way out is through, and the only way through is together.
13:04 · In our next episode, we’ll tune back into the world of living things— and see how our rapidly changing climate involves much more than the atmosphere.
13:12 · It affects every living, breathing, organism on this planet— including you and me.

World Weather Attribution, 11 13, 2023







When an extreme weather event occurs, people often ask: is climate change to blame?
For decades, climate scientists have answered that question in general terms – that as the planet warms, we can expect many of these weather events to become more frequent and extreme.
But in recent years, advances in attribution science have allowed researchers to answer the question in much greater detail.
Founded in 2015 by Dr. Friederike Otto and Dr. Geert Jan van Oldenborgh, World Weather Attribution scientists quantify how climate change influences the intensity and likelihood of an extreme weather event. They often do this using weather data and computer modelling, and often immediately in the aftermath of the extreme event.
To encourage actions that will make communities and countries more resilient to future extreme weather events, World Weather Attribution studies also evaluate how existing vulnerability worsened the impacts of the extreme weather event.
To learn more about World Weather Attribution or to view our studies, go to https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/
Follow us on Twitter: https://twitter.com/WWAttribution
Film produced by Geoff Marsh.

For years, we were told it wasn’t possible to link specific weather events to global warming — and that made communicating about climate change difficult: When extreme weather events were in the news, climate change was often left out of the story. This week, we tell the story of how that changed. We talk to the scientists who figured out how to model the role of climate change in events like Hurricane Harvey — the climate detectives who blew the case of extreme weather wide open.Guests: Dr. Peter Stott, UK Met Office; Dr. Friederike (Fredi) Otto, Grantham Institute for Climate Change and the Environment; Dr. Stephanie Herring, NOAACalls to Action: Help out climate scientists from your couch! Climate scientists rely on accurate weather data to produce and test their models. But lots of historical weather data is still locked away in handwritten records from the 1800s, like old ships’ logs. Now, you can help rescue that data — by transcribing old temperature and weather logs! Check out the project Weather Rescue, which connects volunteers with documents that need transcribing. Especially good if you’re a pro at deciphering cursive handwriting… Talk about the weather! If an extreme weather event linked to climate change occurs in your region, talk to your friends and family about how climate change is affecting the weather they’re experiencing. One goal of scientists like Fredi Otto is to help get climate science into the conversation — and that only works if people HAVE that conversation. People like you! A call for redesigning American streets



September 6, 2018: A call for redesigning American streets


Duration: 00:21:09
Released: 2018

Open Episode in Spotify
Open Series in Spotify
In this week’s podcast we’ll explore how America’s streets can be redesigned to benefit bicyclists and pedestrians—and we’ll explain why doing so may even help mitigate the effects of climate change. A new study from Anne Lusk, research scientist in the Department of Nutrition at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, analyzed how bicyclists and pedestrians responded to various placements of trees along cycle tracks—barrier-protected bicycle-exclusive paths between the road and the sidewalk. The research shows that the placement of these trees can play an important role in how people walking and biking perceive traffic, pollution, heat, and even safety. But the benefits extend beyond just those using the street—and could even be a factor in mitigating the effects of climate change. These trees may make it more likely that people will bike—helping to reduce pollution. And increased greenery can also help cool cities, which often suffer from a heat island effect, which means they’re significantly warmer than more rural areas. Lusk says all of this highlights the need to re-think how we’re designing streets to encourage more people to walk and bike instead of drive.

It’s become clear to farmers and home gardeners alike that climate change is affecting the gardening landscape, literally. The climate is warming, pests are moving into different regions, and there’s a growing need for vegetable varieties that are resilient to the stresses of this new age.In the world of organic farming, the job of creating those new varieties falls to a plant breeder: someone who, often painstakingly, crosses plants until they create a new variety. Dr. Jim Myers, one of the most accomplished plant breeders in the country, has lots of experience with this.Myers created the Indigo Rose tomato, a strikingly purple variety with the same antioxidants as blueberries. He also created the green bean cultivar predominantly used by Oregon producers, and is debuting two new varieties of low-heat habanero peppers next month, dubbed “Mild Thing” and “Notta Hotta.”Myers joins Ira Flatow from Corvallis, Oregon, where he’s a professor of agricultural science at Oregon State University. They discuss his decades-long career in plant breeding and what he sees as the biggest challenges for the plant breeders of the future. Subscribe to this podcast. REGINA BARBER: Hey, Short Wavers. It’s Gina here with a request– follow us on whichever app you’re listening from. We love sharing cool and important science stories with you. [MUSIC PLAYING]

NATHAN ROTT: Hello, Gina.
BARBER: So, Nate, over the years, you’ve reported a ton on wildfires and fought some in a previous life, I heard.
ROTT: Yes, a previous, younger, more lithe life. Yes, that is correct.

BARBER: And Nate, it seems like a lot of the world is experiencing them right now. Like, fires are happening in France and Spain. Canada and even Oregon is fighting dozens of fires right now. So, with all of your expertise, riddle me this.

BARBER: Huh.
ROTT: –within those two sentences, Gina, there is so much nuance, and so, we’ll get into that.
ZEKE HAUSFATHER: There’s a lot of different regional trends that are underneath that.
ROTT: Yeah, so that’s Zeke Hausfather. He’s a climate scientist in California. And he says that, for example, in North American forests, like where we are, the trend is definitely more burning.
HAUSFATHER: The typical fire burns about three times more area than it did 30 years ago or 40 years ago, which is largely driven by changes in conditions. The vegetation is drier, and so when a spark catches, it’s more likely to burn a larger area.

BARBER: That’s so much.
ROTT: Yeah, it’s a lot, which means that in certain areas, there are more fires burning bigger and hotter, which, in some cases, means more smoke from those fires can travel a very long way and make a beautiful sunset, but muddy up a perfectly normal vacation.

ROTT: Yeah.

ROTT: [CHUCKLES] Vague is a very diplomatic way of putting it, Gina. And–
BARBER: Yeah.
ROTT: –there’s a reason for that. You know, scientists just don’t have a lot of long-term data on wildfire smoke exposure to give people definitive guidelines, which leaves a lot of people like you and me wondering how to go about their days when there’s a lot of smoke in the air.
[MUSIC PLAYING]
BARBER: So today on the show, what to do when the world’s on fire.
ROTT: We talk about the changing wildfire landscape, what’s driving the trends, and what you can do about it.
BARBER: You’re listening to Short Wave, the science podcast from NPR.
BARBER: OK, Nate, so you said earlier that wildfires are actually decreasing globally. This is just wild to me. Like, how is that possible?
ROTT: Yeah, I mean, OK, so when we say wildfires, that includes lots of different types of environments and vegetation– forests, yes, but also, you know, grasslands and shrublands and savanna. And as anyone who messed around with fireworks as a kid or had a little pyro streak maybe like me, you will know that fire burns a lot faster and quicker in lighter vegetation, like grasses, than it does in, like, a forest, right?
BARBER: Yeah.
ROTT: So most of the area–
BARBER: Yeah, definitely.
ROTT: –that burns every year are grasslands, shrublands, and savannas, not forests.
BARBER: OK.
ROTT: And so, the reason that, globally, there’s less land burned is largely because there’s less grasslands and shrublands and savannas burning mostly in Africa, which, you know, is a really big continent. So that brings down the global scale.
BARBER: I love this. This is, like, fascinating, these nuances. OK, so, now, there’s these two pretty bad forest fires in France and Spain. And–
ROTT: Yeah.
BARBER: –outside of these fires, is Europe another place where there are fewer fires recently?
ROTT: Well, honestly, Gina, this is, like, a really active area of research, like what are the trends in wildfire are in Europe. But when our producer–
BARBER: Yeah.
ROTT: –Berly McCoy spoke to Zeke Monday about the current fires, he said the area burned was higher than average for the European Union, so–
BARBER: OK.
ROTT: –not record-setting yet. Of course, that could change. But he said these fires are understandably getting a lot of media attention because there are two big fires burning at the same time near a lot of–
BARBER: Yeah.
ROTT: –people. So it might seem like a trend, but it might not necessarily be.
BARBER: So, I mean, could this be just, like, a normal fire year for Europe? I remember, like, four years ago, a big fire in Spain. Like, is this–
ROTT: Yeah.
BARBER: –just normal?
ROTT: Yeah, I mean, look, it could be. But, you know, Zeke pointed out that there is a trend that is related to many wildfires today in Europe and North America everywhere. The fires that are burning in Spain and France both coincided with an extreme heat wave.
BARBER: OK, I see where this is going.
ROTT: Yeah, climate change– don’t know if you’ve heard of it, small thing–
BARBER: Yeah.
ROTT: –happening globally.
BARBER: Yeah, the climate crisis, it’s like this cartoon villain, right? It’s very predictable.
ROTT: Yeah, well, unlike a generic cartoon villain, you know, it’s not easily vanquished by Captain Planet and his gang of trusted friends.
BARBER: Yes.
ROTT: Zeke says that rising temperatures nurture fires that might otherwise just die out. So, like, take Canada, for example.
HAUSFATHER: So, every one degree centigrade, or roughly two degrees Fahrenheit, of warming during the fire season in Canada– so May to September– is associated with an 80% increase in the amount of area burned that year.
BARBER: 80%– that’s a huge jump for just, like, a couple of degrees Fahrenheit.
ROTT: Yeah, it’s massive. And he says, since the 1960s, the fire season has warmed up about four degrees Fahrenheit on average. So–
BARBER: Wow.
ROTT: –that translates to a huge amount of burned area in Canada because when it’s warmer, things just dry out quicker, so there’s literally more fuel for the fire.
BARBER: So doesn’t this also have to do with humans not doing, like, prescribed burns to clear the underbrush?
ROTT: In the United States, yes, that’s definitely true. So, in many parts of the country, not just the Western US, forests are adapted to fire. In many cases, they need it ecologically. And, you know, Native communities used fires for centuries to forests, but since at least the 1930s, we’ve been suppressing forest fires, putting them out as quickly as we can.
BARBER: I mean, Nate, only you can prevent forest fires.
ROTT: Yes, God bless Smokey Bear. It’s not Smokey the Bear, Gina. It’s Smokey Bear. Don’t let the Forest Service come after you.
BARBER: I had no idea, honestly.
ROTT: Yeah. And look, like, Smokey’s slogan was great to protect people and homes and, you know, maybe some timber, but it’s not so great to keep fuel levels down in those forests.
HAUSFATHER: When fires do occur in those forests, there’s so much undergrowth that’s accumulated that the fires are much more catastrophic. They reach up into the canopy of the trees. They become what we call crown fires that actually kill the trees–
BARBER: Geez.
HAUSFATHER: –rather than what historically has happened in Western forests, where you have these low-level fires that kill the undergrowth, but don’t reach up and actually kill the trees. The boreal forest is a different beast.
ROTT: Yeah, and the boreal forests in Canada, the ones that are smoking up parts of the US right now, those have never needed prescribed burning in the same way.
HAUSFATHER: The boreal forest–
BARBER: Wow.
HAUSFATHER: –in Canada is 4 and 1/2 times the size of Texas. And so, historically–
BARBER: What?
HAUSFATHER: –when fires burn in those forests, they’re just allowed to burn themselves out. You know, they haven’t had the same history of fire suppression that we have in the US that has built up fuel.
ROTT: So what he’s kind of saying is, it is normal for these big fires to happen in Canada, but what’s not normal is how often these huge fires are happening.
BARBER: So, historically, how often is normal for them to burn?
ROTT: So, typically, in Canada’s western boreal forest, Zeke says big fires would happen, you know, once every 50 to 200 years.
BARBER: That is not happening right now.
ROTT: No, it is much more frequent. And–
BARBER: Yeah.
ROTT: –when we’re talking about boreal forests, you know, for you non-ecology nerds out there, you know, we’re talking about these dense forests that stretch across the Northern Hemisphere, and temperatures are rising at higher latitudes faster than they are closer to the equator.
HAUSFATHER: What we’re seeing now is considerably more frequent fires, because these areas that used to be much wetter– you know, much of the the northern boreal resembles a swamp– are now much drier because of higher temperatures.
ROTT: And it’s not necessarily that more fires are starting, you know, which, in both the US and Canada, is often caused by lightning, sometimes caused by people. It’s that a warmer climate is creating the conditions for fires to get going and burn a lot more vegetation when they do.
BARBER: OK, so I grew up in the Pacific Northwest, and there weren’t a lot of wildfires. And then I had my own kid, and then wildfires and smoke were just part of the summers. And honestly, I thought I was going to just, like, avoid all that and move to the East Coast.
ROTT: Yeah.
BARBER: And once I’m here, I’m not going to have any of that smoke.
ROTT: Yeah.
BARBER: But for listeners in the same boat as me– like, now, I’m inhaling this smoke– like, what are the recommendations for staying healthy?
ROTT: Well, so the biggest piece of advice I could give you, Gina, is to monitor the air quality to figure out your exposure to risk. So, in the US–
BARBER: OK.
ROTT: –there’s an air quality index for how polluted–
BARBER: Yeah.
ROTT: –the air is in a certain area. You know, it’s based on how many pollutants are in the air, and that includes particulate matter, these tiny little particles that are so small, they can get into your bloodstream.
BARBER: Oh, my gosh.
ROTT: You know, there’s been a lot of research that shows that it’s particularly risky for pregnant people. So I’d highly recommend people use AQI as kind of a quick pulse check to figure out how good the air quality is. It goes from green, where the air pollution isn’t a risk to people, all the way up to maroon, which means it’s a risk for everybody. And there is limited guidance for, you know, when you should limit outdoor activity, for example. But Lisa Patel, a pediatrician and environmental scientist at Stanford Medicine Children’s Health, says it may not be a good enough tool for wildfires.
LISA PATEL: These air quality guidelines were built off the burning of fossil fuels. There was a study that was done on children between zero to five that found that wildfire smoke is about 10 times as toxic. 10 times as many children showed up to the emergency room with respiratory complaints.
ROTT: And it’s not just kids, right? Like, inhaling that smoke can lead to inflammation, which is linked to cancer, to heart and lung disease, and to dementia.
BARBER: Oof. So, what else can we do to limit our exposure to wildfire smoke?
ROTT: Yeah, so spending more time inside, you know, though, I should say, you know, staying inside won’t totally keep you from being exposed, especially in older homes with a lot of drafts. But, you know, staying inside is one piece of advice– wearing a mask when you go outside, recirculating the air in your car, you know, so you’re not sucking air directly from outside into the car. And using an air filter indoors goes a long way. Lisa says you can make one with a HEPA filter duct taped to a box fan. I’ve actually been to places where they’re doing this in Missoula, where I grew up. They are creating them for people that can’t afford air filters in their house. For a few weeks in 1987, trash was temporarily headline news: a barge filled with waste that would no longer fit in New York City’s overflowing landfills spent months wandering up and down the East Coast with nowhere to dump its smelly, rotting cargo. The trash barge’s travels triggered a long overdue public rethink of the wisdom of sending all of our waste to landfills—including food. But fast forward more than thirty years, and food still takes up more space in American landfills than anything else. About 30 to 40 percent of food produced in the US gets thrown away, rather than eaten. What’s more, putting all that rotting food inside landfills produces a lot of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Our ancestors knew exactly what to do with food waste; the earliest descriptions of composting were written on clay tablets more than 4,000 years ago. So why didn’t the GarBarge kick off a composting craze? And why is it so hard for us to keep food waste out of landfills? This episode, Gastropod visits the future of food waste: the high-tech facilities as well as the innovative policies that promise to keep our discarded food out of landfills, keep methane from escaping into the atmosphere, and turn those food scraps into something useful. Can a state the size of California really keep 75 percent of its food waste out of landfills, as it has pledged to do by 2025—and what will happen if it does? Listen in for compost blow-dryers, fruit-sticker bingo, and a lot of microbes! A new study from Harvard T.H. Superfund sites are some of the most polluted areas in the country, containing highly toxic waste such as asbestos, lead, and dioxin. Cleaning them up, which follows a systematic, science-based process as required by law, can take decades.There are more than 1,300 of these sites across the US, from Florida’s Panhandle to the banks of the Rio Grande in New Mexico. They’re found in nearly every state, often near residential areas. The EPA estimates that 78 million people live within three miles of a Superfund site—nearly 1 in 4 Americans.But these waste dumps face a growing threat: the worsening effects of climate change. The EPA has determined that more than 300 Superfund sites are at risk of flooding. The actual number of flood-prone sites, however, may be more than twice that amount, according to a 2021 Government Accountability Office report. Floodwaters can move toxic waste into neighboring communities, which threatens drinking water, agriculture, and broader ecosystem health.Read more at sciencefriday.comTranscripts for each segment will be available after the show airs on sciencefriday.com. Extreme Heat Is the New Normal
New York Times Opinion, 08 28, 2026

Video (15:42)




Description
We filmed “A New Inferno,” the short documentary above, in Phoenix, one of the hottest cities in America, through some of the city’s hottest days of 2025, during one of the hottest years on record globally. On one of our production days, temperatures reached 118 while we were filming outside.
In the face of extreme heat, we documented firefighters and paramedics of the Phoenix Fire Department saving lives in real time. We wanted to call attention to a specialized technique of ice bag immersion for people facing life-threatening heat stroke. We hope that telling their story and showcasing the efficacy of this strategy will encourage wider adoption of this protocol across the country.
Yet this procedure is ultimately a stopgap, as firefighters do their best to adapt to the climate crisis in front of them. The underlying story of heat in Phoenix is one of broader, interlocking crises: homelessness and substance use disorders that are deeply entangled with urban heat, each amplifying the other, illustrating how climate change affects the disenfranchised most brutally.
With our film, we aim to reframe how the public thinks about heat: as an invisible, silent killer reshaping the rhythms of urban life.

How America’s hottest city is trying to cool down

Description
Can trees help save Phoenix from extreme heat?
Subscribe and turn on notifications 🔔 so you don’t miss any videos: http://goo.gl/0bsAjO
It’s time to stop looking at trees as a form of “beautification.” They are, instead, a living form of infrastructure, providing a variety of services that include stormwater management, air filtering, carbon sequestration, and, most importantly for a city like Phoenix, Arizona, they cool the environment around them.
Trees can lower neighborhood temperatures in three ways: 1) Their shade prevents solar radiation from hitting paved surfaces like concrete and asphalt, which absorb energy and rerelease it into the air as heat. 2) Their leaves pull heat from the immediate area in order to evapotranspirate water that’s drawn from the soil. And, 3) If you’re standing under one, a tree protects your body directly from the sun’s rays. If you’ve ever made a summer visit to a dry, hot city like Phoenix, you’ll know how important shade is for making any outdoor experiences tolerable.
As Phoenix deals with a rising frequency of extreme heat waves — which aren’t only deadly, but also cause worrisome spikes in energy demand — the city is looking to trees as part of its heat mitigation strategy. Phoenix isn’t devoid of trees, but they’re distributed unevenly across the city. A quick glance at a satellite image of the metro area reveals substantial green splotches in the north and east and brown ones in the south and west, where many lower-income neighborhoods are located.
So Phoenix recently pledged to reach “tree equity” by 2030, under an agreement with American Forests, a national tree organization. I visited Phoenix recently to take a look at the current state of the city’s urban forest. In this video, we use drone imagery and thermal cameras to understand how the urban design of the city contributes to extreme heat, and what it can do to cool down.

How melting glaciers contributed to the flooding disaster in the Himalayas


Transcript
AMNA NAWAZ: Welcome to the “News Hour.”
The scale of the disaster in the Himalayas is becoming clearer tonight after catastrophic flooding tore through parts of Nepal and neighboring Tibet.
Scientists now believe the disaster was likely triggered by the collapse of a glacier high in the mountains, unleashing a torrent of water, mud, and debris that swept away bridges, roads, and entire communities.
GEOFF BENNETT: President Trump today called the devastation in Nepal brutal.
The death toll stands at least 390, with more than 1,400 others still missing.
That’s as rescue crews race to reach survivors in some of the world’s most difficult terrain.
In the valleys that carve through the highest peaks in the world, villages are now buried in mud.
This is Nepal’s Nuwakot district.
Yesterday’s floods left behind a layer of sludge so high, it reached rooftops and trapped trucks as if in quicksand.
Survivors recounted the terror as it all unfolded without warning.
JANAK BAHADUR, Flood Survivor (through translator): It came in suddenly and exploded like a bomb.
The river looked small from a distance, but it suddenly started overflowing and swept through this place.
GEOFF BENNETT: Geological experts believe a glacier collapse some 30 miles north of Kathmandu was likely what caused the disaster.
These satellite images show the glacier along those snowy peaks there at the bottom before the collapse.
And this is what it looks like now, the surrounding rivers swollen by the floodwaters and debris rushing downstream.
Cell phone video showed the torrent starting to barrel toward this hydroelectric dam.
Within seconds, it bursts through the other side and engulfs the entire site, this border crossing between Nepal and Tibet, the autonomous region in China, now completely destroyed by the ensuing landslides.
Nepalese officials say the floods have swept away dozens of bridges and damaged some 25 miles of roads.
That, combined with the already treacherous terrain of the Himalayas, have made rescue efforts especially difficult.
Nepal’s army says it’s airlifted more than 100 people to safety using helicopters.
On the ground, crews trudge through knee-deep mud with the aid of search dogs to locate the missing, hoisting them onto their backs, many survivors transported to hospitals in Kathmandu.
But as the search grinds on, many families have no choice but to wait for news they fear may never come.
SUBINA TAMANG, Wife of Missing Man (through translator): All I want is that my husband comes back to me safely in one piece.
I do not want anything else.
CHAMINDI SHRESHTHA, Mother of Missing Man (through translator): My son is stuck in the floods.
He is a truck driver.
And he said he was driving.
There is no news of him.
We are not able to find out anything.
GEOFF BENNETT: The scale of this catastrophe is being felt across the region.
Officials in China say they’re searching for hundreds of people still missing in Tibet, where floodwaters stretched for miles across the vast plateau.
Authorities said a new lake was formed in the deluge.
A spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry vowed to send aid to Nepal, which has significantly fewer emergency resources than its neighbor.
LIN JIAN, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson (through translator): The mudslide has caused massive casualties and left many missing in both China and Nepal.
The two sides are having close communication and coordinating efforts for search-and-rescue.
GEOFF BENNETT: Among the missing, some 500 foreign nationals.
The U.S.
State Department this morning confirmed three Americans had been rescued, but as many as 90 may have been affected by the floods.
SADHGURU JAGGI VASUDEV, Indian Spiritual Leader (through translator): I wish to bring to your notice that there has been a terrible… GEOFF BENNETT: In an emotional message today, the Indian spiritual leader known as Sadhguru said a group had been on a holy pilgrimage in the area and got caught in the floods.
He said 22 of them were U.S.
citizens.
And for more on what caused the devastating floods, we’re joined now by Dan Shugar, who heads the waterSHED Lab at the University of Calgary.
Thanks for being with us.
DAN SHUGAR, waterSHED Lab Director, University of Calgary: Thank you.
GEOFF BENNETT: So scientists believe the deadly flood in Nepal may have started when a massive chunk of ice snapped off a glacier high in the Himalayas, unleashing this devastating cascade into the valley below.
Walk us through how that might have happened.
DAN SHUGAR: That was certainly our initial thought as to what happened based on the information that we had yesterday from some preliminary satellite information.
It’s changed a little bit since then, but the general story is still the same.
At about just under 5,000 meters elevation is a glacier that in the satellite imagery that we saw yesterday essentially two days ago was there, yesterday was gone, and the flood resulted downstream.
Since then, we have found that glacier ice - - chunk of glacier ice that essentially disappeared downstream was part of a much larger mass of bedrock, so a gigantic chunk of the mountainside that collapsed, essentially exploding as it descended a vertical kilometer to the valley bottom, melting all that ice, and then flowing out and generating the floods that we saw in those horrific videos.
GEOFF BENNETT: What makes that part of the Himalayas so vulnerable?
DAN SHUGAR: That’s a good question.
I suppose it would be a couple of things, one, incredibly steep topography and then huge relief, so massive differences between the low points and the high points, lots of glaciers, lots of glacial lakes, which weren’t an issue in this particular disaster, but certainly in other ones.
A lot of seismic activity.
The Gorkha earthquake wasn’t that long ago, and we saw very similar sort of disasters unfold, in fact, just on the other side of this mountain.
And the human part of that equation, I think, is important.
Unlike in Western North America, in much of the Himalaya, you have settlements in these incredibly high, narrow valleys that essentially are putting people and infrastructure and livelihoods at risk when these landslides or these floods come down.
GEOFF BENNETT: The other human element at play, it strikes me, is climate change.
What role does climate change play here?
What can scientists say with confidence about the connection between rising temperatures, retreating glaciers, and disasters like this one?
DAN SHUGAR: We can speak in generalities, because it’s a little bit hard to speak about the specific event just yet because we haven’t done any sort of attribution study.
As temperatures rise, glaciers will melt, will thin vertically, destabilizing the valley walls that they formerly were sort of help – hoping – or helping to hold up.
Additionally, as air temperatures rise, the permafrost is changing, and so permafrost is just ground that remains frozen year-round year after year.
But in some areas, both at high altitudes, but also in the north, permafrost is destabilizing because of warming temperatures.
And that can cause large landslides like this as well.
And then a third factor, I think would be changes in precipitation patterns, not only in terms of intensity, but in terms of when during the year they occurred.
Water can get underneath the glaciers, allowing them to slide a little bit more rapidly, any number of ways that that extra water can sort of enhance or increase the likelihood of one of these kinds of events.
GEOFF BENNETT: Dan, what lessons can be learned from this disaster?
DAN SHUGAR: I think that these landscapes, these steep mountain landscapes, are continually evolving due to climate change.
And the global community, not just the government of Nepal or China or India, need – the global community, we need to be stepping up to help mitigate these risks and to enhance the resiliency of people living in these environments that are subject to these disasters that, when there’s a climate change link, we in the rich West are largely responsible for.
GEOFF BENNETT: Dan Shugar with the waterSHED Lab at the University of Calgary, thanks for joining us this evening.
DAN SHUGAR: Thank you.

10:15 · Rising temperatures lead to double-whammy droughts and heatwaves.
10:19 · And that leaves forest floors full of dried-up plants that serve as fuel for wildfires to ignite— spreading faster, farther, and more often.
10:28 · Plus, Earth’s polar ice caps are melting, transforming solid ice to slush and seawater.

10:38 · So while some communities are already facing a problem of not enough water, others are facing a problem of too much.

World Weather Attribution — understanding climate change and extreme weather
World Weather Attribution, 11 13, 2023

Video (5:59)




Description
When an extreme weather event occurs, people often ask: is climate change to blame?
For decades, climate scientists have answered that question in general terms – that as the planet warms, we can expect many of these weather events to become more frequent and extreme.
But in recent years, advances in attribution science have allowed researchers to answer the question in much greater detail.
Founded in 2015 by Dr. Friederike Otto and Dr. Geert Jan van Oldenborgh, World Weather Attribution scientists quantify how climate change influences the intensity and likelihood of an extreme weather event. They often do this using weather data and computer modelling, and often immediately in the aftermath of the extreme event.
To encourage actions that will make communities and countries more resilient to future extreme weather events, World Weather Attribution studies also evaluate how existing vulnerability worsened the impacts of the extreme weather event.
To learn more about World Weather Attribution or to view our studies, go to https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/
Follow us on Twitter: https://twitter.com/WWAttribution
Film produced by Geoff Marsh.

10 Years After Flint, The Fight To Replace Lead Pipes Continues



10 Years After Flint, The Fight To Replace Lead Pipes Continues


Duration: 00:13:12
Released: 2024
Series: Short Wave

Open Episode in Spotify
Open Series in Spotify
Ten years ago, Flint, Mich. switched water sources to the Flint River. The lack of corrosion control in the pipes caused lead to leach into the water supply of tens of thousands of residents. Pediatrician Mona Hanna-Attisha recognized a public health crisis in the making and gathered data proving the negative health impact on Flint’s young children. In doing so, she and community organizers in Flint sparked a national conversation about lead in the U.S. water system that persists today. Today on the show, host Emily Kwong and science correspondent Pien Huang talk about the state of Flint and other cities with lead pipes. Efforts to replace these pipes hinge on proposed changes to the EPA’s Lead and Copper Rule. Have questions or comments for us to consider for a future episode? Email us at shortwave@npr.org — we’d love to hear from you!See pcm.adswizz.com for information about our collection and use of personal data for sponsorship and to manage your podcast sponsorship preferences.NPR Privacy Policy




Transcript
EMILY KWONG, HOST:
You’re listening to SHORT WAVE…
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
KWONG: …From NPR.
Hey, SHORT WAVErs. Emily Kwong here. So 10 years ago, Dr. Mona Hanna-Attisha was a pediatrician at Hurley Medical Center, living in Flint, Mich. The city was near bankruptcy, and to save money, Flint decided to switch water sources from Lake Huron to the Flint River on April 25, 2014.
MONA HANNA-ATTISHA: We had greenish and brownish water, and it smelled weird, and it was giving people rashes, and they were losing hair.
KWONG: And families in Flint kept telling her, something’s not right with the water.
HANNA-ATTISHA: They were asking, was it OK to use this tap water to mix their baby’s formula?
KWONG: State and city officials said there was nothing to worry about. And Mona told her patients the same thing.
HANNA-ATTISHA: For a year and a half, I was telling my patients that, of course, everything’s OK. Like, how can - how could our drinking water not be OK? Like, this is America. It is the 21st century. All the folks in charge, despite all these concerns, were saying everything was OK.
KWONG: But everything was not OK.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
KWONG: Over a glass of wine, one of Mona’s high school friends who used to work at the EPA implored her to look into this issue.
HANNA-ATTISHA: And she literally stared me down. She was like, Mona, it doesn’t have corrosion control.
KWONG: The Flint water system lacked something important called corrosion control. Corrosion control changes the chemistry of the water to make it less likely to leach lead from the pipes. And without that corrosion control, the lead in Flint’s pipes got into the water supply.
HANNA-ATTISHA: And that is the moment that I heard about the possibility of lead being in the water, and that’s the moment my life changed.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
HANNA-ATTISHA: We need water to survive. It’s a medical and public health necessity. And the younger you are, the more our bodies are made up of water.
KWONG: The CDC says that no amount of lead in children is safe. For kids, lead poisoning can have serious consequences. It can damage their brains and nervous systems, causing learning and behavioral problems and issues with hearing and speech down the line. Mona saw a crisis in the making and began looking for any data she could on kids’ blood lead levels. And in September 2015, a year and a half after that water switch, she went public with her results…
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
HANNA-ATTISHA: This research is concerning. These results are concerning.
KWONG: …Showing that the number of children in Flint with elevated levels of lead in their blood had gone up.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
HANNA-ATTISHA: And when our national guiding organizations tell us primary prevention is the most important thing and that lead poisoning is potentially irreversible, then we have to say something.
KWONG: At first, the state dismissed her findings. But Mona Hanna-Attisha was right. It’s been 10 years, and the city’s water quality has improved. Flint switched back to Lake Huron, and thousands of lead pipes have been replaced.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
KWONG: But there is still a lot of work to be done in Flint to replace them all. And the truth of the matter is there are cities and towns all over the country facing their own issues with water quality, aging infrastructure and inadequate laws that don’t protect people from lead poisoning. Flint is an example of how speaking up with science can turn a crisis around. So 10 years on, we’re bringing in science reporter Pien Huang to focus on those trying to stop another crisis in another city - Chicago. You’re listening to SHORT WAVE, the science podcast from NPR.
(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)
KWONG: So to help us understand the emerging lead crisis in Chicago, we’ve got science reporter Pien Huang in the studio. Hi, Pien.
PIEN HUANG, BYLINE: Hey, Emily.
KWONG: Hello.
HUANG: It’s great to see you.
KWONG: Good to see you, too.
HUANG: And it’s also so cool that you got to talk to Dr. Mona.
KWONG: It was so cool. And Mona is still on the front lines of trying to make life better for kids in Flint, where more than two-thirds of children live in poverty. She’s the founding director of the Pediatric Public Health Initiative, which connects families to programs and services to alleviate that poverty. One of them, Rx Kids, gives new moms in Flint a no-strings-attached check of $7,500.
HANNA-ATTISHA: In a city that so many folks know as a city that failed kids is a city that’s learning, that’s leading with science, that’s leading with prevention to promote kind of the health and development of kids by boldly kind of eradicating infant poverty.
KWONG: I asked her what she thought of the situation in Chicago, and she didn’t hold back on her thoughts and feelings.
HANNA-ATTISHA: Chicago has a long history of lead advocates, but also a long history of lead misuse. Chicago continued to use lead in their service lines until it was restricted in 1986 and built into the code - if you wanted water from the main, you were mandated to use lead in your plumbing. So Chicago has the most lead lines than any other city in our nation. And, you know, if you respect the science of lead, if you understand that it has no safe level, lead should not be the straw that is delivering our drinking water to so many children and families.
HUANG: And, Emily, that lead is still in the water even now. So there was a recent JAMA Pediatrics study that found that most children under the age of 6 in Chicago are probably drinking leaded water.
KWONG: Most children - wow. OK. And that research was spearheaded by Benjamin Huynh at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, right?
HUANG: Yeah, exactly. Yeah. So he is an assistant professor of environmental health and engineering there, and his focus is on data science and environmental justice. In this case in particular, he’s got personal ties to the topic.
BENJAMIN HUYNH: So I’m from Chicago. And, you know, those of us in Chicago, we’ve known for a long time that most of our pipes are made out of lead.
HUANG: Including the house that his parents live in. In Chicago, there are around 400,000 homes that have lead pipes connecting the water main to the house. And Ben wanted to know, what does that actually mean for people drinking water from those taps?
KWONG: So how did Ben figure this out, like, that so many kids were drinking leaded water? What data did he use?
HUANG: Yeah. So it’s rooted in the fact that Chicago has a free water testing program. It’s for people who want to test their tap water for lead. And so far, this program has run about 38,000 tests. People have voluntarily collected water samples from their home, sent them to the city. And while these tests are free, Ben says not everybody uses them.
HUYNH: We found that the people who took those tests - they’re more likely to be in white neighborhoods, like, wealthier neighborhoods, and also neighborhoods that are less likely to have lead in the first place.
KWONG: Oh, so there was a huge sampling bias in this data.
HUANG: Right, exactly. And he had to correct for that. So he took that data, and he combined it with other sources of data, so data on local health, demographics, survey results on how many people use tap versus filtered or bottled water as their main drinking source. And then with the help of machine learning, he and his team figured out an estimate. They figured out that 68% of young children in Chicago are drinking tap water with lead.
HUYNH: On top of that, you know, we’re seeing Black and Hispanic neighborhoods are more likely to have lead exposure, but also less likely to be tested for lead.
KWONG: But the federal government does allow for some lead to be in the water. So at what point does the Environmental Protection Agency say, this is too much lead in the water - this is the cutoff?
HUANG: The EPA does have something called the Lead and Copper Rule. And this rule sets an action level for lead at 15 parts per billion.
KWONG: OK.
HUANG: And when water systems find that amount of lead in the water, they’re supposed to initiate that corrosion control that we mentioned earlier.
KWONG: So is Chicago in compliance with this 15-parts-per-billion limit?
HUANG: Yeah. I mean, the city says that it is, and they’ve done everything that they’re supposed to be doing.
KWONG: Sure.
HUANG: But there are other places that might not be.
KWONG: OK.
HUANG: I talked to Elizabeth Southerland. She’s formally with the EPA. And she says that audits from the agency actually showed that in some 90% of these cases where there are excess levels of lead in the water, those cases never even got reported to the federal government.
ELIZABETH SOUTHERLAND: This was probably the worst reported and enforced regulation in the history of the drinking water program.
HUANG: Yeah. And many researchers and advocates say the rule was weak and inadequate. Now even the EPA itself says that those regulations need to change. So last year, the EPA proposed the Lead and Copper Rule improvements, and those are expected to be finalized by October this fall.
KWONG: OK. I’m pulling up their website now. So let’s see what could happen if these proposed changes to the Lead and Copper Rule were to take effect. One proposed rule change is that every water system in the country produce a map of where their lead pipes are. That could be huge.
HUANG: Yeah, totally.
KWONG: Also on this list are calls for improving water sampling and lowering that lead action level from 15 parts per billion to 10 parts per billion. OK.
HUANG: There are some people who think that it should be even less than that, but that would significantly lower the trigger level for lead.
KWONG: OK. And then the last thing - ah, requiring the vast majority of water systems to replace all their lead pipes within the next 10 years.
HUANG: And many people are saying, because the lead protections for the drinking water haven’t really been working, this is what we really need to fix the problem. But you said the vast majority, and I want to…
KWONG: Yeah.
HUANG: …Point that out, because that’s a really important point, because in that proposed rule, Chicago gets an exemption because it simply has too many pipes. The regulation, as it’s proposed, is really concerned with what’s realistic and feasible. And so what the EPA is saying is that it’s realistic to expect a city to replace around 10,000 lead service lines a year, and this is based on what other cities have already done. So since most cities have under 100,000 pipes, they should be able to make that deadline. But Chicago, with its 400,000 lead pipes, would get around 40 years or more to switch out their pipes.
KWONG: Wow.
HUANG: And that 40-year timeline has community advocates, like Chakena Perry with the Natural Resources Defense Council, pretty upset.
CHAKENA PERRY: That’s decades, that’s generations of children and adults, you know, consuming lead-contaminated water. It’s incomprehensible to tell a resident that they have to wait that long for safe drinking water.
HUANG: Chakena and others are really pushing for the EPA to close up those exemptions when they issue the final rule in the fall.
KWONG: So to be determined, really, how this rule might impact Chicago in the long run.

For a few weeks in 1987, trash was temporarily headline news: a barge filled with waste that would no longer fit in New York City’s overflowing landfills spent months wandering up and down the East Coast with nowhere to dump its smelly, rotting cargo. The trash barge’s travels triggered a long overdue public rethink of the wisdom of sending all of our waste to landfills—including food. But fast forward more than thirty years, and food still takes up more space in American landfills than anything else. About 30 to 40 percent of food produced in the US gets thrown away, rather than eaten. What’s more, putting all that rotting food inside landfills produces a lot of methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Our ancestors knew exactly what to do with food waste; the earliest descriptions of composting were written on clay tablets more than 4,000 years ago. So why didn’t the GarBarge kick off a composting craze? And why is it so hard for us to keep food waste out of landfills? This episode, Gastropod visits the future of food waste: the high-tech facilities as well as the innovative policies that promise to keep our discarded food out of landfills, keep methane from escaping into the atmosphere, and turn those food scraps into something useful. Can a state the size of California really keep 75 percent of its food waste out of landfills, as it has pledged to do by 2025—and what will happen if it does? Listen in for compost blow-dryers, fruit-sticker bingo, and a lot of microbes! Mexico’s Riviera Maya has been particularly affected, with the influx reaching thousands of tonnes of seaweed each day.
As the algae decomposes on beaches, it can release toxic gases, raising health concerns for residents and tourists. Scientists also warn that the accumulation of sargassum can damage seagrass ecosystems and affect beach stability.
The crisis is putting pressure on Mexico’s tourism industry, while the Mexican Navy has stepped up efforts to collect the seaweed before it reaches the shore.
But some businesses are looking at sargassum differently.
Companies including Carbonwave and Sargablock are developing ways to transform the invasive algae into products such as bio-fertilizers, footwear and construction materials.
Could an environmental crisis become a new source of sustainable materials?

Transcript
0:04 · [music] Welcome to Inside Latin America and to Mexico’s Riviera Maya. For the last decade, growing amounts of algae called sargassum have been washing up on beaches across the Caribbean, transforming once pristine coastlines and threatening the communities that depend on them.
0:25 · From the beaches of Puerto Rico to the fishing villages of the Dominican Republic, this phenomenon is taking a toll. And 2026 brought record quantities with more than 12 million tons detected across the region. But where is it all coming from and why now?
0:42 · This is the Sargasso Sea. Scientists say around 2010, changing currents began moving seaweed from here into warmer waters, forming the Great Atlantic Sargasso Belt, a vast band of floating algae stretching from West Africa across the Atlantic. Then, nutrient pollution, including fertilizer runoff carried by rivers, helped fuel its explosive growth.
1:06 · Experts agree the regional response still doesn’t match the scale of the problem. But with so much sargassum arriving, governments are being forced to act while private citizens are looking to upcycle this seaweed in an effort to turn this new reality into an opportunity.
1:25 · 9,000 tons a day. That’s how much sargassum washed up on Mexico’s Caribbean coast at the height of this year’s season.
1:34 · With its main tourist beaches under threat, the Mexican government has invested resources in tackling the problem.
1:41 · It enlisted the Navy in a process that starts with sea monitoring.
1:45 · Once blooms are located, especially designed vessels collect as much as they can.
1:51 · Barriers redirect what the ships miss, and divers work daily setting up additional nets and anchoring them beneath the surface.
2:00 · Every part of this process is extremely labor-intensive. If this ship has to be continuously repositioning itself so it can drag in all that sargassum. Once it’s full, it will go back to land and it will have to all be unloaded again before being taken to a processing plant.
2:17 · The goal is to keep the sargassum from reaching the beaches where growing evidence shows prolonged exposure to the decomposing seaweed can be toxic.
2:26 · And if you were to like hang around it for a long time, it would probably cause like respiratory distress and some other issues, but um in some places in the Caribbean, like it’s it’s very strong and it persists for weeks at a time and they are actually seeing adverse human health effects from the hydrogen sulfide.
2:41 · But removing sargassum is also expensive.
2:44 · Putting this option out of reach for many island nations in the Caribbean. The result is beaches that look like this. And when beaches become unusable, people whose livelihoods depend on tourism and fishing suffer, too.
2:59 · People come here, see this, and turn right around and leave.
3:05 · From Guadeloupe to Puerto Rico, more than 70% of people in the Caribbean live along the coast and depend on it to survive. And experts agree, without a joint international approach to sargassum and soon, the human and economic toll will only grow.
3:22 · This phenomenon can fundamentally change how people interact with the beach. For more on that, we spoke to Brigitta van Tussenbroek, a biologist with Mexico’s National Autonomous University, who’s been researching how sargassum is affecting communities along the coasts.
3:38 · Well, if you just think of the village community, of course, their connection with the sea is getting less because you don’t want to go to the beach on the Sunday afternoon with your family when you’ve got the what the amounts of sargassum there. If it’s a fishing community, um it’s more difficult for the boats to go out. Of course, for the tourist industry, it’s a disaster. And a lot of them, the tourist complex which have money, they can attend it to a certain degree. They can put up barriers.
4:08 · They can put small boats which collect the sargassum. They can try to replenish the beach which is eroded.
4:15 · You just mentioned erosion. Can you tell me a little bit about how sargassum is having an effect on what’s already a problem?
4:23 · Sargassum just being there causes erosion. Then sometimes bad practices. So, they remove the sargassum from the beach, but they take a lot of sand with it, which is another problem. And the other problem the major, I think, which I think was one of the major problem because it’s my area of research, it kills the sea grasses in the nearshore. And sea grasses are very important to maintain stable beaches.
4:49 · Do you think of sargassum as a plague?
4:51 · It’s a marvelous seaweed. I I’m still amazed by it. It’s a a seaweed which spends its whole life floating in the ocean. It forms these enormous rafts in the open sea. And the open sea is a desert, basically, for a lot of organisms. And then in the middle of the desert, you have this really biodiverse a raft with small critters, with a lot of bacteria, with epibionts which which grow on the sargassum. It’s beautiful.
5:23 · But having these huge masses of biomass decaying, getting on the beach, and then getting into the sea, it it causes a enormous disequilibrium of of whole life here in these systems.
5:36 · We’ve spent the last few days looking at all the efforts on various different scales of trying to get rid of the sargassum, take it out of the sea, uh clean it from the beaches. It feels like a titanic effort.
5:49 · I think at least the people who make the decisions I I think they still don’t understand the scale they have to work at. But we should do 100 times more or 1,000 times more. So, it should be so much more and I think this should be a really, uh, coherent strategy of managing the sargassum.
6:09 · Are you concerned?
6:10 · Well, I think it’s very difficult to be positive in the in the scenario, isn’t that?
6:16 · Because, as I say, most likely, um, this is not going to stop. This ecosystem is already damaged, uh, beyond the level I won’t ever see it recovering.
6:29 · So, I think we we have to be realistic in this this scenario and I think it it’s very difficult to be realistic, of course, because it it doesn’t look very nice. But, either really scale up a lot and invert a lot and and I really try to diminish the quantity of sargassum getting to the shore or adapt.
6:50 · But what does adapting look like? For a series of entrepreneurs in this region, the answer lies in turning this sargassum into products that can have life beyond the sea. Today’s sargassum harvest in Puerto Morelos, on Mexico’s Caribbean coast, ready to be processed and turned into bio-fertilizer. It’s a time-sensitive operation. Tons of seaweed must be weighed, cleaned, and pressed before it starts to decompose.
7:21 · Carbonwave is a company specializing in upcycling sargassum, filtering it in multiple steps to extract nutrients that boost crop yields and reduce the need for chemical fertilizer. After years of development, its creators say they have finally secured export agreements with the US, Colombia, and Ecuador.
7:40 · We already prove that sargassum can be turned into something that is reliable financially that can create incomes, right? That can create economy along the communities here.
7:54 · In fact, the process sargassum that Carbonwave doesn’t use for agricultural products ends up on people’s feet. Sargasso Sandals mixes sargassum powder with EVA foam, the same material Nike and Adidas use in sneakers to make its soles. Each pair is between 10 and 15% sargassum.
8:14 · This is the fiber that I need.
8:16 · And not far from Carbonwave’s plant, Omar Vasquez is using sargassum to make building blocks.
8:22 · Sargablock is an artisanal process. Each block contains 40% sargassum. The rest is other organic materials. They can make up to 6,500 blocks per day [music] using some 40 tons of sargassum. Sargablock says they’ve already donated 21 small homes made of this material to poor families in this community. And they say interest in this product is growing, certainly locally. This truck is going to a local business around here that’s just starting a construction project.
8:54 · But Omar dreams of taking this product far beyond Mexico’s coasts.
8:59 · And I went to Africa, I went to Ghana, and the problem that they have with sargassum it’s major. Nobody talks about those countries because they don’t have the money that we have in Mexico because tourism they don’t go there as here. So, where I see myself bringing Sargablock all over the world and donating houses to all over the people.
9:17 · In Mexico alone, at least 200 projects are now looking for ways to turn a growing environmental problem into an economic opportunity. And while none of these solutions can single-handedly absorb the millions of tons of sargassum washing ashore each year, they are showing that this unwanted seaweed may have value beyond the beach.
9:40 · Governments and citizens alike are rushing to adapt the best they can to a phenomenon that is no longer just a seasonal nuisance, but rather an increasingly permanent fixture of coastal communities along the Caribbean. Thanks for watching Inside Latin America. Now back to Doha with more news.

Description
Wildfire smoke can carry thousands of living microorganisms, like bacteria and fungi, across long distances. Some of them could potentially infect humans. With wildfires on the rise, experts are studying the risk this poses to our health.

Transcript
0:01 · [Narrator] Wildfire smoke is loaded with harmful particles like charred plant matter, incinerated materials, and noxious gases. But it’s also carrying stuff that’s alive, thousands of teeny-tiny microorganisms like bacteria and fungi.
0:15 · But why doesn’t the heat from a wildfire kill all these microorganisms?
0:19 · Well, not all parts of a wildfire are hot.
0:23 · When we look at fire on the scale of a microorganism, there are likely pockets of cold air, areas that are not being burned at all.
0:32 · [Narrator] In those tiny pockets of cooler air, microorganisms can catch rides on bits of carbon, or water vapor, rise high into the atmosphere and travel long distances. And some could potentially infect humans. Some health experts are already noticing a concerning relationship between wildfire smoke exposure and rates of infection. One study in California found an uptick in fungal infections after wildfires within a 200-mile radius of hospitals. And climate change is making wildfires more intense and more impactful.
1:08 · Compared to the yearly average in the 1970s, the average wildfire season in the US is now 105 days longer, burns six times the number of acres and has three times as many large fires.
1:21 · Fires are affected by dry conditions and warmer conditions. Climate change is causing more of those extremes. More extreme conditions, more extreme wildfires. They go together, hand by hand.
1:34 · [Narrator] Though there are still many unknowns, risk is growing for more people.
1:40 · We would expect that we’re all just gonna become exposed on a regular basis. We’d have to look out for that in places that we wouldn’t normally be on the lookout. (gentle music)

Description
A first animated video in the 6-part Mold in the Home Video Series. It is an introduction to the series and explains when mold in the home rises to the level of a problem that must be addressed.
The Mold in the Home Video Series is created by the Environmental Health Investigations Branch of the California Department of Public Health. It is designed to answer basic questions about mold in the home using plain language in English and Spanish.

If you need additional information, or are having difficulty accessing this content, please contact askehib@cdph.ca.gov to request this information in an alternate format


Transcript

Intro
0:06 · Mold is in the air everywhere but you can’t see it It is not an issue until mold in your home finds water and starts to grow.
0:15 · Water can come into the home through roofing problems, plumbing leaks, bathroom moisture, and air gaps around windows and doors.


Signs of Mold Problem
0:26 · You have a problem when mold appears near a leak or other dampness in the home.
0:31 · Signs of a mold problem include the smell of mold.
0:35 · Mold has a musty odor.
0:38 · Sometimes you can’t see the mold because it is hidden behind wall paper, dry wall, or paneling, or is on the underside of carpets.
0:48 · The smell lets you know that it is an important problem.
0:52 · If someone cleans or paints over the mold, it will return.
0:56 · This is because the water problem causing mold to grow is not fixed.


Prevention of Mold
1:04 · Mold is common around bathroom tiles, windows, showers, and sinks.
1:09 · It can be hard to keep these damp places completely free of it But you can usually prevent this mold from growing by cleaning it regularly and increasing the air flow.
1:21 · For more information, see the next videos in this series.
1:25 · Visit the CA Department of Public Health’s website cdph.ca.gov/Mold for information about mold in the home.

Your pantry’s sweetest ingredient has an extremely bitter history. The sap-producing grass known as sugarcane has been grown and enjoyed by humans for at least 10,000 years, but it was only relatively recently that it went from a luxury to an everyday ingredient—a change that also triggered genocide, slavery, and the invention of modern racism. In this episode, how the Crusades got Europeans addicted to the sweet stuff, and how that appetite deforested southern Europe and kicked off the trade in enslaved Africans, before decimating indigenous populations in the New World and codifying racism into law. It’s a dark story that involves Christopher Columbus’ mistress, the early human rights advocate whose campaign to save indigenous people encouraged the horrors of the transatlantic slave trade, and a trip to southern Louisiana, where we met Black sugarcane farmers to explore sugar’s troubling legacy there. Most of the 600 billion pounds of waste that Americans produce every year ends up in landfills. All that trash can have huge impacts on the environment. But modern landfills have found a new use for all that trash — they’re turning it into energy. In spite of their reputation as “dumps,” these landfills are feats of engineering, more akin to construction sites.
One of North America’s biggest landfills lies on the outskirts of Las Vegas. The Apex Landfill is not only one of the country’s largest, it’s also one of the busiest. Why don’t we just burn our trash
DW Planet A, 08 13, 2021

Video (10:45)




Description
Waste to energy plants are seen as green innovations for countries where landfills dominate, as they reduce methane and generate renewable energy. But will these incinerators really make our trash problems go up in flames?
We’re destroying our environment at an alarming rate. But it doesn’t need to be this way. Our new channel Planet A explores the shift towards an eco-friendly world — and challenges our ideas about what dealing with climate change means. We look at the big and the small: What we can do and how the system needs to change. Every Friday we’ll take a truly global look at how to get us out of this mess.
Read More (Links):
Open burning: https://theconversation.com/health-crisis-up-to-a-billion-tonnes-of-waste-potentially-burned-in-the-open-every-year-152778
Waste around the world: https://datatopics.worldbank.org/what-a-waste/trends_in_solid_waste_management.html
Waste to energy as a solution (IEA): https://www.iea.org/articles/will-energy-from-waste-become-the-key-form-of-bioenergy-in-asia
Waste to energy as a solution (Project Drawdown): https://drawdown.org/solutions/waste-to-energy/technical-summary

0:00 Intro
0:39 Why we need better waste management
2:00 Waste to energy
6:04 The Waste Hierarchy
6:51 A waste solution for the Global South?

Transcript

Intro
0:01 · These skiers are all here because of trash.
0:05 · That’s because underneath this slope is a huge garbage incineration plant.
0:10 · It processes 400,000 metric tons of waste a year and turns it into energy and heat for Copenhagen.
0:18 · It also recycles 90% of the city’s metal waste.
0:22 · Some say such incineration plants could be key for solving our global trash problem.
0:28 · But is that true?
0:30 · Or are we going to end up just getting burned?


Why we need better waste management
0:39 · Globally, we produce over two billion tons of household waste annually, with high income countries generating an outsized amount compared to their populations.
0:50 · 37% of global waste ends up in landfills, polluting groundwater and producing methane.
0:57 · Less than 20% of the world’s trash is recycled or composted.
1:02 · In the Global South many people have no access to trash collection, and it often ends up in rivers — a primary source of ocean plastic.
1:12 · To get rid of as much trash as possible, as fast as possible, around one billion tons of waste are openly burned every year.
1:22 · “Open burning generates high levels of black carbon, which is soot, which has a really strong global warming effect.”
1:31 · Zoë Lenkiewicz is one of the founding members of Wasteaid, and has been a waste manager for over 20 years.
1:38 · “It also generates dioxins and furans, which are known to cause cancer.
1:41 · All of this is going into the local air, wherever people are burning waste.”
1:48 · Women are more directly impacted, as they are often responsible for disposing of household waste.
1:53 · Burning trash this way is a serious problem. But done differently, there are advantages to it.


Waste to energy
2:01 · Here’s where controlled burning, aka incineration, comes in.
2:04 · Incinerators first appeared where it was hard to landfill, in London in 1874, then in New York City, in 1885.
2:12 · “The incineration process itself, it reduces the volume of the waste [by] 90 percent.”
2:19 · Ella Stengler is the managing director of the umbrella organization for European waste to energy operators.
2:25 · “And it fulfills the kind of sanitary task because it destroys the pollutants which are embedded in the waste.”
2:32 · The generated heat can also be turned into energy. It’s called, unsurprisingly, waste to energy.
2:38 · In the US, where there’s a lot of space and cheap energy in the form of oil, waste to energy wasn’t so competitive, and many plants were closed.
2:46 · But more and more plants were built in the EU.
2:50 · Today they provide power to 18 million Europeans, and heat to 15 million.
2:56 · They’re a common waste management option for countries like Denmark and the Netherlands, which have almost completely eliminated landfilling.
3:05 · Environmental organizations see potential in waste to energy as a transition step toward a more circular economy, especially in countries without much space, that need more energy.
3:18 · Here’s how the plants work: The garbage is dumped into a big pit — from there it’s fed into the furnaces.
3:25 · They burn extremely hot, and the waste is reduced in a matter of minutes.
3:30 · The heat from the fires generates steam, which turns turbines to create electricity.
3:35 · The steam can also be used for heating.
3:38 · The 10% that doesn’t burn is called bottom ash, and metals can be recovered from it.
3:44 · The rest can then be used as construction material.
3:50 · So the process reduces the volume of waste, creates energy, and part of the residue can even be recycled.
3:58 · What’s not to love?
4:01 · Well, there are a few reasons why the world isn’t full of waste to energy plants with ski slopes on top.
4:07 · One of those reasons is fly ash, which is everything caught by the filters.
4:11 · It needs to be disposed of in a hazardous waste facility.
4:15 · Another reason is cost.
4:16 · “If there would be a waste to energy plant built, it should be equipped with a state-of-the-art technology, which is expensive.
4:27 · And you need to train the staff to properly operate it and also authorities to monitor it.”
4:33 · Even without ski slopes, waste to energy plants can cost over one billion US dollars to build.
4:39 · Without the latest technology and monitoring, pollution can reach unsafe levels, and impact people living nearby.
4:47 · And they also emit a lot of CO2: in the EU, around 52 million tonnes per year.
4:56 · That’s like 430,000 cars each driving a million kilometers.
5:02 · “Policymakers and industries put incineration in the same type of energy group as renewables, like wind or solar or even nuclear.”
5:15 · This is Tatiana Lujan.
5:16 · She leads the plastics team for ClientEarth, and is also working to implement the EU’s circular economy directive.
5:24 · “But when you look at the greenhouse gas emissions of incineration, they’re actually pretty close to coal and gas, and way far from wind, solar, nuclear.
5:36 · A study commissioned by ClientEarth found that controlled incineration generates between 59 and 73% of the emissions that coal would.
5:44 · Classifying this energy as renewable can divert funding from more sustainable waste management technologies like recycling.
5:51 · So, where it can be correctly built and managed, controlled incineration is better than a landfill – but it’s by far not the cleanest option to handle waste, no matter how much energy is won.


The Waste Hierarchy
6:04 · Have a look at this “waste hierarchy pyramid” – bear with me, it’s less complicated than it looks.
6:09 · At the very bottom of the pyramid is open burning or dumping, the worst possible way to get rid of trash.
6:15 · Disposal without energy recovery is next, so landfilling or incineration without energy generation.
6:22 · Then here’s where waste to energy, which is an umbrella term for a few different methods, comes in.
6:29 · Then comes recycling.
6:31 · Even better is to re-use things, often called upcycling, and at the top is prevention and reduction.
6:38 · Yeah, the whole world is pretty far from the top.
6:42 · That is why waste to energy is seen by some as a quick “solution” for countries struggling with their waste.


A waste solution for the Global South?
6:51 · Not surprisingly, plants are opening up around the world, like in China, Indonesia and India.
7:02 · Africa’s first waste to energy plant just opened, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.
7:08 · But it has proven to be more complicated than just opening up plants and burning the problem away.
7:14 · One reason is that the composition of waste varies widely throughout the world.
7:22 · “You can’t take one model that works in a wealthy country like a cookie cutter and expect it to work in a low-income country because it’s a completely different market.”
7:34 · In India, household waste is around 50 percent organic matter, like food scraps, which are too wet to burn.
7:41 · And because of the lack of centralized waste collection, trash there is often mixed together.
7:48 · “I don’t think segregation is happening at all in majority of the Indian cities.
7:55 · So that’s a major, major problem.”
7:57 · Pritpal Randhawa has been conducting long-term studies on waste management in India for the past 10 years.
8:02 · “The waste has to be segregated and the undesirable material should be separated from that waste, and only the waste with high calorific value should be burned.
8:14 · But that is not something which is happening actually.”
8:18 · Calorific value is a measure of a substance’s heating power — in other words, how easily it burns.
8:24 · Crude oil and mixed plastics come in at around 40 megajoules per kilogram.
8:29 · Food is about 16.
8:31 · Without waste separation, lots of food scraps find their way to the furnaces, forcing the plants to add additional fuel.
8:39 · This makes the whole facility extremely inefficient.
8:42 · Countries also need to have a place to store the hazardous waste.
8:46 · So if incineration isn’t a silver bullet for the Global South, what are other options?
8:52 · “It’s not very complicated at all – the ideal situation would be management of waste at the decentralized level.”
9:01 · And not only decentral, but diversified: specifically suited to the environment and economy of an area.
9:10 · In many cities in India, for example, waste pickers collect recyclables, which are processed informally.
9:15 · Biogas generated from organic waste can be a source of fuel from Benin to Mumbai.
9:20 · And plastic can be made into building material.
9:25 · “With waste management, absolutely one size does not fit all.
9:28 · And you really need to look at what’s most appropriate for that local area.”


When incineration makes sense
9:34 · Waste to energy plants can work, but a trash collection system and a strong environmental regulator are both necessary.
9:41 · These can be really hard to come by.
9:44 · Even with them, countries need to do some careful reflection before building new plants.
9:48 · “When you create incineration, you’re making huge investments and locking yourself in a system that you’re going to have to continue feeding and feeding and feeding.
10:00 · And that creates a disincentive for transitioning to a real circular economy.”
10:08 · So before more trash burning facilities join the global system, policymakers should look at funding more sustainable methods of waste disposal – like recycling, reusing and most importantly, reducing our waste in the first place.
10:22 · So what do you think?
10:24 · To burn, or not to burn?
10:28 · If this video made you think at all…
10:30 · If this video make you think at all, come back every Friday for new ones.
10:33 · And don’t forget to subscribe.
