title: What Does Extreme Heat Do to the Body
text:
Transcript
0:01 · MILES O’BRIEN: At the iconic Sydney Opera House, I met a scientist looking for an answer.
0:06 · Ollie Jay runs the Heat and Health Research Center at the University of Sydney.
0:13 · Lay the context for us a little bit on Australia, its climate, and the heat impacts you deal with here.
0:21 · We have an increased prevalence of heat waves.
0:23 · They’re greater intensity, the maximum temperature records are being beaten regularly.
0:28 · Among, uh, high income countries, we’re actually the most susceptible to the impacts of extreme heat on human health and well-being.
0:35 · For a researcher such as yourself, trying to find solutions, ways to adapt, this is the perfect laboratory, isn’t it?
0:41 · JAY: Absolutely.
0:42 · We take time to understand the nature of the problem before we start trying to develop solutions, because we don’t want to go down that route that a lot of academics do of finding solutions to problems that don’t exist.
0:52 · O’BRIEN: Ollie and his team are looking for smarter, more efficient ways to keep people safe and cool as the global thermostat rises.
1:01 · ♪ ♪ That was on his mind when I met him on a steamy Saturday at the University of Sydney Cricket Club Oval.
1:11 · (bat cracks) A match like this can last two long days, six to eight hours each.
1:19 · That was big!
1:20 · (cheers and applause) On the sidelines, Ollie Jay and his team were setting up a curious contraption they call the EMU.
1:30 · It’s a flightless Australian bird, but also something called the Environmental Measurement Unit.
1:35 · O’BRIEN: Mm-hmm.
1:36 · Like MaRTy in Phoenix, EMU measures four key parameters: air temperature, humidity, radiant temperature and wind speed.
1:47 · We measure temperature in this device right here.
1:50 · We can move air in a certain way across that temperature sensor to get a very accurate read on what the temperature of the air is in the shade.
1:57 · O’BRIEN: Humidity is measured in that same white chamber.
2:01 · Above it is a copper sphere that is painted matte black.
2:07 · It measures radiation that comes directly from the sun and bounces off the various surfaces surrounding an athlete.
2:15 · JAY: And then using all of this information, we can model how hot someone’s going to get, and therefore what their rate of dehydration might be.
2:21 · And, you know, potentially how much water they need to drink in order to maintain hydration.
2:29 · O’BRIEN: A short walk away from the cricket oval is Ollie’s lab.
2:33 · And that’s where he’s built another novel tool to better understand how heat affects the human body.
2:39 · It’s a climate chamber.
2:42 · Think of it as a science oven, and I’m on the menu.
2:47 · JAY: Just be careful of the step there.
2:49 · Here we go, Miles.
2:50 · O’BRIEN: You’re not messing around.
2:52 · JAY: No, we’re not messing around. O’BRIEN: All right.
2:54 · Reporting for scientific duty.
2:55 · I was finally going to find out what it’s like to be an order of French fries, waiting under the heat lamp on a short-order shelf.
3:05 · Before I got this far, I swallowed a horse pill.
3:08 · Right down the gullet there.
3:10 · A thermometer with a tiny transmitter inside that tracked my core temperature.
3:15 · I’m hot stuff.
3:16 · They took my blood pressure.
3:18 · Applied a strap to track my heart rate and a mask that measured the amount of oxygen I was consuming, to help estimate how much heat my body was generating on its own.
3:30 · JAMES SMALLCOMBE: If you can just blow out for me.
3:31 · (blows) Yep, that’s tight enough, that’s perfect.
3:34 · Your cardiovascular system seems to be in pretty good nick, uh, Miles, we’ve got, you know, great blood pressure and your resting heart rate’s nice and, uh, nice and low, so.
3:43 · Objective evidence demonstrating your very good health.
3:46 · O’BRIEN: He put it to the test by simulating one of the worst weather disasters in modern U.S. history: the heat wave in Chicago in 1995.
3:57 · More than 700 people died.
3:59 · Researchers concluded a working air conditioner would have prevented half the fatalities.
4:05 · And living alone doubled the risk of death.
4:07 · It became a stark lesson in how vulnerability and isolation can turn extreme heat into a mass-casualty disaster.
4:17 · Almost for the first time, it placed extreme heat on the radar of public health officials and actually seeing that it is responsible for excess death and morbidity.
4:27 · O’BRIEN: The tragedy exposed something deeper than weather.
4:31 · It was about inequality, and neglect.
4:35 · That summer, Chicago made it painfully clear heat doesn’t strike evenly, and it kills quietly.
4:44 · We’re doing this from the perspective of trying to understand the settings that the most vulnerable are going to be in, and then developing solutions that are fit for purpose in those settings.
4:54 · O’BRIEN: Here in the chamber, the temperature was 104 degrees Fahrenheit, with humidity between 50% and 60%.
5:03 · It was pretty miserable.
5:06 · I feel like a cheeseburger just off the grill.
5:08 · The human body cools itself by sweating, but that only works if the sweat can evaporate.
5:14 · At this temperature and humidity, it can’t.
5:19 · The air is nearly saturated.
5:21 · The sweat just sits there, and the body keeps heating up.
5:27 · It’s a huge challenge for human survival.
5:30 · What we know is that the people who are most vulnerable won’t have access to air conditioning.
5:34 · They most likely won’t have access to things like cooling shelters as well.
5:38 · They’ll be sheltering at home in place.
5:40 · So the question is, what type of activities, what type of risk reduction cooling strategies can these people use that is most effective at blunting that physiological heat strain that generates inside the body that we know is harmful to human health?
5:53 · O’BRIEN: He’s exploring cooling strategies for people who can’t afford to live in air-conditioned comfort.
6:00 · Practical, low-cost ways to survive the heat.
6:04 · Things like immersing your feet in water so they act like radiators.
6:09 · And using fans which, under the right conditions, can significantly reduce the effects of heat stress.
6:16 · These are the kinds of things that can help the most vulnerable among us, during a heat wave like Chicago in 1995.
6:26 · With the proper prior planning on that, could those deaths have been preventable?
6:31 · Most of them?
6:32 · There’s a, there’s a saying, um, in the heat health space that every heat-related death is preventable.
6:40 · O’BRIEN: Globally, heat kills about a half-a-million people every year.
6:45 · And in the U.S., the fatalities are growing at an alarming rate.
6:50 · In 2023, more than 2,300 died from heat in the U.S.
6:55 · About three times more than a decade ago.
6:58 · Far greater than the average toll for hurricanes and wildfires.
7:03 · They grab the headlines, but heat has always been the most lethal consequence of climate change, by far.
7:11 · Outside this window in Sydney, intense heat is everywhere– quiet, invisible and relentless.
7:20 · Ah.
7:22 · (sighs) Sheesh.
7:23 · After I’d mopped myself up, Ollie and I went from the frying pan to the fire.
7:31 · He took me on a walking tour of the University of Sydney campus.
7:35 · Born and raised in Wales, with a stop in Canada along the way, Ollie actually earned his PhD studying cold temperatures.
7:45 · But in 2014, Sydney beckoned.
7:48 · Suddenly, he was on the opposite end of the earth and the thermometer.
7:53 · Australia being a hot place, and it is a hot place, I figure that if, Australian-based researchers, if we can’t get a handle on these problems, and we can’t find a solution, then there’s very little chance that anyone else will.
8:06 · O’BRIEN: Plenty of scientists study the climate and the relentless rise of temperatures.
8:10 · But far fewer connect the dots to the impact on human health.
8:15 · How heat affects real bodies, in real time, in a warming world.
8:20 · It’s a mistake to overlook human physiology as you try to come up with some answers here, right?
8:25 · If you think about it from a health perspective, obviously, the hot weather is a problem.
8:29 · But the real problem is the hot person in the hot environment.
8:32 · ♪ ♪ O’BRIEN: It was time for us to solve that problem.
8:36 · We met up with his partner Allison and their adorable, precocious daughter Lottie.
8:41 · ALLISON: Ready to go to the beach?
8:43 · O’BRIEN: They took me to Coogee Beach, a short walk from their home in Sydney.
8:49 · Becoming a parent has changed the way he thinks about his work.
8:54 · It’s sharpened his focus and redoubled his resolve to solve.
9:00 · There are lots of solutions, but I think what we’ve got to do is focus on not just climate change mitigation, ensuring that the choices that we make don’t aggravate the problem in the future, but also got to face that we’ve got to adapt to a warmer world.
9:13 · We need to do both of them at the same time.
9:15 · It would be bad if all of that back and forth led to inertia and apathy. JAY: Well, it’s exactly right.
9:21 · People need to have hope in order to act.
9:22 · Otherwise, we just bury our head in the sand and try to pretend it’s not happening when it is.
9:26 · O’BRIEN: In the sand. JAY: Here we are.
9:28 · O’BRIEN: I see what you’re doing there, man.
9:30 · Nicely done, nicely done. (Ollie laughing) ♪ ♪

title: What is Climate Change
text:
Transcript

Introduction to Climate Change
0:00 · Our planet has been draped in ice sheets, filled with boiling-hot oceans, and dimmed by volcanic ash – all before anything more complicated than a single-celled organism showed up.
0:10 · So climate change is nothing new around here… when it happens gradually, over millions of years.
0:17 · But something new has happened in the last few centuries.
0:20 · People like us…except, wearing hats like this… began burning fossil fuels like coal, oil, and natural gas to make energy.
0:29 · Most of us aren’t wearing hats like those anymore.
0:31 · But we’re still powering our daily lives and industries with those fuels, releasing billions of tons of carbon dioxide every year.
0:41 · And that’s caused Earth’s climate to change in the span of just a few human lifetimes, the geological blink of an eye.
0:48 · Hi! I’m Dr. Sammy, your friendly neighborhood entomologist, and this is Crash Course Biology!
0:56 · Hey, do you guys smell that?
0:58 · …smells like…
1:00 · theme music?
1:01 · [THEME MUSIC] Now, I know what you’re thinking.
1:12 · “Wait, isn’t this Crash Course Biology?”
1:15 · And yeah, this episode is heavy on the gases, low on the golgi bodies.
1:19 · And that might leave you wondering, what does climate change have to do with the science of life?
1:25 · Here’s the thing: life and climate are tied together, like that tangled pair of headphones at the bottom of your backpack.
1:30 · You know, like you tug one end and then a knot tightens, which is looped around a paperclip, somehow snagged on that tiny notebook where you drew hearts around your crush’s name, which after several tugs is now lying open on the floor and…I’m breaking into a cold sweat just thinking about it.
1:46 · But back to the point, we can’t talk about life without talking about climate —which doesn’t mean last week’s thunderstorm or a one-day temperature swing – that’s weather.
1:58 · Climate is long-term weather conditions averaged over many years.
2:03 · To understand the difference between them, just remember that knowing the weather will help you decide if you should grab an umbrella before you head out, but knowing the climate will help you decide if you should invest in a good air conditioner.
2:15 · While the weather might impact your choice of clothing for the day, the climate directly impacts where and when different kinds of life can survive.


The Greenhouse Effect
2:24 · We owe today’s climate to the fact that our little green-and-blue marble of a home isn’t just floating in space unprotected.
2:31 · It’s wrapped up in an atmosphere; a big, invisible, gassy jacket.
2:35 · Which, granted, sounds pretty weird when you put it that way.
2:38 · But without it, we wouldn’t exist.
2:40 · This jacket is made of different kinds of gases.
2:43 · And a small fraction of them, known as greenhouse gases, absorb solar energy like, super well.
2:49 · We’re talking about gases like methane, water vapor, and most importantly carbon dioxide – also known as CO2.
2:58 · They account for less than half of one percent of our atmospheric jacket.
3:03 · But they’re a part of what makes it so good at trapping heat, sort of like all the little white feathers in your puffy coat.
3:09 · When sunlight beams down from space, most of it travels through those gases with no problem.
3:14 · The energy from that sunlight gets absorbed as it strikes the Earth, warming the surface.
3:19 · That type of warming is normal and seasonal.
3:22 · The Earth naturally bounces some of that solar energy back toward space.
3:27 · Where some of it exits the atmosphere and heads right back out into the inky ether.
3:32 · But the rest of that energy gets trapped by the Earth’s gassy jacket.
3:36 · Specifically by those super absorbent greenhouse gases, which suck up heat and bounce it back down to us again.
3:44 · This warming process is called the greenhouse effect.
3:47 · Unsurprisingly, It works the same way as a greenhouse – using layers of glass to trap heat inside.
3:54 · And it keeps Earth at a nice, cozy, insulated average of 14 degrees Celsius.
4:00 · Without it, our Earth would be a chilly average of -18 degrees Celsius.
4:06 · Great for storing ice cream!
4:08 · Not so good for rainforests, swimsuits, or us for that matter.
4:13 · So, the greenhouse effect is a natural, helpful process that makes Earth habitable for all of life!
4:18 · But you can have too much of a good thing.
4:21 · When our atmospheric jacket contains more carbon dioxide, for example, it gets really good at trapping heat.
4:28 · Like, too good.
4:30 · And the hotter things get, the more water evaporates and joins the atmosphere— and remember, water vapor itself is a greenhouse gas, so that in turn absorbs even more heat, creating a looping system of cause-and-effect that just keeps reinforcing itself.


Measuring the Greenhouse Effect
4:46 · And while dressing in layers is great if you’re hiking in the Alps, it’s really hard for our planet to shed its extra coats.
4:52 · So all of that heat gets stuck going from the ground to the atmosphere like the worst game of hot potato ever played.
4:59 · When I learned about this, I was like, “Wow, what a revelation!
5:03 · I can’t believe we’ve only recently figured this out!”
5:05 · But it turns out that this isn’t new knowledge; we’ve known how, and why, this could happen for nearly 170 years.
5:16 · Let’s pay a visit to the Theater of Life… [Inquisitive music] Back in 1856, Eunice Foote, an American scientist and suffragette, was thinking about how the Sun’s warmth affected different gases.
5:27 · In those days, the scientific community was a bit like a fort with a handmade “no girls allowed” sign out front.
5:34 · But Foote wasn’t deterred, and ran her experiments anyway.
5:38 · She filled tubes with different combinations of gases, including carbon dioxide.
5:42 · After putting some tubes in the Sun and some in the shade, she compared their temperatures, trying to find the hottest gas.
5:50 · All the tubes in direct sunlight warmed up.
5:52 · But none as intensely as the tube that contained carbon dioxide.
5:57 · The temperature had soared to 51.7 degrees Celsius, hot enough to burn your fingers.
6:04 · From that insight, Foote theorized that if our atmosphere ever contained more carbon dioxide, the whole planet would warm up as a result, which would mean a lot more than a few scalded fingers.
6:16 · And sure enough, today, that’s exactly the situation we’re in.
6:20 · Foote was one of the first scientists to recognize carbon dioxide’s potential to affect Earth’s climate.
6:25 · But she wasn’t the only one to connect the dots.
6:28 · For example, just a few decades later, another scientist named Dr. Svante Arrhenius observed that burning coal releases carbon dioxide.
6:37 · As a fossil fuel, coal forms from the decomposed, carbon-based bodies of plants and animals that lived and died a long time ago.
6:46 · And I’m talking before the dinosaurs.
6:48 · So no, I’m afraid that means you aren’t gassing up your car with the remains of a T-Rex.
6:53 · When we burn those fossil fuels— whether it’s in the form of coal, oil, or natural gas— carbon dioxide gets released into the atmosphere.
7:00 · When Arrhenius ran the numbers, he predicted that carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels could warm our climate within a few thousand years if we kept burning them at their current rate.
7:14 · But we’ve far outpaced his estimates.
7:16 · Our emissions of carbon dioxide have grown and grown and grown — and so has the mountain of evidence that those emissions are warming our planet.
7:25 · Some oil and gas companies have worked to promote uncertainty around the existence of climate change and what’s causing it.
7:32 · While they have only very recently acknowledged its existence, as of 2023, they’re still trying to deflect from what’s causing it.
7:40 · But the scientific consensus on this is overwhelming.
7:44 · You can learn much more about that in our Climate & Energy series.
7:47 · We’ve only been reliably taking direct measurements of Earth’s global temperature since the 19th century.
7:52 · But that measly slice of time shows a steady rise in temperature of about 1.1 degree Celsius since 1880.
8:01 · And we know that that’s unusual because we’ve learned to read Earth’s much longer climate diary, in the form of ice cores.
8:07 · See, when snow hardens into ice, tiny bubbles of air remain trapped in the gaps between snowflakes.
8:13 · These gases and water molecules stay frozen, like entries in a frosty journal.
8:19 · So by drilling deep down into polar ice, we can snoop on what the atmosphere was like hundreds of thousands of years ago.


Carbon Sinks
8:27 · Ice cores show us that carbon dioxide levels have fluctuated over the past 800,000 years.
8:32 · And temperatures have fallen and risen alongside them, too.
8:36 · But when people started burning fossil fuels, carbon dioxide levels began to spike quickly, like really, really quickly.
8:44 · And they haven’t stopped rising.
8:45 · Before the Industrial Revolution, for every million molecules of air in our atmosphere, around 280 were carbon dioxide molecules.
8:54 · But by 2022, that number had increased to 422 —the highest concentration of CO2 our planet has seen in 4 million years.
9:06 · And that surge in carbon dioxide affects more than just the temperature.
9:10 · As the amount of carbon dioxide in our atmosphere rises, it impacts all of Earth’s systems.
9:15 · Just like yanking on the end of that tangled mess of headphones impacted all of the other items in my bag (and eventually, everybody around us when stuff started falling out).
9:24 · It’s all connected, is what I’m saying.
9:26 · For example, the ocean is our planet’s largest carbon sink.
9:31 · It’s sort of like a big storage container for carbon.
9:34 · In fact, the ocean holds 50 times more carbon than the air or soil do.
9:40 · But a chemical reaction happens when carbon dioxide meets water, it creates an acid.
9:45 · So that influx of carbon has already turned the ocean 30% more acidic since the 19th century.
9:53 · As carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases trap more heat, there’s more energy pouring into our planet than going out.
9:59 · That means more energy is pumped into the ocean, fueling hurricanes and typhoons to become more frequent and more intense.


Environmental Justice
10:07 · As the whole planet gets hotter, that triggers all kinds of changes.
10:11 · Spring arrives earlier, leading to shorter winters and longer summers.
10:15 · Rising temperatures lead to double-whammy droughts and heatwaves.
10:19 · And that leaves forest floors full of dried-up plants that serve as fuel for wildfires to ignite— spreading faster, farther, and more often.
10:28 · Plus, Earth’s polar ice caps are melting, transforming solid ice to slush and seawater.
10:34 · And that’s causing ocean levels to rise and encroach on land.
10:38 · So while some communities are already facing a problem of not enough water, others are facing a problem of too much.
10:45 · And because these adverse changes layer on top of existing social inequalities, they disproportionately affect lower-income communities and people of color, making climate change not only a scientific issue, but a matter of environmental justice that has spurred some researchers to political action.
11:02 · For example, climate scientist Nicole Hernandez Hammer witnessed first-hand, through her field research, the sea-level rise alongside Miami Beach’s Latino communities.
11:12 · But these communities were not included in conversations about climate change or the dangers of rising sea levels.
11:18 · So, Hammer took action, moving into environmental outreach and education.
11:23 · And, while the threat is still there, these communities are now in conversation about climate change, and able to plan and advocate for the future of their environment.
11:33 · And the good news more broadly is we know exactly why these tangled, complex effects are happening.
11:39 · The more we burn those fossil fuels, the more greenhouse gases we release —and that’s driving sweeping changes all over our planet.
11:47 · And these changes are impacting life at all levels from the tiniest bacterium, to the elephants of Botswana, to you and me.
11:55 · We can slow these impacts by breaking up with fossil fuels.
11:58 · But we also have to invest in nature’s carbon sinks —such as soils and forests— which pull carbon out of the atmosphere and back into the land, where it can’t keep heating things up.


Review & Credits
12:09 · It won’t be the easiest breakup.
12:12 · We’ve designed whole societies and global systems around fossil fuels.
12:16 · We should fully expect to be listening to Jazmine Sullivan on repeat with a gallon of Rocky Road.
12:21 · But this is one relationship we can’t afford to stay in.
12:24 · So, in order to halt emissions, we have to both invent new systems and work more efficiently within old ones, and to do that, we’ve got to get a whole planet’s worth of people on board.
12:35 · And if you’ve ever been part of a group project, you know that last part isn’t easy.
12:39 · Thankfully, when faced with global crises, humans have one great thing going for us: we are creative.
12:46 · I mean, we’ve been to space, we’ve got electric cars, we made furbies for some reason.
12:53 · So yes, It’s going to take all of our creativity and cooperation to tackle.
12:58 · But the only way out is through, and the only way through is together.
13:04 · In our next episode, we’ll tune back into the world of living things— and see how our rapidly changing climate involves much more than the atmosphere.
13:12 · It affects every living, breathing, organism on this planet— including you and me.
13:18 · This series was produced in collaboration with HHMI BioInteractive.
13:22 · If you’re an educator, visit BioInteractive.org/CrashCourse for classroom resources and professional development related to the topics covered in this course.
13:32 · Thanks for watching this episode of Crash Course Biology, which was filmed at our studio in Indianapolis, Indiana, and was made with the help of all these nice people.
13:41 · If you want to help keep Crash Course free for everyone, forever, you can join our community on Patreon.

title: Why managing chronic health conditions begins at home
text:
Description
The recognition that health care extends beyond the walls of hospitals and doctor’s offices is growing. In Greensboro, North Carolina, advocacy groups, sociologists and medical practitioners are taking a creative approach to uncovering the root causes of disease, with a particular focus on poor housing conditions that can lead to chronic illness. John Yang reports.

title: Why managing chronic health conditions begins at home
text:
Transcript
0:00 · JUDY WOODRUFF: Let’s take a look now at an innovative approach to health care.
0:04 · John Yang tells us about an effort in North Carolina that tries to treat the housing conditions that contribute to chronic illnesses like asthma before they become health emergencies.
0:15 · KRISHNAVENI BALAKRISHNAN, Greensboro Housing Coalition: You can see mold growth all along the wall here.
0:21 · JOHN YANG: There is so much mold in the Greensboro, North Carolina, rental property that inspectors Krishnaveni Balakrishnan And Ken Cook are examining that the residents moved out after only a few weeks.
0:33 · KRISHNAVENI BALAKRISHNAN: There’s mold on the children’s pillows.
0:36 · The family that lives here, they have five children.
0:38 · One of them is asthmatic, and the mold in the home is causing not only that child, but also the rest of the family to become sick.
0:45 · There’s a lot of moisture issues, a lot of mold on the ceiling, on the family’s belongings.
0:51 · The home is not habitable.
0:52 · JOHN YANG: The residents say the landlord’s suggestions for getting rid of the mold didn’t work.
0:58 · They had to pay for a hotel while still paying rent here.
1:00 · KRISHNAVENI BALAKRISHNAN: You can tell where it’s been wiped.
1:02 · JOHN YANG: Balakrishnan and Cook don’t work for the city.
1:05 · They work for an advocacy group called the Greensboro Housing Coalition.
1:10 · They’re part of an innovative approach aimed at improving the health of low-income residents.
1:14 · KRISHNAVENI BALAKRISHNAN: There’s some mold in the doorsill.
1:17 · JOHN YANG: Doctors, housing advocates, and community activists say taking care of houses like this can be a form of preventive medicine.
1:25 · By getting rid of unhealthy environments, they can keep people out of the emergency room.
1:34 · Researchers say asthma accounts for 93 percent of the respiratory illnesses in Greensboro emergency rooms and clinics.
1:42 · On this day, one of them is Alveno Stanford’s 14-year-old son, Jacob.
1:45 · ALVENO STANFORD, Parent: And I noticed how his chest would like come out more than usual.
1:50 · So, I could tell the chest was just, like, coming out more.
1:53 · JOHN YANG: It’s not the first time Jacob’s made a costly emergency room visit.
1:58 · ALVENO STANFORD: Three times a year.
1:59 · Like, this year, he may come three.
2:02 · Year before that, he may come like two or three.
2:04 · And it’s been at least 10 times with him.
2:08 · JOHN YANG: Greensboro’s efforts are part of a growing interdisciplinary approach, attacking the causes of conditions like asthma to try to improve health and reduce medical costs.
2:20 · Stephen Sills is a University of North Carolina-Greensboro sociologist.
2:29 · He looks for patterns in asthma cases using data from the Cone Health system, the city’s major hospital operator and a partner in the project.
2:37 · Then he uses Google Maps Street View to plot substandard housing.
2:41 · STEPHEN SILLS, University of North Carolina-Greensboro: We map that, block by block, neighborhood by neighborhood.
2:45 · Where are more of these respiratory illnesses coming from?
2:49 · And we see that there’s three areas in Greensboro that really are the concentration of poor roofing, absent gutters, broken and cracked foundations, cracked windows, missing shingles and siding.
3:05 · JOHN YANG: And they’re the same areas where asthma cases are concentrated, underscoring the link between poor housing and poor health.
3:13 · All these conditions you just described would exacerbate or trigger asthma?
3:17 · STEPHEN SILLS: Exactly.
3:19 · Exacerbate is a good word there.
3:20 · If I’m living in a house where the roof is leaking, the pipes are leaking, there’s mold and mildew, the carpet hasn’t been replaced in years, all are triggers for someone who has a respiratory condition like asthma.
3:35 · JOHN YANG: Sills’ students use the data to make referrals to the Greensboro Housing Coalition.
3:41 · It turns the traditional approach to delivering health care on its head.
3:44 · STEPHEN SILLS: So often, the physician is thinking about the biology of the individual?
3:49 · What’s wrong with this person?
3:51 · How can I treat that problem that is a biological, medical problem?
3:55 · What drug can I give them, or what behavior can I ask them to change?
4:00 · In this case, the treatment is for the community.
4:04 · The problem isn’t the individual.
4:06 · The problem is the structure around the individual.
4:08 · JOHN YANG: Sills’ research provides hard data to support the coalition’s work at an apartment complex in the impoverished east Greensboro neighborhood of Cottage Grove.
4:18 · JOSIE WILLIAMS, Greensboro Housing Coalition: So, you can see the roofing and all the stuff up here, very old.
4:23 · JOHN YANG: Josie Williams of the Greensboro Housing Coalition documents conditions there.
4:28 · Sewage coming up through the drain.
4:29 · JOSIE WILLIAMS: Yes, sewage was coming up in the drain.
4:32 · That’s why the water is so dark.
4:34 · So, the way they were turning this on and off was by pliers.
4:37 · JOHN YANG: And the people are paying rent for this?
4:39 · JOSIE WILLIAMS: Yes.
4:41 · JOHN YANG: There were 177 apartments, and 100 cases of asthma.
4:45 · JOSIE WILLIAMS: We walked into an apartment one day, and the sewage from the bathroom had come out of the toilet onto the floor, into the living room.
4:54 · And the family had been living like that for three weeks.
4:56 · JOHN YANG: Three weeks?
4:57 · JOSIE WILLIAMS: Mm-hmm.
4:58 · We walked into another apartment complex where the ceiling was leaking, and it was raining, and the mother was catching the water with an inflatable pool in the middle of the floor.
5:09 · JOHN YANG: One of the asthma cases, 7-year-old Shah Mei (ph), whose family immigrated from Myanmar.
5:16 · Dr. Beth Mulberry is her pediatrician.
5:18 · DR.
5:19 · BETH MULBERRY, Mustard Seed Community Health: They were living without heat.
5:20 · It was below 20.
5:21 · They had a huge water problem.
5:25 · Their carpet was soaked.
5:26 · She was needing to be on maintenance medication, allergy medication, oral.
5:33 · And then she was on a rescue inhaler, which she was using fairly regularly at that point.
5:37 · JOHN YANG: The Housing Coalition helped the family find better housing, and Shah Mei quickly improved.
5:45 · DR.
5:46 · BETH MULBERRY: I think it was about two months.
5:47 · So, it’s pretty quick and pretty amazing change.
5:52 · She has not used her rescue inhaler since July.
5:56 · JOHN YANG: The complex has since been sold, and the coalition is working with the new owner to improve it.
6:04 · Led by Josie Williams, the Housing Coalition holds monthly neighborhood meetings to help residents press for other changes in the area.
6:11 · At their most recent session, they discussed a corner store.
6:14 · JOSIE WILLIAMS: Anything healthy in that little store?
6:17 · Alcohol, cigarettes?
6:18 · What else you see in that little store?
6:20 · Snacks?
6:21 · What else?
6:22 · You have the power to create those changes.
6:23 · JOHN YANG: The recognition that health care extends beyond the walls of hospitals and doctors offices is growing.
6:33 · In October, federal officials approved a five-year pilot program allowing North Carolina Medicaid to pay for such services as removing mold, controlling pests and repairing heating and air conditioning.
6:46 · DR.
6:47 · BETH MULBERRY: We really need to start making an investment in what are the root causes of these chronic illnesses.
6:54 · And a lot of this has to do with our people that are living in poverty, the inability to rent a place where they expect changes to be made if it’s an unhealthy environment for them.
7:08 · JOHN YANG: A prescription for good health that cannot be filled at a pharmacy.
7:12 · For the “PBS NewsHour,” I’m John Yang in Greensboro, North Carolina.

title: World Weather Attribution — understanding climate change and extreme weather
text:
Description
When an extreme weather event occurs, people often ask: is climate change to blame?
For decades, climate scientists have answered that question in general terms – that as the planet warms, we can expect many of these weather events to become more frequent and extreme.
But in recent years, advances in attribution science have allowed researchers to answer the question in much greater detail.
Founded in 2015 by Dr. Friederike Otto and Dr. Geert Jan van Oldenborgh, World Weather Attribution scientists quantify how climate change influences the intensity and likelihood of an extreme weather event. They often do this using weather data and computer modelling, and often immediately in the aftermath of the extreme event.
To encourage actions that will make communities and countries more resilient to future extreme weather events, World Weather Attribution studies also evaluate how existing vulnerability worsened the impacts of the extreme weather event.
To learn more about World Weather Attribution or to view our studies, go to https://www.worldweatherattribution.org/
Follow us on Twitter: https://twitter.com/WWAttribution
Film produced by Geoff Marsh.

title: Vanishing Act
Vanishing Act
text:
Description
Shane meets species on the brink of oblivion, and the people who won’t let them slip away.

title: Vanishing Act
text:
Transcript
(“Ready or Not” by Fugees plays) (Shane) The story of our planet is a tale of equal and opposite forces: Life… (female singer) Ready or not, here I come (Shane) …and death.
We’ve never known one without the other.
(female singer) And take it slowly Ready or not (Shane) From the first primordial cell, to the loftiest tree, to beasts we’ve never known, each species walks its own path… …but they all end in the same place.
(female singer) Ready or not (Shane) Extinction is Mother Nature’s way of pruning the Tree of Life.
(female singer) Ready or not (Shane) And she is a tireless arborist.
Ninety-nine percent of all the species that ever existed no longer do.
(female singer) I play my enemies like a game of chess (thunder, explosions) (Shane) Of Earth’s eight million living species, one has become a force of nature in its own right.
And, ironically, we humans– the only species that can fathom extinction– are driving it faster than any other species in our planet’s history.
What fate awaits the Tree of Life in the Age of Humans?
And can we change course before putting our future in peril?
Welcome to the age of humans, where one species can change everything, and what we do reveals who we truly are.
This is Human Footprint.
(serene music) For most of our history, the world was a pretty scary place.
Colossal predators hunted massive herbivores.
And we were definitely on the menu.
(roaring) Today, there aren’t many places where the land still pulses with the ancient rhythms of giants.
(animals grunting) Where you’re grateful for the safety of a safari vehicle.
People travel thousands of miles to experience Africa’s megafauna, yet these iconic animals are dwarfed by the titans that roamed North America in the not-so-distant past.
(“To Live & Die in L.A.” by Tupac Shakur plays) (engine revving) The sprawl of L.A. feels a world apart from the Serengeti… (Tupac) It never rains in Southern To live and die in L.A. (Shane) But if you want to meet the giants that once ruled this continent, this is the place to do it.
(chorus) To live and die in L.A. (vocalizing) (Emily) This is my favorite critter here.
This is a giant ground sloth.
(Shane) Yeah, what makes this your favorite?
(Emily) It’s a sloth and it was giant.
(laughter) (Shane) Need you say more?
(bicycle bell rings) Meet paleontologist Emily Lindsey.
Her commute through L.A.’s urban jungle helps her connect with the present… (relaxing music) …but when she gets to the La Brea Tar Pits, her thoughts turn to the ancient world.
(Emily) This is called a short-faced bear.
(Shane) The idea that there was an animal this large is deeply disturbing to me.
How much bigger is this than, like, a polar bear?
(Emily) A lot.
(laughter) (Shane) Today, La Brea is almost as iconic as Disneyland or Hollywood, drawing visitors from around the world.
But at the start of the 20th century, people flocked here for another reason.
(Emily) The L.A. basin is the richest oil basin of its size in the world.
In the early 20th century, we were producing about a quarter of the world’s oil.
(Shane) In those days, Rancho La Brea was a rich source of the densest form of crude oil: asphalt.
(Emily) They were digging it up and shipping it up to San Francisco, where it was being used to pave the roads.
(Shane) In some places, finding asphalt didn’t even require digging.
(Emily) And because the other thing we have a lot of in L.A. is earthquakes, there are places where these fissures occur in the ground.
(Shane) Here, the asphalt seeps up to the surface in shallow, sticky pools.
Before long, miners noticed bones– a lot of them.
They assumed the bones belonged to cattle from the ranch they were digging on until a traveling geologist took a closer look.
(Emily) And he was like, “That’s not a cow bone.”
It was the saber of the saber-toothed cat.
Exactly what part of the cow do you think this came from?
(laughing) (Emily) Over time, plants, animals, big, small, get stuck in there.
(Shane) At La Brea, the miners had stumbled onto the world’s largest deposit of Pleistocene fossils– an entire ecosystem sealed in an asphalt time capsule.
Soon, a new kind of excavation was underway.
(Emily) In about two and a half years, they collected about a million fossils.
Whoa.
(rhythmic music) Is, like, this density, like, normal for the pits?
(Emily) Yeah, it’s just bone on bone, on bone, on bone, on bone.
It makes them really challenging to excavate.
So, imagine playing, pick-up sticks.
But every stick is, like, a different size and shape and also fragile and also priceless.
And then, somebody has dumped a bunch of cement on top of it.
(Shane) In the last century, scientists have excavated over five million fossils here, representing 40,000 years of ecological history.
(Emily) This is our dire wolf wall.
So, there’s 400 skulls of dire wolves on this wall.
That represents maybe 10% of the dire wolves that we’ve discovered so far at the tar pits.
(serene music) (Shane) Thousands of apex predators died in the pits, along with the massive herbivores they hunted.
Then, suddenly, mysteriously… the megafauna stopped getting stuck.
(Emily) Through intensive radiocarbon dating, we were able to figure out exactly when they stopped getting stuck, which is a proxy for when they stopped being on the landscape.
So, these are the very last animals of their kind that we know of at La Brea, and in many cases, in all of North America.
This is the last dire wolf.
(Shane) Like, the last.
The last one that we know of.
(Shane) Wow.
(Emily) 13,000 years ago.
The last saber-toothed cat that we know of, 13,000 years ago.
This is a piece of the last American lion.
-13,000 years ago?
-Yeah.
13,000 years ago was a bad year.
So, what happened 13,000 years ago?
Gosh.
(Emily) So, this is a Columbian mammoth and these are one of the species here that we know overlapped with and interacted with the first humans in the Americas.
We find a lot of mammoth kill sites.
(Shane) It takes a brave person to point to one of these things and say, “You hungry?”
(Emily) Yeah.
(laughter) (Shane) Humans are brave.
We’re also smart, social, and skilled at making and using tools, which is why, in the late 1960s, paleontologist Paul Martin proposed an idea to explain these extinctions: the “overkill hypothesis.”
(dramatic drumming music) (Emily) We know that humans are perfectly capable of hunting species to extinction.
(Shane) Before the overkill hypothesis, experts attributed the loss of North American megafauna to the end of the last Ice Age.
But Martin questioned how these animals had survived so many previous warming periods, only to vanish when humans arrived.
Overkill had an intuitive appeal amidst the growing environmental movement.
It was easy to envision us hunting species to extinction.
(Emily) One of the counterarguments is, well, you know, these small bands of hunter gatherers couldn’t possibly have, like, driven all the mammoths to extinction.
(Shane) Megafauna kill sites do exist, but they’re rare.
